en: [The Seventeen Stages of Yogic Practice] / What is the *yogācārabhūmi*?
It should be understood as consisting of seventeen stages (*bhūmi*).
Which are the seventeen? The summary verse:
[The first] five are associated with the five consciousnesses; the mental stage is threefold.
Accompanied by both applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), and either with or without meditative concentration (samādhi).
It is both with mind and without mind; it consists of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
likewise, it is endowed with the three vehicles; and it is supreme, being both with remainder and without remainder.
The stage associated with the five bodies of consciousness;
the stage of the mind;
the stage with applied thought and sustained thought.
The stage that is without applied thought and consists of sustained thought only;
the stage that is without applied thought and without sustained thought;
and the stage of meditative concentration.
The level of non-concentration;
the level with mind; the level without mind.
The stage consisting of hearing;
the stage consisting of reflection;
the stage consisting of cultivation.
The stage of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, and the stage of the bodhisattva.
The stage with substrate and the stage without substrate— these seventeen stages are, in brief, called the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

What is the stage associated with the five groups of consciousness? Briefly stated, the stage associated with the five groups of consciousness consists of the five groups of consciousness themselves by way of their intrinsic nature, as well as their basis, their object, their concomitants, and their function.
What are the five groups of consciousness?
They are eye-consciousness, and the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties. What is eye-consciousness?
It is the discernment of visible forms based on the eye.
What is the basis of visual consciousness?
The eye is its simultaneous basis;
the mind is its immediately preceding basis.
The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which contains all seeds, is the appropriator of the basis, and is comprised within maturation (*vipāka*), is the basis of seeds.
Summarizing these, there are two kinds of bases:
the material and the immaterial.
In that regard, the eye is material; that which is other than it is immaterial.
What is the eye?
It is a translucent form derived from the four great elements, which serves as the support for visual consciousness; it is invisible and possesses resistance.
What is the mind?
It is the consciousness that has passed away immediately after visual consciousness.
What is consciousness containing all seeds?
It is the maturation that has arisen, containing all seeds, based upon the prior cause of delighting in conceptual proliferation.
What is the objective support of visual consciousness?
It is form that is visible and resistant;
furthermore, it is of many kinds.
In brief, it consists of color, shape, and informative intimation.
What is color?
It is as follows: blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, sunshine, light, darkness, cloud, smoke, dust, mist, and the uniform color of the sky.
What is shape?
It is as follows: long, short, square, round, minute, large, even, uneven, elevated, and depressed.
What is informative action (*vijñapti*)? It is, for example: taking up, putting down, contracting, standing, sitting, lying down, approaching, and passing beyond, and so forth.
Furthermore, what is color? It is that which resembles form and is the objective domain of visual consciousness.
What is shape? It is the accumulation of matter that has the form of distinctions such as long and so forth.
What is informative matter (*vijñapti*)?

It is the non-arising of that very accumulated matter— which has arisen and ceased— due to a contrary cause, such that it does not arise in its place of birth, but rather [arises] in another location, whether immediately adjacent or separated by a gap,
whether near or far, or even in that very same location.
Or, there is the production of abnormalities in a particular region.
In this context, "color" (varṇa), "luster" (ābhāsa), and "radiance" (bhāsa) are synonyms.
Configuration (saṃsthāna), accumulation (pracaya), long (dīrgha), short (hrasva), and so forth, are synonyms.
Manifestation (vijñapti), action (karman), activity (kriyā), effort (ceṣṭā), movement (īhā), and vibration (parispanda) are synonyms.

For all perceptions of color and shape, the following are synonyms: the range of the eye, the object of the eye, the range of visual consciousness, the object of visual consciousness, the focal point of visual consciousness; and the range of mental consciousness, the object of mental consciousness, the focal point of mental consciousness.
Furthermore, that very same thing may appear as gold, or as something of poor color, or as something situated between those two, resembling their respective colors.
What is the accompaniment?
It consists of those mental factors (caitasika-dharma) that arise simultaneously with and are associated with it;
namely:

Attention, contact, feeling, perception, and volition—whatever other mental factors there are that arise simultaneously and are associated with visual consciousness, these furthermore have a single object but multiple aspects; they are co-existent yet each functions individually.
All of them are produced from their own seeds, and being associated, they possess aspects, objects, and bases.
What is action?
It should be understood as being of six kinds.
First of all, its primary function is the representation of its own object as a cognitive support.

Furthermore, there is the representation of specific characteristics; furthermore, the representation of the present time; furthermore, the representation of a single moment; furthermore, the representation of a single moment; furthermore, the mental consciousness follows along in two modes.
The persistence of the wholesome and the afflicted, the persistence of the origination of karma, and furthermore, the appropriation of desirable and undesirable fruits— this is the sixth function.
[Ear-consciousness] What is ear-consciousness?
It is the discernment of sound based upon the ear.
What is the basis? The co-existent basis is the ear;
the immediately preceding basis is the mind; the seed-basis is that very storehouse-consciousness which contains all seeds.
What is the ear?
It is a translucent form derived from the four great elements, which serves as the support for auditory consciousness; it is invisible and possesses resistance.
The distinction between the mind and the seed is as previously explained.
What is the object?
Sounds are of many kinds; they are non-demonstrable and possess resistance (*sapratigha*).

They are as follows: the sound of a conch, the sound of a kettledrum, the sound of a drum, the sound of a clay drum, the sound of dancing, the sound of singing, the sound of instrumental music, the sound of cymbals, the sound of women, the sound of men, and the sound of wind and forest trees.

Manifest sound, unmanifest sound; meaningful sound, meaningless sound; limited sound, moderate sound, loud sound; the sound of a river, the sound of clamor; the sound of recitation, private study, teaching, discussion, and definitive resolution—these and many other such sounds [are examples].
Furthermore, sound has as its cause appropriated great elements, unappropriated great elements, or both appropriated and unappropriated great elements.
Among these, the first is that which has internal conditions.
Thus: the second is that which has only external conditions;
the third is that which has both external and internal conditions.
Furthermore, it is agreeable,
disagreeable, and that which is contrary to both.
In this context, "sound" (śabda) has the following synonyms: resonance (ghoṣa), tone (svara), etymological derivation (nirukti), noise (nāda), and vocal intimation (vāgvijñapti).

The range of the ear, the object of the ear, the range of auditory consciousness, the object of auditory consciousness, the objective support of auditory consciousness, the range of mental consciousness, the object of mental consciousness, and the objective support of mental consciousness— these are synonyms.
The companion and the action are to be understood as being like visual consciousness.
[Olfactory consciousness:
What is olfactory consciousness?
It is the discernment of odors based upon the nose.
What is the basis? The co-existent basis is the nose;
the immediately preceding basis is the mind.
The seed-basis is that very storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) which contains all seeds.
What is the nose?
It is the translucent matter derived from the four great elements which serves as the basis for olfactory consciousness; it is invisible and possesses resistance.
The distinction between the mind and the seed is as explained previously.
What is the object?
Odors are of many kinds, invisible, and resistant; they are either fragrant, foul-smelling, or neutral odors to be smelled.
For example, there are many such odors as the odor of roots, the odor of heartwood, the odor of leaves, the odor of flowers, the odor of fruits, and so forth.
In this context, "odor" refers to synonyms such as "that which is smelled," "that which is to be smelled," "that which is to be sniffed," and so forth.

The range of the nose, the object of the nose, the range of olfactory consciousness, the object of olfactory consciousness, the focal point of olfactory consciousness, the range of mental consciousness, the object of mental consciousness, and the focal point of mental consciousness— these are synonyms.
The companion and the action are to be understood as previously described.
[ Tongue-consciousness ] What is tongue-consciousness?
It is the discernment of tastes based upon the tongue.
What is the basis?
The tongue is the simultaneous basis;
the mind is the immediately preceding basis.
The seed-basis is precisely that storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) which contains all seeds.
What is the tongue?
It is the translucent matter that serves as the basis for tongue-consciousness; it is invisible and possesses resistance.
The distinction between the mind and the seed is as previously explained.
What is the object?
Tastes are of many kinds, invisible, and resistant.
They are further [classified as] bitter, sour, pungent, astringent, salty, and sweet; they are either pleasant, unpleasant, or conducive to equanimity, and are to be tasted.
In this context, "rasa" (taste/flavor) is synonymous with that which is to be relished, consumed, eaten, drunk, licked, sucked, and enjoyed.

The range of the tongue, the object of the tongue, the range of tongue-consciousness, the object of tongue-consciousness, the focal point of tongue-consciousness, the range of mind-consciousness, the object of mind-consciousness, and the focal point of mind-consciousness— these are synonyms.
The companion and the action are to be understood as previously described.
[Body-consciousness] What is body-consciousness?
It is the discernment of tangible objects based upon the body.
What is the basis? The coexistent basis is the body;
the immediately preceding basis is the mind.
The seed-basis is that very storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) which contains all seeds.
What is the body?
It is the translucent matter derived from the four great elements, which serves as the basis for body-consciousness, is invisible, and possesses resistance.
The distinction between the mind and the seed is as previously explained.
What is the object?
It is the tangible, which is of many kinds, invisible, and resistant.
Namely: earth, water, fire, air; lightness, heaviness, smoothness, roughness, cold, hunger, thirst, satiety, strength, weakness, disease, old age, death, itching, fainting, and sliminess.
Fatigue, rest, softness, straightness, and so forth— these are the many kinds of tangible objects.
Furthermore, that which is to be touched is either pleasant to the touch, unpleasant to the touch, or neutral toward equanimity.

In this context, "the tangible" (spraṣṭavya), "that which is to be touched" (spṛśya), and "that which is to be felt by touch" (sparśanīya) are synonyms for hardness, fluidity, mobility, heat, and so forth.

The domain of the body (*kāyagocara*), the object of the body (*kāyaviṣaya*), the domain of body-consciousness (*kāyavijñānagocara*), the object of body-consciousness (*kāyavijñānaviṣaya*), the focal point of body-consciousness (*kāyavijñānālambana*); the domain of mind-consciousness (*manovijñānagocara*), the object of mind-consciousness (*manovijñānaviṣaya*), and the focal point of mind-consciousness (*manovijñānālambana*)—these are synonyms.
The companion and the action are to be understood as previously described.
[The arising of consciousness:
In that case, the eye is impaired,
and the form has not come into range.
And the mental attention arising from that is not present;
thus, the arising of that visual consciousness does not occur.
And because the eye is unimpaired,
the form has come into range,
and the attention arising from those [conditions] is present;
Then, from that, there occurs the arising of his visual consciousness.
Just as it is with visual consciousness, so too should auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses be understood.
The consciousnesses are to be understood as follows: [the minds associated with consciousness].

In that regard, when visual consciousness arises, three types of mind are perceived in succession: the adventitious (*aupaniṣadika*), the investigative (*paryeṣaka*), and the determinative (*niścita*).
Among these, the first is precisely the visual consciousness itself.
There are two types of mental consciousness.
In that regard, subsequent to the determinate mind, both affliction and purification are to be seen;
therefore, that [consciousness] is a result of outflow (*naiṣyandika*).
Visual consciousness also proceeds as wholesome or unwholesome,
but not by the power of its own conceptualization;
and both mental consciousness and visual consciousness remain wholesome or afflicted only so long as that mind is not distracted elsewhere.
Just as it is with the arising of eye-consciousness, so it should be understood for all [consciousnesses] up to body-consciousness.
[The Simile of Consciousness] In this regard, the basis should be seen as like a vehicle for one who has set out for another country;
the companions of the five groups of consciousness are like those seeking companions.
The object of focus is like that which is to be done;
its activity is like one's own capacity.
This is another way of explaining it.
For a householder, their support should be regarded as like a house;
their objective support as like enjoyments;
and their companions as like female and male servants.
Action accompanied by resolve.
The first stage, the stage associated with the five collections of consciousness, in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, is completed.
[The Second Stage: The Mind] What is the stage of the mind?
It, too, is to be viewed in five aspects.
By way of intrinsic nature, basis, object, assistance, and function.
What is intrinsic nature?
It is that which is mind, mentation, and consciousness.
What is the mind?

It is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which is endowed with all seeds, has attained the state of being a basis, is established as a basis, and is comprised of the appropriator and maturation.
What is the mind (*manas*)?

It is that which has ceased immediately after any of the six groups of consciousness; it is the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) which is always associated with four afflictions characterized by ignorance, the view of self, the conceit "I am," and craving.
What is consciousness?
It is that which is present for the cognition of an object.
What is the basis?
The immediate basis is the mind (*manas*).
The seed basis is as explained previously.
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) which contains all seeds.
What is the object?
All phenomena (dharmas) are the object. Specifically, however, it consists of the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the unconditioned.
And it consists of invisible and non-obstructive form, the six sense bases, and all seeds.
What is the accompaniment?
It is as follows:
attention, contact, feeling, perception, volition, desire, and resolve.
Mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, faith, moral shame,
dread of blame, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, vigor, pliancy, heedfulness, equanimity, non-violence, attachment, aversion, and ignorance.

Pride, views, doubt, anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, guile, arrogance, harmfulness, lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, restlessness, lack of faith, laziness, negligence, forgetfulness, distraction, lack of clear comprehension,

remorse, torpor, applied thought, and sustained thought— mental factors of this class, which are co-existent and associated, are called "companions," as they have a single object but various aspects and arise simultaneously.
Each functions individually, is determined by its own seed, is associated [with others], and possesses a mental aspect, an object, and a basis.
What is action?
The first action is the representation of the objects of oneself and others.
Furthermore, it is the representation of specific and general characteristics.
Furthermore, there is the representation of the past, future, and present times;
furthermore, the representation of moments and continuities;
and furthermore, the engagement and subsequent following of pure and impure phenomena and actions.
Furthermore, it is the grasping of desirable and undesirable fruits, and the production of the outflow resulting from those as the cause for the other groups of consciousness.

Furthermore, it is indeed this [mental consciousness] alone that, in every respect and entirely distinct from all other groups of consciousness, discriminates its object, contemplates the object, becomes intoxicated, becomes deranged, sleeps, awakens, falls into a faint, recovers from a faint, initiates bodily and vocal actions, achieves detachment, falls away from detachment, severs the roots of virtue, reconnects the roots of virtue, passes away, and is reborn.
How does it conceptualize the object? By means of seven kinds of conceptualization. What, then, are they?

Conceptualization is of eight kinds: that which is based on signs, that which is signless, that which flows spontaneously, that which is investigative, that which is analytical, the afflicted, and the non-afflicted.
What is conceptualization based on signs?
It is that which occurs in one whose sense faculties have matured with respect to objects previously experienced.
What is the signless [conceptualization]?
It is the conceptualization of the future based on the past, as well as that of an infant who is not yet skilled in conventional discourse.
What is that which flows by its own natural force?
It is that which, when an object is present, proceeds solely by its own natural impulse through the power of the object itself.
What is the investigative [mental application]? It is that which belongs to one who is searching for and examining phenomena.
What is the investigative [mental application]? It is that which belongs to one who is investigating after [an object] has been sought out, examined, and established.
What is the afflicted [mind]? That which is accompanied by longing for the past, accompanied by delight in the future, and [accompanied by attachment] toward the present.

It is a volitional thought accompanied by attachment, a volitional thought of ill-will, or a volitional thought of cruelty— any volitional thought associated with any one or another of the primary or secondary afflictions.

What is the non-afflicted? It is that which is wholesome or indeterminate, consisting of the discrimination of renunciation, the discrimination of non-malice, and the discrimination of non-harming, by means of this or that [particular state].

Alternatively, it is the conceptualization associated with wholesome factors such as faith, whether it pertains to deportment (*airyāpathika*) or to the arts (*śailpasthānika*), or the conceptualization of one who is creating a magical emanation (*nirmāṇa*).
To this extent, there is conceptualization of the object.
How does one contemplate the object of focus?
By way of what is practiced through yoga, by way of what is not practiced through yoga, and by way of what is neither practiced through yoga nor not practiced through yoga.
How is it "in accordance with reality"? It is by not superimposing what is non-existent through the four perversions,
such as the perversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent.
Through the perversion of perceiving pleasure in suffering, through the perversion of perceiving purity in the impure,
and through the perversion of perceiving a self in what is not-self.
Nor does one deny what truly exists through false view—that is, through false views such as "there is no giving" and so forth.
Rather, in the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*), one observes and fully understands the object as it really is;
or else, by means of perfectly pure supramundane knowledge, one awakens to phenomena as they truly are.
Thus, it is established by means of yoga.
The opposite of this should be understood as that which is improperly undertaken.
How is it that one contemplates phenomena neither by way of what is produced through yoga nor by way of what is not produced through yoga?
By relying on neutral wisdom (*avyākṛtā prajñā*), one contemplates phenomena;
in this manner, one contemplates the object of focus.
How does one become intoxicated?
By virtue of having a naturally weak body, by not being accustomed to drinking alcohol, by drinking excessively strong alcohol, and by drinking alcohol in excessive quantities.
How does one become insane?

Through the projection of past karma, through an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), through terror and fear, through injury to the vital points (*marman*), and through possession by malevolent spirits (*bhūta*).

How does one sleep? By way of the natural weakness of the physical basis, by way of the fault of exhaustion and fatigue from labor, by way of heaviness from food, by way of mental attention to the sign of darkness, by way of resting from all activities, by way of habituation to sleep, and by way of being induced by others.
For example, one who is being carried away by a spell, or by medicinal herbs, or by some power, falls asleep while being put to sleep.
How does one wake up?
By the inability to endure that obsession (paryavasthāna) intensified by sleep; by sleeping while maintaining mental attention toward what must be done; and by the intervention of others.
How does one fall into a swoon?

Through the derangement of wind and bile, through injury, or through excessive purging—namely, by the purging of feces or the purging of blood—and through the excessive mental exertion of one who has been purged.
How does one emerge from fainting?
By the subsiding of that very obsession of fainting.
How does it set physical and vocal action in motion?

It does so by being preceded by knowledge corresponding to those physical and vocal actions; then by the generation of desire; then by the undertaking of effort; and finally by the setting in motion of the winds that are conducive to physical and vocal action, preceded by that effort.
How does one cultivate detachment?
By means of the maturation of the faculties conducive to detachment; by obtaining conformable instruction from others;
by avoiding obstacles to it; and by cultivating right, non-erroneous mental attention.
How does one fall away from detachment?

By being naturally of dull faculties; by attending to the signs, marks, and characteristics of that [state] while the wholesome side is still new; by practicing while undertaking dharmas conducive to falling away; by being shrouded by afflictions; and by being under the influence of evil friends.
How does one completely sever the roots of virtue?

It is by being endowed with a nature of intense evil intention and conduct; by obtaining friends who conform to that [evil path]; by reaching the culmination of the intensification of that obsession with wrong view;
and by attaining a lack of restraint and a lack of remorse regarding all evil conduct.
In that regard, the seed is also the wholesome root;
non-attachment and the others are also the wholesome root.

And by means of establishing the continuum in opposition to the manifestation of the roots of virtue, through the uprooting of the seeds that constitute the total destruction of those roots of virtue.
How does one reconnect the roots of virtue?

By means of having naturally sharp faculties; by observing the engagement of friends, kinsmen, and companions in meritorious deeds; by approaching holy persons and hearing the true Dharma; and by attaining certainty through the arising of doubt.
How does one pass away?
By means of having a limited lifespan.
Furthermore, that death occurs—both at the proper time and at an improper time—due to the exhaustion of the life-span, the exhaustion of merit, and the failure to avoid unfavorable conditions.
It should be understood that this applies to a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, and even an indeterminate mind.
How is it through the exhaustion of the life-span?
It is when someone here, having exhausted the full extent of the life-span as it was projected, passes away;
this is called "death at the [proper] time."
How is it through the exhaustion of merit? It is when someone here passes away due to a deficiency of the necessary requisites.
How is it through the failure to avoid dangerous circumstances?
As the Blessed One said:
"There are nine causes and nine conditions for the death of one whose lifespan is not yet exhausted."

Which nine? He eats immoderately; he eats unwholesome food; he eats undigested food; he does not eliminate what is raw; he retains what is cooked; he does not employ medicine; he does not know what is suitable or unsuitable for him; he wanders at improper times; and he does not lead a celibate life.
That very same [death] is further called "untimely death."
How does one die with a wholesome mind?
It is when a certain person here, at the time of death, recollects wholesome states previously practiced,
or is reminded of them by another.
By means of which, at that time, wholesome factors such as faith and so forth manifest in his mind; these continue to function as long as gross perception persists,
but when the movement of perception becomes subtle, the wholesome mind turns away.
The mind remains strictly in an indeterminate state;
for at that time, he is incapable of directing his attention toward the wholesome states previously practiced, nor can he be made to remember them by others.
How does one die with an unwholesome mind?
It is when, for example, a certain person at the time of death either personally recollects unwholesome states previously practiced,
or is reminded of them by others.

At that time, unwholesome states associated with greed and so forth do not manifest in his mind, up to and including the coarsest perceptions; as before, everything is just as in the case of the wholesome.
Therein, one who dies with a wholesome mind dies a peaceful death;
intense painful sensations at the time of death do not descend upon his body.
One who dies with an unwholesome mind dies with a painful death; moreover,
intense painful sensations pertaining to the time of death descend upon his body.
Furthermore, for one dying with a wholesome mind, the perception of forms is unconfused;
however, for one with an unwholesome mind, the perception of forms is confused.
How does one die with an indeterminate mind?

Whether one has performed wholesome or unwholesome deeds, or neither, if one dies without personally recollecting them nor being reminded by others— neither with a wholesome mind nor with a defiled mind—
one dies neither with a happy death nor with a painful death.

Furthermore, when that person who has performed wholesome or unwholesome deeds is dying, they either remember for themselves the wholesome or unwholesome dharmas previously practiced, or are reminded of them by others. At that time, whichever [state] becomes more powerful due to its greater frequency of practice, toward that the mind inclines and is released from the other.
If, however, both have been practiced equally, then whichever of the two he first recollects or is made to recollect, his mind does not turn back from it nor does it divert elsewhere.

At that time, making those two causes predominant—namely, the cause of delighting in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and the cause of wholesome and unwholesome karma—he, while passing away, experiences that fruit projected by previous karma.
In this case, one who has performed unwholesome deeds experiences here the preliminary signs of the undesirable fruit of unwholesome karma previously committed.
For example, he has visions of many distorted forms as if in a dream.
With reference to this, the Blessed One said:

"Whatever former evil, unwholesome karma has been committed and accumulated by him, at that time it hangs over him, hangs down upon him, and hangs all around him—just like the shadow of mountains or mountain peaks during the hour of sunset."
And so it is said.

And this person should be known as one who goes from light to darkness. Conversely, however, one who abides in the fruit of previous wholesome karma and performs wholesome deeds here [in this life] should be known as one who goes from darkness to light.
In this regard, there is this distinction:
At the time of death,
a vision of various beautiful forms appears to him, like a dream, while his mind remains undisturbed.
In that regard, for one who has committed excessive unwholesome deeds, perspiration arises from seeing those distorted signs;
horripilation occurs through the pores of the skin;
and there occur such things as the flinging about of hands and feet.
The voiding of urine and feces occurs;
furthermore, such phenomena as touching the sky, rolling of the eyes, and the flowing of foam from the mouth arise.
If, however, he is one who acts with middling intensity, some of his transformations occur while others do not;
they are not all complete.
For everyone, at the time of death, before reaching the state of indistinct consciousness, the self-attachment practiced over a long period of time manifests.
Consequently, under its influence, there arises a longing for personal existence in the form of "May I not cease to be.
This serves as the basis for the manifestation of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*):
at that time, self-love (*ātmasneha*) arises in the stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*) and the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
Yet, that stream-enterer or once-returner, having repeatedly scrutinized that self-love, suppresses it and does not tolerate it.
Just as a stronger man, when fighting with a weaker man, overpowers the weaker one, so too should the principle be understood in this case.
But for those non-returners, that self-attachment does not manifest at all at that time.
In that regard, the severing of the vital points (*marmaccheda*) occurs in all places of birth except for the hell realm and the heavenly realm;
furthermore, it is of two kinds:
intense and slight.
It is intense for those who have performed evil deeds and slight for those who have performed good deeds;
moreover, among the Northern Kurus, it is slight for all.
For those passing away from the realm of form (rūpadhātu), death occurs with all their sense faculties intact.
Furthermore, for those passing away from the desire realm, the death of some who possess all their faculties and the death of some whose faculties are incomplete is called untamed death;
whereas the death of those who are pure and liberated is called tamed death,
and the death of those who are impure and unliberated is called untamed death.
Then, at the time of death, for those who have performed unwholesome deeds,
consciousness first abandons the upper part of the body as its basis,
and that upper part of his becomes cold.
Furthermore, he releases it only as far as that region of the heart.
Furthermore, for those who have performed wholesome deeds, consciousness abandons the physical basis starting from the lower part;
the lower part of his body becomes cold until it reaches the region of the heart,
and from that point at the heart, the departure of consciousness is to be understood.
Thereupon, the entire basis becomes cooled.

Because that attachment to one's own existence has arisen immediately [after death], because that basis (the body) has been permeated by the cause of former delight in conceptual proliferation and has been permeated by wholesome and unwholesome karma— taking these two causes as the predominant conditions—

the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) manifests from its own seed, appearing in that location without interruption, through the conjunction of simultaneous cessation and arising, like the lowering and raising of the ends of a balance scale.
Furthermore, that intermediate state possesses all the sense faculties.
Moreover, for those who have committed evil deeds, the intermediate state has an appearance like that of a black woolen blanket or like the pitch-black darkness of night.
Furthermore, for those who have performed wholesome deeds, it is like the appearance of a bright white cloth or a moonlit night;
and that [realm] becomes the range of the pure divine eye.
At that time, that previous longing for a personal existence no longer manifests, because consciousness has been brought to cessation.
However, the craving for the manifold of sense objects continues to manifest.
And the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which has the very form of that place where he is to be reborn, arises;
its vision, like a divine eye, is unimpeded as far as the place of birth.
His movement is also unimpeded, just like that of one possessing supernatural powers (*ṛddhimat*), extending as far as the very place of rebirth.
With that eye, he sees the beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) who belong to his own class, as well as their place of rebirth and his own.
For those who have committed evil deeds, his vision is purified downward.
And one who goes downward moves with face cast down; those going to the gods move upward;
whereas those going to the human realm move horizontally.
Furthermore, that intermediate state (antarābhava) remains for seven days if the conditions for rebirth are not obtained;
however, if the conditions are obtained, there is no fixed duration.
If they are not obtained, it dies and remains again for seven days, continuing in this manner for up to seven weeks without obtaining the conditions for rebirth.
Thereafter, he necessarily obtains the condition for rebirth.
And for him who has passed away after seven days, his manifestation [of rebirth] occurs sometimes in that very same place and sometimes elsewhere in a different realm.
If the performance of another action were to change, it would change that intermediate state seed.

Furthermore, its synonyms are as follows: it is called the "intermediate state" (*antarābhava*) because it manifests in the interval between the state of death (*maraṇabhava*) and the state of birth (*upapattibhava*).
It is also called a "scent-eater" (*gandharva*) because it moves by means of scent and is nourished by scent.
It is called "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because, depending upon that [mind], it proceeds to the place of rebirth by way of the mind.
Furthermore,
it is called "actualization" (*abhinirvṛtti*) because it brings about birth by facing toward it, both through the movement of the body and through the movement of the object of perception.
Furthermore, that intermediate state (antarābhava) should be understood as excluding the sphere of rebirth in the formless realm (ārūpyopapattyāyatana).
Furthermore, if that perpetrator of unwholesome karma— having been a sheep-butchers, a poultry-keeper, a pig-breeder, or established in one or another of such groups of those who lack restraint—

has committed and accumulated evil, unwholesome karma leading to rebirth in hell, he sees beings of exactly that kind and those very actions within his place of rebirth, [seeing] those sheep and so forth as if in a dream.
Due to his delight in former habituation, he runs right toward them.
And having been obstructed by that form of the place of rebirth, that intermediate state ceases to exist and the state of rebirth is produced for him.
Then, for one passing away from there, the perception of a confused form occurs exactly as it did previously during the state of death.
And the application of arising and cessation should be understood as before.
There he is born by spontaneous generation, with the six sense-bases fully complete.
With such a thought, he approaches them, thinking: "I shall play, rejoice, and enjoy myself together with these; I shall learn the arts."
There, due to his perversion, he is driven by various karmic causes and experiences great torment;
otherwise, without such a vision, he would have no desire at all to go there.
How much less, then, could there be going?
Therefore, one does not go from here, and consequently, one is not reborn there.

Just as it is with the hells, so should one understand rebirth among the pretas who resemble those in hell. Furthermore, when being reborn among other animals and pretas, or among the classes of gods belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), he sees beings similar to himself rejoicing at their place of birth. Then, having produced there a longing for delight as before, he goes [there].
And in that case, for one who is obstructed at the place of rebirth, death and rebirth are to be understood as previously described.
[Descent into the Womb:
Therein, through the coming together of three conditions, the descent of the embryo into the mother’s womb occurs:
the mother is healthy and in her fertile period.
The mother and father are in love and have come together,
and the gandharva is present;
yet, if there is a threefold obstacle therein—

It is not produced by defects of the womb, nor by defects of the seed, nor by defects of karma. In that regard, what are the defects of the womb? If the womb is obstructed by wind (*vāta*), or obstructed by bile (*pitta*), or obstructed by phlegm (*kapha*); or if it is shaped like the middle of a sesame seed, or shaped like the middle of a barley grain; or if its opening is like the face of a cart, or like the mouth of a conch shell; or if it possesses male organs, or is crooked, or is afflicted with disease, or is astringent—one such as this is [a defective womb].
The defects of the womb are to be understood.
What are the defects of the seed? If the impurity is emitted by the father and not by the mother, or if it is emitted by the mother and not by the father.
Or it is not released from both;
or it becomes putrid for the mother, or for the father, or for both—such are the defects of the seed to be understood.
What are the faults of karma?
If the mother or the father has not performed or accumulated karma conducive to [the birth of] a son, or if both have not done so;
or if that sentient being has likewise not performed or accumulated karma conducive to [becoming] a mother or father.
Or else, such parents may have performed and accumulated karma conducive to having a different kind of son;

or that sentient being may have performed and accumulated karma conducive to having different kinds of parents—karma conducive to being of great renown or not of great renown. Such categories of karmic faults are to be understood.
Due to the absence of these defects and the presence of three conditions, the descent of the embryo occurs.

While still in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), through a desire for play and the like upon seeing beings of a similar class, he generates the wish to go to the place of rebirth. At that time, a perverted perception arises regarding the semen and blood produced by his mother and father.
In this regard, such is the perversion:
He sees his mother and father engaging in sexual intercourse with one another;
yet at that time, no such intercourse actually occurs between the mother and father.
With a perverted mind, he then perceives this as something created by illusion.
Seeing that misconception, attachment arises in him toward it.
If he desires to become a woman, attachment for a man and a desire for cohabitation arise;
if he desires to become a man, attachment for a woman and a desire for cohabitation arise.
Then he approaches that vicinity;
a desire for sexual union with a woman arises in the woman, and a desire for sexual union with a man arises in the man.
And because of the arising of those desires, he sees either only the man or only the woman.
And as he draws closer to that place, his vision of the other parts of her body gradually fades away;
only the sight of the female organ or the male organ remains present before him,
and there he encounters resistance.
His passing away and rebirth are to be understood as before.

[Rebirth: If one has little merit, one is reborn into low families; at the time of death and at the time of entering [the womb], signs appear such as a clamorous noise and the sensation of entering a thicket of reeds or a dense forest.
If one has performed wholesome deeds, they are reborn into high families;
for such a person, there appears as a sign the manifestation of calm and sweet sounds, as well as the climbing of palaces, celestial mansions, and other such elevated places.
In that case, when the passion of the impassioned mother and father has reached its peak intensity, the semen is released last of all;
and at the conclusion of that, a drop of both semen and blood necessarily appears.
Furthermore, those two drops of semen and blood, having become mixed within the mother’s womb, remain bound together as a single mass, just like boiled milk turning into a solid state;
therein the *ālayavijñāna*—which contains all seeds, is comprised of maturation (*vipāka*), and is the appropriator of the basis (*āśrayopādātṛ*)—coagulates.
How, then, does conception occur?
By means of that mass of semen and blood in which the embryo has been produced, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which possesses a perverted object of perception, ceases.

Simultaneously with its cessation, by the power of that very [consciousness] which possesses all seeds, another mass of semen and blood— homogeneous with it, mixed with other subtle sense-faculties and great elements, and endowed with sense-faculties— is produced.
Consciousness established in that state is called "the bound rebirth-linking" (*pratisandhi*).
That is the stage of the *kalala*; and those great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the sense-faculties within that *kalala* arise together with the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) alone.
Furthermore, the great elements that serve as the bases for the faculties arise together with those very same great elements of the faculties and the body-faculty.
Then, taking those great elements of the faculties as their material cause (*upādāya*), the faculties such as the eye arise in succession.
With the manifestation of the sense faculties and their bases, the entire basis becomes fully formed and acquired.
Furthermore, that *kalala* form is said to be "coagulated" (*sammūrcchita*) with those mental states and mental factors through mutual security and well-being;
and by the power of the mind, it does not undergo putrefaction.
Furthermore, through the benefit or injury of that [body], there is the benefit or injury of the mind and mental factors;
therefore, it is said that these are mutually characterized by *yogakṣema* (shared security and well-being).
And at that time, the region where that consciousness coagulates is his heart-region;
for in this way, from whichever region that consciousness passes away, in that very same region it first coagulates.

Furthermore, that consciousness containing all seeds has its seeds complete for those whose nature is to attain parinirvāṇa, whereas for those whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa, it is deficient in the seeds for the three types of enlightenment.
And whatever personal existence whatsoever is produced, all of it should be understood as being accompanied by the seeds of all personal existences.

Within the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), there also exists the seed (*bīja*) of that which belongs to the form and formless realms; likewise, within the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), there exist the seeds of those belonging to the desire and formless realms; and within the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), there exist the seeds of those belonging to the desire and form realms.
Furthermore, as that *kalala* grows, there is a simultaneous growth of both name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*), due to the increasing expansion of both.
That growth, moreover, should be understood to continue until the completion of the physical basis (*āśraya*).
In this process, matter (*rūpa*) increases and attains greater expansion by depending upon the earth element.
Furthermore, the water element gathers that very [embryo];
the fire element matures it;
and the wind element differentiates its limbs and arranges them.

Furthermore, regarding that manifestation of personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) which contains all seeds, although it has both pure and impure karma as its cause, one should see that delight in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) alone is the primary cause.
However, for the fruits such as lineage, power, physical form, lifespan, and enjoyments, pure and impure karma is the primary cause.
And regarding that personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), fools conceive of it as "I," or "mine," or "I am";
whereas for the noble ones (*ārya*), it is simply "suffering.
Furthermore, by its very nature, while in the state of the womb, consciousness—which is neither suffering nor established in pleasant feeling—accumulates.
And that very feeling therein is comprised within maturation (*vipāka*).
All other felt experience (*vedita*), however, is either born of maturation or conditioned by objects.
Among these, pleasure and pain arise at one time through the manifestation of their respective conditions.
At times, it does not arise.
And that continuity of the seed-series is beginningless;
even though it is beginningless,
it becomes renewed through the repeated acquisition of the fruits of maturation, due to the perfuming by specific wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
When the fruit has manifested, it becomes fresh through the grasping of that fruit; and once the fruit has manifested, that seed becomes one whose fruit has been utilized.
In this way, the continuity of saṃsāra proceeds until one attains parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, those seeds therein whose fruit has not yet been received may be such that their fruit is to be experienced upon rebirth.
Some [karmas] are to be experienced in subsequent lives;
furthermore, the full completion of those personal existences occurs over hundreds of thousands of eons from their own seeds.
Whatever other fruit arises, that too arises from its own seed alone.
In this case, the seed of one whose lifespan has been exhausted has already yielded its fruit;
however, the seeds of remaining personal existences have not yet yielded their fruit, and thus they are not fruits that have been consumed.

Furthermore, even if the fruit of a certain seed is to be experienced within that particular personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), it may not be experienced due to a deficiency of conditions; yet, in the case of that which is to be experienced indeterminately (*aniyata-vedanīya*), that seed remains in that very state.
Therefore, because every personal existence contains the seeds of all [other] personal existences, one who is attached to any single one must be said to be attached to them all.
One who is becoming detached from one thing must be said to be detached from all things.

Furthermore, regarding those seeds within those personal existences (*ātmabhāva*) that belong to the side of the afflictions (*kleśapakṣya*), there is the designation "dysfunction" (*dauṣṭhulya*) and "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*). However, regarding those which belong to the side of maturation (*vipākapakṣya*) and those belonging to other neutral sides (*avyākṛtapakṣya*), there is only the designation "dysfunction," not the designation "latent tendency."
Furthermore, regarding those seeds belonging to the side of wholesome dharmas such as faith, they are neither designated as "latent tendencies" (anuśaya) nor as "dysfunction" (dauṣṭhulya).
For it is because of their arising that the basis (āśraya) becomes functional (karmanya), not non-functional.

And for this reason, because the entire basis is permeated by *dauṣṭhulya* and has *dauṣṭhulya* as its intrinsic nature, the Tathāgatas designate it as suffering, namely, as the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

Furthermore, synonyms for "seed" (bīja) should be understood as belonging to this class: element (dhātu), lineage (gotra), nature (prakṛti), cause (hetu), the existing body (satkāya), conceptual proliferation (prapañca), the storehouse (ālaya), appropriation (upādāna), suffering (duḥkha), the basis for the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭy-adhiṣṭhāna), and the basis for the conceit "I am" (asmimāna-adhiṣṭhāna).

Furthermore, at the time of final nirvāṇa, for pure yogins who have undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), the basis undergoes a transformation such that it is devoid of the seeds of all afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*).
It also renders the conditions for the seeds of all wholesome and neutral phenomena deficient,
and one attains mastery over internal conditions.
[The embryonic stage:
Furthermore, that embryo becomes endowed with all its major and minor limbs after thirty-six weeks.
Thereafter, it develops over four days,
as stated by the Blessed One in the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*: "Furthermore,
it becomes complete after nine months or even longer."
If it is completed in eight months, it is complete but not "supremely complete.
If it is in six or seven months, it is indeed incomplete or deficient.
Furthermore, during that stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the nourishment for its growth occurs through the coarse essence produced within the mother's womb.
Furthermore, in the even more subtle stages beginning with the *kalala*, nourishment should be understood to occur through a very subtle essence.
And that embryo has eight stages.

What are the eight stages? They are: the stage of the *kalala*, the stage of the *arbuda*, the stage of the *peśī*, the stage of the *ghana*, the stage of the limbs (*praśākhā*), the stage of hair, body hair, and nails, the stage of the sense faculties (*indriya*), and the stage of the secondary sexual characteristics (*vyañjana*).
In that context, *kalala* is the internal fluid bound within the *śarīra*;
*arbuda* is that which has become solidified both internally and externally like curdled milk, yet has not yet reached the stage of flesh;
and *peśī* is that which has become flesh but is still soft.
When it has become solidified and capable of being handled, it is called *ghana*.
From that very state, through the formation of flesh, there is the manifestation of the signs of the major and minor limbs, which is the stage of *praśākhā*.
Following that, there is the manifestation of hair on the head, body hair, and nails; this is the stage of *keśaromanakhaprādurbhāva*.

Thereafter, the manifestation of the sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth, is the stage of the faculties (*indriyāvasthā*). Thereafter, the manifestation of their physical bases is the stage of the marks (*vyañjanāvasthā*).

Then, due to the influence of past karma, and because of the mother's failure to avoid unwholesome things, as well as the winds within the womb that arise from such avoidance and are concordant with them, deformities of the hair, deformities of the complexion, deformities of the skin, and deformities of the limbs are produced.
How does the deformity of the hair arise?
First of all, he has previously committed a sinful and unwholesome deed that must be described as such.
Or, his mother frequently consumes food and drink consisting mostly of alkaline and salty flavors, by which the fetus comes to have dull hair and body hair.
How does the disfigurement of the complexion occur?
As before, karma is the cause;
the present condition is that the mother resorts to excessive heat, such as the sun's glare or fire.
By that, his complexion becomes dark and swarthy;
or, if she dwells in an excessively cold inner chamber,
by that his complexion becomes white.
Or again, she consumes food that is excessively hot,
whereby a reddish coloration arises in her.
How does a deformity of the skin arise?
As before, past karma is the cause;
the present condition is that the mother excessively indulges in sexual intercourse.
By which there arise in him eruptions of ringworm, or eruptions of scabies, or eruptions of leprosy, or various skin diseases.
How does deformity of the limbs occur?
Karma, as before, is its cause.

The present condition is the mother’s engagement in modes of conduct such as running, jumping, leaping, and so forth, by which, due to her failure to avoid uneven terrain, deformity of the limbs arises or there may be a deficiency of the sense faculties.
If it is a female, she remains on the mother's left side, leaning against the spine with her chest facing forward;
if it is a male, he remains on the mother's right side, leaning against the chest with his back facing forward.
Furthermore, when that embryo has reached full development, internal winds arise in the mother— who can no longer endure the excessive burden of the fetus—
and these produce pain for her. Then, winds born of the maturation of karma (*karmavipākaja*) and belonging to the category of birth (*upapattyaṃśika*) arise within the embryo itself.
They turn the fetus so that it is head-downward and feet-upward;
then the fetus emerges while still enveloped by its membrane.
As it emerges, however, that membrane remains within the womb.
And the moment of emerging from the birth canal is called the state of being born. Once born, he gradually experiences the contact pertaining to rebirth,
as follows:
He conforms to the designation of visual contact— that is, by training in the conventions of worldly conduct—
and he dwells in a family,
that is, as a consequence of aging and the maturation of the sense faculties.
And he performs actions, namely, worldly crafts and occupations;
and he experiences sense objects, namely, desirable and undesirable forms and so forth;
and he undergoes suffering, namely, that which has its conditions in past karma or its conditions in the present.
And how it is led by conditions—that is, either by the conditions for going to the five realms of existence or by the conditions for going to nirvāṇa.

And for those beings, in whichever category of beings the manifestation of their personal existence occurs, the homogeneity of those beings performs its function as a condition through four conditions:
by providing the application of the seed-nature, by the accumulation of nourishment, by the arrangement of protection, and by training in the performance of bodily and vocal actions.
For example: first, the mother and father provide the semen and blood;
then, having recognized that [the child] has been born, they cause it to drink, nourish, and grow with appropriate food and breast milk.
Then, as he wanders here and there, they provide protection against improper conduct and erratic behavior.
Subsequently, they instruct him in conversation and social discourse as his growth continues and his faculties reach maturity;
and they, in turn, instruct others.

Thus these beings experience pleasure and pain throughout beginningless time, yet they do not attain the transcendence of pleasure and pain until— having approached the awakening of the Buddhas, through the influence of the voice of others and through wise mental attention within themselves— they reach the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).
This state is indeed very difficult to understand, namely:
"Nothing whatsoever belongs to me anywhere;
nor am I anywhere, belonging to anyone, in any way.
In this manner, there occurs the passing away and rebirth of internal phenomena.
[Regarding] dissolution and evolution: how, then, does the dissolution and evolution of external things occur?
It occurs through karma conducive to dissolution and evolution.
If karma conducive to destruction has become manifest, then their destruction occurs through an external condition of destruction;
it does not occur, however, as in the case of internal beings, through the exhaustion of their lifespan.
For what reason?
For instance, external entities are material, gross, composed of the four great elements, and characterized by stable continuities, whereas internal entities are not so. Furthermore,
the karma that causes those receptacle worlds to evolve and dissolve is necessarily projected for the duration of an eon.
Neither above that nor below.
Furthermore, regarding that which is reckoned as a sentient being, there is no fixed rule for its timing;
for such beings are the products of various karmic formations.
Therefore, for them, it occurs even beyond a kalpa, and from there downward, as far as ten years.
Furthermore, that dissolution (saṃvarta) should be understood as being threefold:
the dissolution by fire dissolves everything from the Avīci hell up to the Brahmāloka;
the dissolution by water dissolves the entirety of the second dhyāna.
The destruction by wind extends as far as the entirety of the third dhyāna.
In the fourth dhyāna, however, those gods belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna arise together with their celestial palaces,
and they pass away together with their celestial palaces.
Therefore, for them there is no dissolution,
nor is there any cause for dissolution.
There are three limits of dissolution.
The second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, this world undergoes dissolution for twenty intermediate kalpas;
it remains dissolved for twenty intermediate kalpas;
and it undergoes evolution for twenty intermediate kalpas.
It remains evolved for twenty intermediate kalpas;
these constitute eighty intermediate kalpas,
which, by way of numerical designation, is one great kalpa (mahākalpa).
There, in that Brahma-world, the lifespan is one kalpa;
it is the very last to be destroyed,
and it is the very first to re-evolve.
Furthermore, the determination of that eon should be understood as follows:

for the gods of the Brahmakāyika realm, twenty intermediate eons (antarakalpa) constitute one eon, and this is how their lifespan is determined; for the gods of the Brahmapurohita realm, forty intermediate eons constitute one eon, and this is how their lifespan is determined.
Sixty intermediate kalpas constitute one kalpa; this is how the determination of the lifespan of the Mahābrahmās is established.
What is the destruction by fire?
It is that time when beings with immeasurable lifespans decline in life-span until they have a lifespan of eighty thousand years;
then, due to their undertaking of unwholesome states, they further decline until they have a lifespan of ten years.

Furthermore, through the cause of undertaking wholesome dharmas by those who have attained spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), their lifespan increases until they reach a life span of eighty thousand years. This period of decrease and this period of increase,
taken together, are called an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*) according to the established numerical system.
Furthermore, that intermediate aeon comes to an end through three calamities: famine, disease, and weapons.
That famine occurs when the lifespan of humans has reached thirty years; moreover, it manifests again and again in such a manner that even boiled old bones provide mere sustenance for survival.
And whatever grain of barley, rice, jujube, horse-gram, or sesame they might occasionally find there by some means, they cast it into the ocean like a precious gem and drag it out.
And those beings, for the most part lacking strength, fall prostrate upon the earth and are unable even to rise;
through such a famine, the majority of beings perish.
Furthermore, that famine lasts for seven years, seven months, and seven days and nights;
beyond that, it should be said to have subsided.
And those beings, having gathered and come together, experience a mild sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
By that cause and by that condition, there is no diminution of their lifespan and the famine comes to an end.
Furthermore, when humans have a lifespan of twenty years,
as that very sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) fades away and they decline, there will then be many epidemics, calamities, and afflictions;
they will be subject to many diseases and for the most part will die.
Furthermore, that disease lasts for them at most seven months and seven days;
beyond that, it is said to have subsided.
Consequently, those beings possess a moderate sense of spiritual urgency.
By that cause and by that condition, furthermore, they do not diminish in lifespan,
and those diseases do not arise.

Furthermore, when the lifespan of humans has reached ten years, due to the disappearance of that very sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), their lifespan begins to decline. At that time, upon seeing one another as sentient beings, a fierce murderous intent arises within them.
Consequently, whatever they grasp—whether grass, pebbles, or potsherds—these become sharp weapons, well-tempered and keen.
Those by whom mutual slaughter is carried out do so for at most seven days;
beyond that, it should be declared that they have emerged from it.
And for those beings at that time, there are three supreme calamities,
namely:
the calamity of lifespan, the calamity of the physical basis, and the calamity of requisites.
Therein, the decline of lifespan is such that it lasts for at most ten years;
therein, the decline of the physical basis is such that the measure of the body becomes at most a span and a fist;
therein, there is the decline of the necessities of life.
Among foods, *kodrava* grain is the foremost; among garments, the hair-blanket (*keśakambala*) is the foremost;
and among ornaments, the sword is the foremost.
All five flavors— ghee, honey, oil, products of sugarcane, and salt— completely disappear. Thereupon,
those beings experience an extreme sense of spiritual urgency.
Furthermore, they do not fall away from their sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having abandoned those unwholesome factors that lead to the decline of life, they proceed by undertaking and practicing wholesome factors that produce vitality.
Gathering together and coming back to one another, they once again increase in lifespan.
They increase in complexion, strength, happiness, sovereignty, and lordship,
until their lifespan reaches eighty thousand years.
In this manner, there are twenty periods of decrease and twenty periods of increase.
When forty cycles of decrease and increase have passed, then, during the very last period of increase, sentient beings pass away from the hells but are no longer reborn there.
When they have all passed away, it should be said that the world has been dissolved, namely by the dissolution of the hells.
Just as by the dissolution of the hells, so too by the dissolution of the animal realm and the dissolution of the realm of hungry ghosts.

Furthermore, among human beings, a certain being who has attained the nature of things (dharmatā) dwells having fully entered the second dhyāna. Following his example, other beings who have also attained the nature of things dwell having fully entered the second dhyāna.
Having passed away from here, they are reborn in the Ābhāsvara heavenly realm.
At that time, it should be said that this world has dissolved, namely by way of the dissolution of the human realm;
and as it is with the dissolution of the human realm, so it is with the dissolution of the divine realms.
And when not even a single sentient being is perceived within the world-system of the five destinies, then even the existence of material requisites is no longer perceived.
When even the availability of the necessary conditions is not perceived, then rain itself is also not perceived;
for when it does not rain, those things which exist in this [world]—

Upon the great earth, the grasses, medicinal herbs, and forest trees wither away. Furthermore, this very solar disc becomes more intensely scorching when deprived of timely rain. Moreover, due to the predominance of the collective karma of sentient beings that leads to destruction (*saṃvartanī-karma*), there appears another sixfold set of solar discs for the purpose of burning the objects of combustion.
Furthermore, those solar disks possess a power of heat four times greater than this solar disk;
moreover, having become sevenfold, they heat it seven times over.
What are the six objects?
The small streams and great rivers, which are dried up by the second solar disk; the great lake Anavatapta, which is dried up by the fourth solar disk.
The great ocean is dried up by the fifth solar disc,
and it is dried up by a portion of the sixth.
Mount Sumeru and the great earth are burned by the sixth and seventh solar disks respectively, because their physical forms are most solid;
from that very point, the flame, impelled by the wind, proceeds burning as far as the Brahma-world.
Furthermore, these consist of three types of entities:
the water-born entity, such as grass and the like, which withers by the first [wind] alone;
and that very same water-entity, which withers by the other five [winds].
The immobile object, whose essence is its body, is that which is consumed by both.
When that world-system has been thus burnt and consumed, as described in detail according to the sūtra, not even soot is perceived, nor is even ash perceived.
To this extent the world is said to have dissolved, namely, by means of the dissolution of the receptacle world;
and twenty intermediate kalpas have elapsed.
And once the world has thus evolved, it remains for twenty intermediate kalpas.
What is the destruction by water?
When seven destructions by fire have passed, then in the second dhyāna there arises an innate water element which,
like the water element dissolving salt, destroys that receptacle world.
And that water-element, together with that very receptacle world, disappears;
having disappeared, it remains in that same state for twenty intermediate kalpas.
What is the destruction by wind? After seven destructions by water have passed, there occurs once more one destruction by fire. Following that, there occurs one destruction by wind.
Immediately thereafter, in the third dhyāna, a natural wind-element arises;
this, like a wind drying a limb, causes that receptacle world to vanish,
and that wind itself vanishes along with it.
For it is observed that when the wind-element becomes aggravated in some individuals, even their bones undergo emaciation;
and having thus dissolved, they remain for twenty intermediate kalpas.
In this way, indeed, the dissolution of the world occurs.
[The Process of Evolution] What is the process of evolution (*vivarta*)?

It should be understood that following the passing of those very twenty intermediate kalpas, the commencement of the kalpa of evolution occurs for sentient beings through the sovereign influence of their karma conducive to evolution.
Therein, first of all, the third dhyāna evolves in space; that is to say, by way of the evolution of the receptacle world.
As it is with the third dhyāna, so it is with the second.
Thus is the first [destruction].
In that case, from the third summit of destruction, beings, having passed away due to the exhaustion of their lifespan and the exhaustion of their merit, are reborn in the third dhyāna;
so it is in every instance.
In this way, from the second summit of destruction, [beings are reborn] in the second dhyāna;
thus it is everywhere.

Furthermore, from the first summit of the world-system's destruction, a certain being, having passed away due to the exhaustion of his lifespan or the exhaustion of his merit, is reborn in the first dhyāna— namely, in the Brahma-world. There he becomes Brahmā, the Great Brahmā.
As he was alone, longing arose within him;
discontent was born:
"Oh, would that other beings too might be reborn here!"

And by his mental volition, other beings as well— due to the exhaustion of their lifespan, or even the exhaustion of their merit— pass away from the second dhyāna and are reborn in the first dhyāna itself;
in this way, these three dhyānas become evolved.
Namely, through the transformation of sentient beings as well;
from that, celestial palaces appear in the sky for the four classes of gods belonging to the desire realm.
And the arising of all those celestial palaces in the sky should be understood as being like a magical creation.
And from among those, beings pass away from the Ābhāsvara heavenly host and are reborn there as before.
Thereafter, a wind-mandala arises here, equal in extent to the trichiliocosm, serving as the foundation for the trichiliocosm and for those beings who do not dwell in celestial palaces.
That, moreover, is of two kinds:
lying on the back and lying on the side;
by means of which their celestial palaces are tilted horizontally and their abodes extend downward.
Then, through the sovereign power of that karma, clouds containing gold arise above it,
from which rain is produced;
and those waters abide within the wind-mandala.
Then the winds, having come together, consolidate the waters and solidify them;
that becomes the golden earth, capable of withstanding the pressure of water from above and below.
When that [wind] has ceased, by the very power of that karma, a cloud containing various elements arises above it,
from which rain is produced;
and those waters settle upon the golden earth.
In the same way, moreover, the winds coalesce and solidify [the elements].

And there, from that pure, foremost, most excellent, and sublime element, Sumeru is produced through the power of the withdrawal of the winds; it consists of four jewels: it is made of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
Furthermore, from that middle element there emerge seven golden mountain ranges,
namely: Yugandhara, Vinataka, Aśvakarṇagiri, Sudarśana, Khadiraka, Īṣādhara, and Nimindhara.
Furthermore, they stand surrounding Mount Sumeru in successive order.
Furthermore, the measurement of Sumeru is eighty thousand yojanas in height as well as in width;
it is submerged exactly eighty thousand yojanas in the waters.
Yugandhara is half the size of that [Sumeru].
From there, the dimensions of the other golden mountains—beginning with Vinataka and ending with Nimindhara—are to be understood as being successively half the size of their predecessors.
Furthermore, the names of the peaks belonging to those very mountains should be seen as corresponding to the specific types and distinctions of those [main] mountains.

Furthermore, outside the four sides of Sumeru, from the lower realm, there are four continents beyond the golden mountains, eight intermediate islands, and the Cakravāḍa mountain, which is half the size of Mount Nimindhara.
By this [Cakravāḍa], the world of four continents is encircled.
And the abodes of the asuras are located below Sumeru, near the waters.
And the Himavat mountain is adjacent to the lake Anavatapta;
below that are the eight locations of the hells.
Of the great hells and the individual hells;
of the hells and the neighboring hells;
and of certain animals and hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, those four continents are as follows: Jambūdvīpa, Pūrvavideha,
Avaragodānīya, and Uttarakuru.
Among them, Jambūdvīpa is shaped like a cart;
Pūrvavideha is shaped like a half-moon;
and Godānīya is circular.
And Uttarakuru is square.
Jambūdvīpa is six thousand five hundred yojanas in circumference; Pūrvavideha is seven thousand yojanas in circumference;
and Avaragodānīya is seven thousand five hundred yojanas in circumference.
Uttarakuru is eight thousand yojanas in extent.
Furthermore, the water that lies between those seven golden mountains is endowed with the eight qualities;
this is the inner ocean,
where there are the abodes of the nāgas.
These eight nāgas remain for an eon and support the earth:
Nanda, Upananda, Aśvatara, Mucilinda, Manasvin, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Mahākāla, and Elāpatra.
Those gods experience the battle with the asuras, and they also undergo it in return.
The strength of Śakra, the lord of the gods, consists of the four classes of nāgas:
the egg-born, the womb-born, the moisture-born, and the spontaneously born;
as well as the four classes of suparṇins.
Born from an egg, born from a womb, born from moisture, and born by spontaneous generation.
And that water which is outside of that inner ocean is the outer ocean.
And from the base of that Mount Sumeru, there are four terraces.
The first terrace, measuring sixteen thousand yojanas, extends out from Sumeru.
The measurement of the remaining [mountains] is half of that [preceding one], respectively.
On the first [level] dwell the Karoṭapāṇis; on the second, the Rudhirapāṇis; on the third, the Sadāmadas; and on the fourth, the Mālādharas.
On the summit of Meru, at the four corners, are four peaks five hundred yojanas in height.
In them dwell yakṣas who have Vajrapāṇi as their leader.
On the four sides of Yugandhara are the royal capitals of the Great Kings:
in the east, west, south, and north respectively, those of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa.
On all the golden mountains are the villages, towns, and districts belonging to those Great Kings.
In the vicinity of Himavat, the king of mountains, there is a golden slope named Surapārśva, fifty yojanas in length and fifty yojanas in width.
It is the abode of the nāga king Supratiṣṭha,
and it serves as the battleground for Śakra, the lord of the gods.

And there was a king of trees named Supratiṣṭhita, surrounded by seven rows of palm trees; and there was a lotus pond named Mandākinī, with a hundred attendants, which served as the pleasure ground for that very Supratiṣṭhita.
There, assuming a form at will, he would pull up the lotus stalks and fibers from that pond and enjoy them.
And he was accompanied by a retinue of five hundred female elephants.
Adjacent to that very place is the great lake Anavatapta, fifty yojanas deep and fifty yojanas wide, strewn with golden sand, endowed with water possessing the eight qualities,
beautiful, lovely to behold, exquisite, and pleasing;
from it flow forth the four great rivers.
Namely, the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Sītā, and the Vakṣu.
And upon that base of Sumeru is situated the city of the gods, measuring ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
elsewhere are the villages, towns, and provinces of those gods.
Sumeru has four faces;
the four continents, Jambūdvīpa and the others,
constitute its four sides.
The side facing Jambūdvīpa is made of beryl;
the one facing Pūrvavideha is made of silver;
the one facing Avaragodānīya is made of gold.
That which faces Uttarakuru consists of crystal.
Surrounding Jambūdvīpa, a golden Cakravartin-path remains submerged in the great ocean, [reaching] up to the beings of the Four Great Kings' realm;
through the appearance of a Cakravartin king, the water of the great ocean dries up by as much as the depth of a knee.
To the south of Lake Anavatapta is a great Jambu tree, after which this continent is named Jambudvīpa.
To the north of that is a great Kūṭaśalmali tree,
where four Suparṇins dwell.
Of those four continents, each continent has two intermediate islands;
among these, one is the Rākṣasa island.
When the receptacle world has thus come into existence, beings pass away from the Ābhāsvara class of gods and are reborn here by means of that same karma to be experienced during the first kalpa,
which is the most supreme and excellent karma belonging to the desire realm.
And at that very time, the fruition of that karma is manifested, and not at any other time.
Those beings at that moment are called "those of the first eon" (*prathamakalpaka*).
They are possessed of form (*rūpin*) and mind-made (*manomaya*); all of this is exactly according to the sūtra.
And at that time, there are no houses, dwellings, or village settlements;
the entire earth is merely level ground.
Then, for those beings, the essence of the earth (pṛthivīrasa) appeared;
in this sequence, there followed the *parpaṭaka*, the forest creeper (*vanalatā*), and the uncultivated, unsown rice—free of husks and without powder.
Subsequently, the husk and the powder came to envelop the grain of the rice.
Then the rice remained in clusters;
then those beings were seen to take possession of it.
Then, from the consumption of its essence and so forth, a deterioration of their complexion appeared among those beings.
Their radiance also disappears;
and whoever eats more becomes paler, and their body becomes heavier.
Consequently, one being begins to despise another.
Due to the manifestation of those unwholesome states, there occurs a progressive disappearance of the flavors and other qualities,
as described at length in the Sūtra.
Consequently, they look at one another, gazing with their eyes fixed upon each other's eyes.
Then they become impassioned.

Thereafter, by means of karma conducive to the state of male and female, the female faculty appears for some and the male faculty appears for others. Then they engage in sexual misconduct through the union of pairs.
Then they are reviled by others;
consequently, for that reason, they build houses.
And, on account of their appropriation of the rice, they also carry out the appropriation of fields.
Consequently, that taking of what was not given—consisting of seizing and dragging away—became known.
Then, for that reason, they established a king as a restrainer;
and he became Mahāsammata.
In this way, the appearance of the circles of Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras occurs in the world according to the Sūtra.
And with the disappearance of that light which was established as its basis, darkness appears in the world;
thereafter, the sun, the moon, and the stars appear in the world.
In that regard, the measurement of the solar disk is fifty-one yojanas,
while that of the lunar disk is fifty. Furthermore,
the solar disk is composed of fire-crystal (tejaḥ-sphaṭika).
Furthermore, the lunar disk is composed of water-crystal (*sphaṭika*).
Moreover, between these two, it should be understood that the lunar disk moves more swiftly and its course is irregular.
Furthermore, the solar disk simultaneously provides illumination to two continents and simultaneously brings darkness to the other two.
There, at one place it is midday, at another sunrise, at another midnight, and at another sunset;
for all the hosts of the moon, sun, and stars, their movement and course follow along half of Mount Sumeru.
Furthermore, that [mountain] is equal to Yugandhara.
Furthermore, when they move in close proximity to Mount Sumeru, then the summer heat is perceived;
when they become separated from it, then the winter cold is perceived.
