For that very reason, their rapid setting should also be understood.
Furthermore, when the lunar disk bends slightly upward at the top, a semicircular appearance is seen;
its far side, being obscured by the near side, is not visible.
Just as the moon becomes curved, it appears more and more fully rounded;
conversely, during the dark fortnight, as it becomes concave, its waning is observed.
Furthermore, because reflections of fish, turtles, and other creatures arise within the great ocean, a dark shadow of the moon is perceived in its center.
Furthermore, the measurement of the stars is as follows: the largest are eighteen krośas, the medium-sized are ten krośas, and the minute ones are four krośas.
In that [world] where the four castes are produced, there occurs the undertaking of karma to be experienced in the five destinies as desirable or undesirable.
Then, by means of a defiled karma conducive to sovereignty, a certain being is born as King Yama.
Immediately thereafter, hell-wardens resembling magical apparitions arise, along with the instruments of torture such as iron and so forth, and the fires of hell manifest.
Then those beings, according to their karma, are reborn there and in other realms of existence.

Having done so, one hundred koṭis of four-continent worlds, one hundred koṭis of Sumerus, one hundred koṭis of the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm, and one hundred koṭis of Brahma-worlds evolve and dissolve simultaneously within the triple-thousandfold world systems;
and these constitute the three world-systems.
A thousand *cūḍika* worlds— namely, a thousand moons, a thousand suns, and so on up to a thousand Brahma-worlds, all condensed into a single unit—

this thousand *cūḍika* worlds is indeed a second-order intermediate (*dvisāhasro madhyama*) world system. A thousand of these intermediate world systems is indeed a third-order great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasro mahāsāhasro lokadhātuḥ*).
Thus, in the eastern direction, in the southern, in the western, above, and below,
there is no end and no limit to the world-systems as they undergo dissolution and evolution.
Just as when a rain-cloud pours down, there is no interval or gap between the streams of water falling in all directions, even so it is in all directions.
There is no end and no limit to the world-systems as they undergo dissolution and evolution.
And that which is the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system is called a "buddha-field," wherein Tathāgatas arise and perform the deeds of a Buddha throughout immeasurable world-systems.
Furthermore, when the world-system has thus evolved, five destinies are discerned: hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, and humans;
and four modes of birth: egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and spontaneously born.
The six supports;
the tenfold time:
the season, the year, the month, and the half-month.
Day, night, kṣaṇa, tatkṣaṇa, lava, and muhūrta;
these are the seven objects of possession.
There are ten requisites for the body.
There are ten enjoyments of sensual pleasures;
furthermore, they are as described in the Middle [Discourse].
There are eight frequent mental explorations.
There are eight worldly conditions:
gain and loss, fame and insignificance, pleasure and pain, blame and praise.
There are three factions:
the faction of friends, the faction of enemies, and the faction of neutrals.
There are three kinds of worldly conduct,
three kinds of discourse,
and twenty-two kinds of agitation.
There are sixty-four classes of beings,
eight stages,
and four modes of entry into the womb.
There are four modes of conduct,
six kinds of livelihood,
six kinds of protection, and seven kinds of suffering.
There are seven kinds of pride,
seven kinds of intoxication,
and four types of legal proceedings.
And there are many bases of legal procedure.
What is the hell realm?
It consists of the aggregates of hell-beings, which are comprised of both seeds and fruits, as well as the karma to be experienced in hell.
Just as with the hell realm, the animal realm, the hungry ghost realm, the divine realm, and the human realm are to be understood accordingly.
What is the egg-born womb? It is those beings who emerge after breaking out of the shell of an egg.
Furthermore, who are they?
For example: swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, and so forth.
What is the womb-born birth?
It refers to those beings who, enveloped by a placenta, emerge after breaking through the placenta.
Furthermore, who are they?
Elephants, horses, cattle, donkeys, and so forth.
What is the moisture-born birth-place?
It refers to those beings who, having encountered this or that moisture, are born.
Furthermore, who are they?
Worms, insects, moths, sesame-destroyers, and so forth.
What is the apparitional mode of birth?
It is those beings who, through the sovereign power of karma, are born with all six sense bases complete, or with some of the six sense bases incomplete.
Who, then, are they?
Namely: hell-beings, gods, and certain animals, hungry ghosts, and humans.
What are the six supports?
They are the supports of foundation;
namely, below, the circle of wind, the circle of water, and the circle of earth.
[This is] the source for the non-falling of sentient beings below; therefore, it is called a "support.
The second is the support as a dwelling-place (*nilayādhāra*); that, moreover, consists of houses, pavilions, and so forth.
This is the source of non-injury toward the outflows;
therefore, it is called the "support."

Furthermore, these—such as houses, pavilions, and so forth—are, in brief, of four types: those produced through volitional effort (*abhisaṃskārika*), those not produced through volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskārika*), those belonging to celestial palaces (*vaimānika*), and those that are emanations (*nairmāṇika*).
The third is the support for abundance of food (*subhikṣa*).
This is the source of edible food; therefore, it is called a support.
The fourth is the support of security.
This is the source for beings not meeting with destruction by means of weapons and the like; therefore, it is called a support.
The sun and moon are the fifth support;
because they are the source for the seeing of forms, it is called a "support.
The sixth is the support of nutriment.
There are four nutriments:
edible food, contact, mental volition, and consciousness.
Because they are the source for the maintenance and support of the body, they are called its "sustenance."
There are seven objects of possession.

Which are they? They are: oneself; mother and father; wife and children; female and male slaves; laborers and servants; friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations; land-property; house-property; shop-property; the basis for meritorious action; and the basis for the application of business activities.
And the seventh item is the storage of treasuries.
And there are ten types of requisites.
Which are they?
Food, drink, vehicles, clothing, ornaments, laughter, song, dance, music, perfumes, garlands, and ointments, household utensils, light, and the attendance of men and women.
There are eight frequent preoccupations.
Which are they?
Those which people frequently preoccupy themselves with in the world.

Namely: the covering of the private parts, the care of the body, the transition between postures, food, sleep, sexual intercourse, the exertion associated with that, and the conversation associated with that.
What is the threefold worldly course?
It is as follows: conversing, chatting, and exchanging greetings; giving and taking in marriage; inviting and being invited; eating and sharing meals;
and providing mutual assistance whenever various affairs arise.
What are the three kinds of discourse?
They are: that which is in accordance with the Dharma, that which is not in accordance with the Dharma, and that which is other than these two.
What is discourse in accordance with the Dharma?
Whatever discourse is noble, conducive to seclusion, and dispels the hindrances of the mind—
as described in detail according to the sūtra—
[what is] unrighteous?
That which is discourse concerning alms-food and so forth for one with a defiled mind;
whereas for one with an indeterminate mind, it is discourse other than that.

There are twenty-two kinds of agitation (*saṃrambha*). What are they? They are as follows: cheating with weights, cheating with measures, cheating with scales; the practice of wrong occupations; quarreling, brawling, strife, dispute, reviling, angering, censuring, threatening, beating, and killing.
Binding, confinement, cutting, banishment, deceit, trickery, dishonesty, and false speech.
There are sixty-four classes of sentient beings.

Which are they? Namely: hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, humans; kṣatriyas, brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras; women, men, eunuchs; the lowly, the middling, the excellent; householders, and renunciants.

Those of difficult asceticism and those of easy asceticism; those possessing vows, those lacking vows, and those who are neither possessing nor lacking vows; those free from passion and those not free from passion; those fixed in the mass of falsehood, those fixed in the mass of correctness, and those fixed in the indeterminate mass; monks, nuns, female trainees, male novices, female novices, laymen, and laywomen; those engaged in abandonment, those engaged in recitation, and those engaged in service; elders, those of middle standing, and newcomers; preceptors, instructors, co-residents, and disciples.

There are those who are newcomers; those engaged in the affairs of the Saṅgha; those desiring gain; those who are honored; those engaged in the affairs of the Saṅgha and desiring gain; those desiring honor; those who are austere; those who are learned; those of renowned great merit; those who have entered the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma; those who uphold the Sūtras; those who uphold the Vinaya; those who uphold the Mātṛkās; ordinary worldlings; those who have seen the Truths; those in training (śaikṣas); those beyond training (aśaikṣas); disciples (śrāvakas); pratyekabuddhas; bodhisattvas; tathāgatas; and universal monarchs (cakravartins).
Furthermore, those wheel-turning monarchs are of four types: those who rule over one continent, those over two continents, those over three continents, and those over four continents.
Among them, for the ruler of one continent, an iron wheel appears;
for the ruler of two continents, one made of copper; for the ruler of three continents, one made of silver; and for the ruler of four continents, one made of gold.

There are eight stages. Which are they? They are as follows: the stage of the womb, the stage of birth, the stage of infancy, the stage of childhood, the stage of youth, the stage of middle age, the stage of old age, and the stage of decrepitude.
In that regard, the embryonic stage consists of the *kalala* and so forth; the postnatal stage follows thereafter. During the stages of infancy and old age, one is not capable of crawling or playing.
The stage of childhood pertains to one capable of that;
the stage of youth pertains to a thirty-year-old capable of enjoying sensual pleasures;
and the middle stage pertains to a fifty-year-old.
The stage of old age is at seventy years;
beyond that is the stage of decrepitude.
There are four modes of entry into the womb.
Which are they? They are as follows:
He enters with full awareness but remains and departs without full awareness;
he enters and remains with full awareness but departs without full awareness;
he enters, remains, and departs with full awareness.
One enters, stays, and exits without clear comprehension;
among these, the first pertains to a universal monarch (cakravartin),
and the second to a solitary buddha (pratyekabuddha).
The third belongs to the bodhisattva;
the fourth belongs to other sentient beings.

What are the six kinds of livelihood? They are as follows: agriculture, commerce, cattle-rearing, service to the king, and the practice of writing, calculation, counting, and sealing; as well as other various crafts.
What is the sixfold protection?
It is as follows: the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, the infantry, the power of stores, and the power of allies.
There are seven kinds of suffering. What are they?
Birth, aging, sickness, death, association with the unpleasant, separation from the pleasant, and the frustration of one's desires.
Pride is of seven kinds. Which are they?
Pride, excessive pride, and pride beyond pride;
The pride of "I am," the pride of overestimation,
the pride of underestimation, and false pride.
What is the sevenfold intoxication?
It is intoxication with health, intoxication with youth, intoxication with life, intoxication with noble lineage, intoxication with beauty, intoxication with power, and intoxication with learning.

What are the four modes of discourse? They are: discourse based on what has been seen, discourse based on what has been heard, discourse based on what has been thought, and discourse based on what has been cognized. What is discourse based on what has been seen?
Whatever has been directly perceived by him with his own eyes, and on the basis of that he engages in discourse with others—this is called "discourse based on what was seen."
What is conventional usage based on what has been heard? It is that which one employs in communication with others based on what has been heard from another.
What is conventional discourse based on what has been thought?
It is that which one communicates to others by taking as a basis something that has not been seen nor heard by oneself, but rather has been personally reflected upon, weighed, and examined.
What is the conventional expression based on what is known?
That which one expresses to others based on what has been internally experienced, attained, touched, and realized by oneself—this is called the conventional expression based on what is known.
What are the numerous bases of legal procedure?
They are also called the bases of etymological explanation;
"bases of conceptual proliferation" and "bases of the compendium of meanings" are their synonyms.
These syllables of the *mātṛkā* should be understood as a compendium of all meanings.

They are as follows: the stages (*bhūmi*), the faculties (*indriya*), the objects (*viṣaya*), phenomena (*dharma*), persons (*pudgala*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), distinctions (*viśeṣa*), activity (*kriyā*), self (*ātman*), other-existence (*parabhāva*), non-existence (*abhāva*), questioning (*pṛcchā*), answering (*visarjana*), giving (*dāna*), taking (*ādāna*), correctness (*samyaktva*), falsity (*mithyātva*), permission (*anujñā*), prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), virtues (*guṇa*), faults (*doṣa*), gain (*lābha*), loss (*alābha*), fame (*yaśas*), infamy (*ayaśas*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), blame (*nindā*), praise (*praśaṃsā*), the essential and the excellent (*sāravarajñāna*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), laziness (*ālasya*), measure (*mātrā*), showing the way (*saṃdarśana*), inciting (*samādāpana*), inspiring (*samuttejana*), and gladdening (*saṃpraharṣaṇa*).
There are seven bases of designation; these, moreover, are the seven case-inflections,
beginning with *puruṣaḥ*, *puruṣam*, *puruṣeṇa*, and so forth.

Designation, conceptualization, communication, comprehension, stability, establishment, accumulation, collection, determination, application, wonder, and so forth; the beginning, middle, and end; wholesome notions, assertions, conventional usage, performance, enjoyment, seeking, protection, shame, compassion, patience, fear, and discernment; parents, children, wife, and all such objects of possession and requisites—all these are to be described. Furthermore, birth, aging, up to the frustration of one's desires, sorrow, lamentation, youth, health, life, association with the beloved, and separation from the unpleasant.

The attainment of desires and their failure; advancing and retreating; looking ahead and looking aside; contracting and extending; walking, standing, sitting, lying down, waking, speaking, and remaining silent; the dispelling of drowsiness and fatigue; eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; practice and non-practice; negligence and non-negligence; the concise and the detailed; decrease and increase; applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*); the proliferation of afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the absence of such proliferation (*niṣprapañca*); strength and weakness; the feasible and the impossible; activity and restraint; application (*yoga*); speed; sequence; time; place; number; completeness and incompleteness; and similarity and dissimilarity.
Mixed, common, perceptible, imperceptible, concealed, and manifest;
cause and effect, discipline, worldly livelihood, requisites, truth and falsehood, benefit and harm... suspicion and curiosity;
timidity and confidence, the manifest and the unmanifest, killing, binding, imprisonment, mutilation, and banishment.
Abuse, anger, striking, threatening, reviling, burning, moistening, drying, fanning, crushing, turbidity, scripture, and inference.
This fivefold entity, beginning with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and ending with karma, should be understood as being subsumed under three bases:

the collection of form (*rūpasamudāya*), the complex of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitasikakalāpa*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is stated excluding other mentally designated phenomena (*prajñaptimanodharma*).
In that regard, first concerning the collection of form (*rūpasamudāya*), all phenomena arise from their own seeds.
How so?
It is said that form is born depending upon the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
And how is derived matter dependent upon them? It is established in them, supported by them, and augmented by them.
For it is thus:
The seeds of all internal and external primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) are established within the internal continuum of consciousness.
In that regard, the seed of derived matter first produces derived matter as long as the primary elements have not yet been produced by the seed of the primary elements.

Once the primary elements have arisen, that derived matter, arising from its own seed while depending upon those [elements], is said to be "born depending on them" (*tadupādāya jāta*), because its birth is preceded by that [dependence].
In this way, the primary elements become its producers.
How, then, does derived matter depend upon them? It is as follows:
Derived matter (upādāyarūpa) that has arisen functions without being separated from the location of the primary elements (bhūta). How is it established there?
Because it shares the same security and vulnerability as the primary elements—namely, the state of being benefited or harmed by them.
How is it supported?
By the non-perishing of that very [action]. How is it nourished?

Depending upon nutriment, or sleep, or the practice of celibacy, or meditative concentration, it undergoes further increase, growth, and expansion based on those; thus it is said to be "sustained by those. Furthermore, this fivefold activity of the great elements (mahābhūta) with respect to derived matter (upādāyarūpa) should be understood.
Furthermore, within an aggregate of form, an atom is never produced; rather,
when it is produced from its own seed, it is produced as an aggregate itself— whether minute, medium, or large.
Furthermore, an aggregate is not built up by atoms;
rather, an atom is designated through the conceptual delimitation of the limits of magnitude.
In that regard, the aggregate as well [is so designated].
It possesses spatial extension; even an atom (paramāṇu) possesses spatial extension. However, an aggregate (samudāya), being composed of parts, is not an atom.
For what reason?
Because the atom itself is a part,
and that exists only for a composite whole, not for the atom.
Furthermore, there are other atoms;
therefore, the atom is not composed of parts.

Non-separation is of two kinds: non-separation in terms of location, and non-separation in terms of being inseparable from a part. For example, there is non-separation in terms of location among the atoms of the primary elements (*bhūta-paramāṇu*)—namely, visible form, sound, odor, taste, and the tangible—whether they are without sense-faculties, devoid of sense-faculties, or possessed of sense-faculties; and there is non-separation in terms of being inseparable from a part when they possess sense-faculties.
Furthermore, there is no separation between their mingling because they occupy the same location;
for example,
[there is no separation] between that very atom of primary matter (*bhūta-paramāṇu*) and the other aggregate consisting of primary matter and derived matter (*bhautika*).

Furthermore, the blending of that entire collection of matter should be seen as an inseparable mixture, like water mixed with various powdered substances and stones, and not like a heap of sesame, mung beans, black gram, and horse gram.
Moreover, all derived matter (upādāyarūpa) rests precisely in the location of the primary elements (mahābhūta); it does not exist apart from the location of the primary elements.
To the extent that a space is occupied by the primary elements, to that same extent it is occupied by derived matter.
For this reason also, derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is said to be dependent upon the great elements (mahābhūta).
And for this very reason, the designation "great element" (mahābhūta) is applied to the [four] great elements;
it is called a "great element" because it has become great (mahatvena bhūtatvāt).
In brief, these constitute fourteen substances within the aggregate of matter (*rūpasamudāya*).

They are as follows: earth, water, fire, air; visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects; and the five sense organs, such as the eye, excluding the mental object (*manogocara*) which is matter itself.
In this context, every aggregate of matter comprised of the material sense organs consists of the elements and substances as they have been specified.
Just as it is with that which is comprised by the material sense-faculties, so too is that which is comprised by the primary elements that serve as the basis for the material sense-faculties.
However, the other aggregate, excluding the material sense-faculties, belongs to other realms.
In that regard, by way of the inclusion of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*), these consist of fourteen substances (*dravya*);
and it is precisely based on this inclusion of characteristics that the designation of a "substantial atom" (*dravyaparamāṇu*) is established.
Furthermore, by way of the inclusion of elements (*dhātusaṃgraha*), whatever aggregate consists of as many elements as it does, it should be stated to be comprised of that many substances.

Furthermore, regarding inclusion by way of inseparability (*avinirbhāga-saṃgraha*): it should be understood that a collection—whether internal or external—is comprised of as many substantial entities (*dravya*) as there are phenomena (*dharma*) perceived within it according to their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). For instance:
In some cases, only a single primary element is perceived within a composite aggregate.

For example: in stones, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, coral, and so forth; in springs, lakes, ponds, rivers, and streams; in flames, lamps, torches, and the like; and in the wind-circles of the east, south, west, and north, as well as in winds with dust and winds without dust.

In some cases, two [qualities] are perceived, such as in snow, moist tree leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth, or again, in heated gems and the like. In other cases, three [qualities] are perceived.
For example,
when those very trees and so forth are heated or again set in motion,
sometimes a tetrad is perceived.
For example, regarding internal collections of form,
as it was said by the Blessed One: "Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, beginning with head-hairs and ending with excrement— this is the internal earth element."
The water element consists of urine and so forth.
That by which this body is heated and thoroughly scorched, and through the excess of which one comes to be designated as "feverish," is the fire element.
Or, it is the air element because of its upward movement and so forth.
Thus, whatever is perceived here exists by virtue of its defining characteristic;
whatever is not perceived does not exist.
Sound exists within every collection of form by way of its constituent element.
Furthermore, in terms of its characteristics, it is sometimes produced through present application.
Wind is also of two kinds: that which is stable in its continuity and that which is unstable in its continuity.
Among these, that which is stable in its continuity is that which functions as a mechanism within various aggregates.
Furthermore, that which possesses a non-stationary continuity is of two kinds: that which moves within a circle and that which moves through the atmosphere.
In that regard, the nature of darkness and the nature of light are called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
Furthermore, that nature of darkness is stable within the intermediate spaces between worlds (*lokāntarikā*);
elsewhere, it is unstable.
Thus, light-form is stable among the self-luminous gods;
elsewhere it is unstable.
Furthermore, both that light and darkness should be understood as a collection in which color predominates.
And due to the efficacy of the seed of the aggregate of form residing within the mind, when both [conditions] are present, sometimes a large aggregate appears immediately after a minute aggregate,
and at other times, a minute aggregate appears immediately after a large one.
By means of which the decrease and increase of aggregates are discerned.
What is solidity?
It is earth. What is that which has reached the state of hardness?
That which is the seed is again solidity; that very element is what constitutes the state of hardness,
such as hair and so forth, or clods of earth and so forth.
What is "appropriated"? That which is internal and grasped.
What is that which has not been approached?
That which is external and non-appropriated.
Furthermore, that which has been approached by the mind and mental factors and has been appropriated as a characteristic is "approached";
by the opposite of this, it is "not approached" and "not appropriated. Furthermore, that which is "approached" is so called because of its approaching toward a self.
"Appropriated" is as explained previously.
In this same way, the water element and the others are to be understood according to their respective applications.
In every aggregate of form, the element of all the great elements (mahābhūta) exists at all times.
For example, it is seen that fire is produced from dry wood when it is rubbed;
likewise, fire is produced from stone; and likewise, liquidity arises in iron, silver, gold, and so forth, when they are intensely heated by fire.

Likewise, just as water emerges from a moonstone, so too do earth and other elements, as well as gold and other substances, manifest through the power of the mind's resolute intention (*adhimokṣa*) in one possessed of such supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
Furthermore, that collection of form proceeds by way of three streams: the accumulative (*aupacayika*), the outflowing (*naiṣyandika*), and that born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Among these, the accumulative is of two kinds: the accumulative that pervades space and the accumulative that nourishes the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The outflowing is fourfold:
outflowing by accumulation, outflowing as maturation, outflowing by transformation, and outflowing by nature.
The born of maturation is twofold: that which is born as maturation, and that which is born from maturation.
That which is born from maturation is "born of maturation" (vipākaja).
Furthermore, that collection of form, when summarized, functions by depending upon six bases:
the base of support, the base of abode, the base of requisites, the base of the seats of the faculties, the base of the faculties themselves, and the base of the range of meditative concentration.

In that collection of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitasika-kalāpa*), both the mind and the mental factors are perceived; specifically, fifty-three mental factors are perceived, such as those beginning with attention (*manaskāra*) and ending with initial and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), as previously specified.
Among these mental factors (*caitasikā dharmāḥ*), how many arise in every state of mind, across all levels, at all times, and in their entirety?
He said:
There are five [mental factors], beginning with attention and ending with volition.
How many of these arise everywhere—that is, in all stages—and yet do not arise at all times or in all instances?
There are only five, beginning with faith and ending with wisdom.
How many are exclusively wholesome and not present everywhere?
Rather, they exist on all stages, but not at all times, nor are all of them present simultaneously.
Those beginning with faith and ending with non-violence are not exclusively afflicted;
they do not exist everywhere, nor in all stages, nor at all times, nor are they all present simultaneously.
Those beginning with attachment and ending with lack of clear comprehension are [afflicted].
How many are present everywhere, yet not on all levels, not at all times, and not in their entirety?
They are those beginning with remorse and ending with investigation (*vicāra*).
In that case, the sense faculty is unimpaired,
the object has come into range,
and when the corresponding attention is present, the arising of consciousness occurs.
How does a faculty become unimpaired?
By two causes:
by way of non-destruction and by way of non-diminution.
How does an object come into range of appearance?

For example: by way of its basis, or by way of its intrinsic nature, or by way of place, or by way of time, or by way of being manifest or unmanifest, or by way of the whole of an entity or a single part of it.

If it is not obstructed by the four types of obstructions— namely, that which conceals, that which renders invisible, that which overpowers, and that which deludes— and is not remote due to the two kinds of remoteness, namely remoteness of place and remoteness of deficiency; [then it is perceived].
How does the manifestation of the mental attention born thereof occur?
It occurs through four causes:
by the power of aspiration, by the power of mindfulness, by the power of the object, and by the power of habituation.
How is it by the power of desire? Where there is attachment of the mind, there a greater degree of mental application arises.
How is it by the power of mindfulness?
Wherever the sign becomes more distinct and is more clearly visualized,
there a greater degree of mental application arises.
How [is it] by the power of the object?
Wherever an object that is more gross or more agreeable is present, there a greater degree of mental application arises.
How is it by the power of practice?
That which has become more familiar and more well-accustomed gives rise to a greater degree of mental application (*ābhoga*) toward it;
otherwise, there would be the constant arising of only a single type of mental attention (*manaskāra*) upon a single object.
Furthermore, there is no simultaneous arising of two moments of the five groups of consciousness, nor does one arise immediately after another.
Immediately following the five body-consciousnesses that have arisen in a single moment, mental consciousness necessarily arises;
after that, it may sometimes become distracted.
Then, either auditory consciousness or one or another of the five groups of sensory consciousnesses [arises];
if that is not distracted,
then it is certainly called mental consciousness.
And that object is conceptualized by those two mental consciousnesses, which function as both determinative and investigative.
In that regard, the arising of either afflicted or wholesome phenomena occurs through two causes:
through conceptualization and through prior impulsion.
In this case, it occurs through both causes within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Furthermore, regarding the five groups of sensory consciousness, the arising of afflicted or wholesome states in the immediately subsequent visual and other sensory consciousnesses occurs solely through the prior impelling force (*pūrvāvedha*) of an afflicted or wholesome mental consciousness; it does not arise from conceptualization,
because those [sensory consciousnesses] are non-conceptual.
For this very reason, it is said that the visual consciousnesses and the others are followers of the mental consciousness.
Regarding what is said— that there is a single mind and subsequent consciousnesses—
how is the determination of a single mind established?
It is by way of a conventional moment of mind, and not by way of a moment of actual occurrence.
What is the conventional single mind?
It is that which, based on a single word, arises as a cognition with respect to a single object for such a duration of time;
and even that which continues in a similar flow is also said to be one.
But the second is dissimilar to that.
In that case, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is distracted without effort toward an unfamiliar object, there is no activity of desire and the other [mental factors].
And that mental consciousness should be described as occurring spontaneously, having only a past object.
The mind that arises immediately after the five groups of consciousness—whether it be investigative or determinative—must be said to have only a present object;
and if it occurs, it does so by taking that very object as its focal point.
In that regard, one makes known the entire characteristic of an object through consciousness;
that very same [object], when not yet made known, is called the "characteristic of the cognizable," which is made known by attention (*manaskāra*).

In that very same [object], that which has the characteristic of being pleasant, unpleasant, or the opposite of both is apprehended by contact (*sparśa*). In that very same [object], that which has the characteristic of being beneficial, harmful, or the opposite of both is apprehended by feeling (*vedanā*).
In that very same [object], that which has the characteristic of being the basis for conventional expression is apprehended by perception (*saṃjñā*).
In that very context, that which is characterized by right, wrong, both, or neither (i.e., contrary) practice is undertaken through volition (*cetanā*).
Therefore, these mental factors (*caitasika*), beginning with attention (*manaskāra*) and ending with volition (*cetanā*), arise everywhere, on all levels, at all times, and in their entirety.
What is attention? It is the mental engagement of the mind.
What is contact?
It is the coming together of the three.
What is feeling? It is experience.
What is perception?
It is the act of perceiving.
What is volition?
It is the mental formation.
What is desire (*chanda*)?
It is the wish to act with regard to a desired object, following after that [object] here and there.
What is resolve?
It is the capacity for ascertainment regarding a determined object, following after that [object] in each respective case.
What is mindfulness? It is the mental verbalization that follows after this or that familiar object.
What is concentration?
It is one-pointedness of mind based on sustained reflection that conforms to the object under investigation, in each respective case.
What is wisdom?

It is the discernment of phenomena with respect to each object to be examined, following after that [object], whether it is conducted through yoga, not conducted through yoga, or neither conducted through yoga nor not conducted through yoga.
In that regard, what is the function of attention?
Its function is the avoidance of mental distraction.
What is the function of contact?
Its function is to provide a basis for feeling, perception, and volition.
What is the function of feeling?
Its function is the arising of craving and equanimity.
What is the function of perception (*saṃjñā*)? Its function is to mentally differentiate (*citrīkāra*) the object and to engage in conventional expression (*vyavahāra*).
What is the function of volition?
Its function is to originate applied thought, bodily and vocal actions, and so forth.
What is the function of desire?
Its function is to generate the undertaking of vigor.
What is the function of resolve?
Its function is the stabilization of the object of focus, whether by way of its qualities, its defects, or neither.
What is the function of mindfulness?
Its function is the recollection and constant recollection of what was long ago thought, done, or spoken.
What is the function of concentration?
Its function is to provide a basis for knowledge.
What is the function of wisdom?
Its function is to investigate in a manner conducive to the cessation of conceptual proliferation and to the purification of afflictions.
In that regard, how is the establishment of the three time periods (adhvan) effected?

First, as for seeds, because they are not distinct from their dharmas, their establishment is like the establishment of those dharmas, by way of having already yielded fruit or not yet having yielded fruit.
Furthermore, as for fruits, that which has the characteristic of having ceased is the past.
When the cause exists, that which has the characteristic of being unarisen is the future;
that which has the characteristic of having arisen but not yet ceased is the present.
How is there the establishment of birth, aging, duration, and impermanence?
In every continuum of consciousness, the entire continuum of seeds is established as co-existent when the conditions are present.
By the power of those conditions, that phenomenon which has never previously arisen within the continuum first arises; this is called "birth," a characteristic of the conditioned.
Aging is the alteration of that very same thing.
Furthermore, that is twofold: alteration as difference and alteration as change.
Among these, when there is the arising of something similar, it is alteration as difference.
When there is an arising of something dissimilar, there is alteration and change of state.
For that which has just arisen, "duration" is the persistence for the mere moment of its birth;
"impermanence" is the non-persistence beyond the moment of birth.
These very [characteristics] constitute the four characteristics of that same phenomenon (dharma) through the differentiation of its states.
There are four conditions:
the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Among these, the seed is the causal condition.

The immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is that consciousness after which there is a fixed rule for the arising of subsequent consciousnesses; it is the condition for those [subsequent] consciousnesses. The object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) is the objective support (*ālambana*) of those mental states and mental factors (*cittacaitasika-dharma*).
The dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) is the basis (*āśraya*) excluding the seed (*bīja*).
For example: for visual consciousness, it is the eye and those factors that are its companions;
likewise for the remaining consciousnesses.
And those [factors] which, being wholesome or unwholesome, lead to the acquisition of desired or undesired fruits—
such as these are dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
In this regard, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is established by way of the seed;

the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) by way of intrinsic nature; the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) by way of that very [nature]; and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) by way of the basis, the companions, and so forth.
Regarding what was said— that "those which are causes and those which are conditions for the arising of consciousness"—
among those very four, one [factor] is both a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*),
being both a cause and a condition.
The remaining ones are indeed conditions.
Regarding what was stated—that there are the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate—what is their distinction? The wholesome is of one kind in the sense of being irreproachable;
it is of two kinds: that acquired at birth and that acquired through application.
It is threefold by way of intrinsic nature, association, and origination;
fourfold as pertaining to merit, pertaining to liberation, pertaining to penetration, and being untainted;
and fivefold as consisting of giving, consisting of ethical discipline, consisting of cultivation, having a desirable fruit, and having the fruit of dissociation.

Wholesome form is sixfold: feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, analytical cessation, and [wholesome] unmanifest form. It is sevenfold when comprised of the foundations of mindfulness, and comprised of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the factors of the path. It is eightfold when comprised of acts of salutation, prostration, rising to greet, and joining the palms; comprised of giving praise for well-spoken words, uttering true eulogies, attending to the sick, and [serving] one's teachers.

It is comprised of service performed with reverence; it is comprised of rejoicing; it is comprised of exhorting others; it is comprised of dedication; and it is comprised of the cultivation of the immeasurables. It is ninefold, being comprised of the paths of preparation, uninterrupted transition, liberation, and excellence; and it is comprised of the weak, medium, and intense mundane and supramundane paths. It is tenfold: that which is based on material things and that which is not based on material things; that consisting of hearing, that consisting of reflection, that comprised of restraint, that comprised of neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint, that comprised of the fundamental and the preparatory stages, and that comprised of the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
It is comprised within the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas and the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, it is of ten kinds: that associated with the desire realm; that associated with the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas; that associated with the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and that which is comprised within the untainted (anāsrava).
Furthermore, it is tenfold: the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*).
Furthermore, it is tenfold: the ten factors of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), from right view up to right liberation and right knowledge.

Furthermore, it is tenfold: the wholesome [karma] conducive to rebirth in the eight meritorious states, that which leads to becoming a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), and that which leads to the imperturbable (*āniñjya*); such are the divisions of the wholesome.
In brief, the meaning of "wholesome" (*kuśala*) is twofold: the pursuit of desirable fruits, and skill in the thorough knowledge of things (*vastu*) together with their results.

Conversely, that which is unwholesome (*akuśala*) is the opposite of wholesome qualities and constitutes an obscuration; this is because it pursues undesirable fruits and because it involves an incorrect thorough knowledge of things.
Furthermore, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is of four kinds:

that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*), that which pertains to postures (*airyāpathika*), that which pertains to crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and that which pertains to emanations (*nairmāṇika*).

Whatever craft one performs for the sake of pleasure or play, neither for the sake of a livelihood nor with the notion of it being work nor through deliberate reflection—that is the indeterminate pertaining to crafts; any other [craft] is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
Just as it is with that which pertains to the arts, so it is with that pertaining to postures and that pertaining to emanations; these are both wholesome and indeterminate.
The eye is of one kind for the seeing of forms;
it is of two kinds: that which is derived from nourishment (*aupacayika*) and that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*);
it is of three kinds: the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*).
It is fourfold: with eyes that blink, with eyes that do not blink, stationary, and non-stationary.
Among these, the stationary belongs to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) and is fivefold, being comprised within the five destinies (*pañcagati*);
it is also sixfold.
It pertains to one's own continuum or another's continuum; it is handsome or ugly, stained or stainless.
It is sevenfold: with consciousness or without consciousness, strong or weak, based on wholesome consciousness, based on unwholesome consciousness, or based on neutral consciousness.

It is eightfold: the physical eye, the divine eye, the eye born as the maturation of wholesome karma, the eye born as the maturation of unwholesome karma, the eye accumulated through food, the eye accumulated through sleep, the eye accumulated through celibacy, and the eye accumulated through meditative attainment.

There are nine kinds: that which is acquired, that which is not acquired, that which was previously acquired, that which was previously not acquired, that which was acquired and then lost, that which is to be abandoned, that which is not to be abandoned, that which has been abandoned, and that which has not been abandoned.
There are no ten kinds.
There are eleven kinds: past, future, present, internal, external, gross, subtle, inferior, superior, distant, and near.
In this way, the ear and so forth, up to the body, are each threefold;
however, there is a distinction in the case of the fourfold [classification].
The ear is threefold: that which is composed of flesh, the divine, and the applied (āvahita).
It is fourfold: stable, unstable, high-pitched like Uccaiḥśravas, and not high-pitched like Uccaiḥśravas.
It is threefold: the nose, the tongue, and that which is luminous, non-luminous, and impaired.
The nose and the tongue are each fourfold:
stable, unstable, with consciousness, and without consciousness.
The body is threefold.
It is fourfold: abiding in dross, not abiding in dross, all-pervading because it accompanies all the sense-faculties,
and stable or unstable, and self-luminous or non-self-luminous.
The mind is of one kind in the sense that it cognizes phenomena;
it is of two kinds: that which falls within the realm of designation and that which does not fall within the realm of designation.
Of these, the former belongs to those whose linguistic conventions are fully developed, and the latter to infants.
Another formulation:
mundane and supramundane;
the threefold mind consists of the mental faculty (manas) and consciousness (vijñāna).
It is fourfold: wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified.
It is fivefold according to the distinction of five states:
the state of cause, the state of fruit, the state of pleasure, the state of suffering, and the state of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
It is sixfold as the six groups of consciousness;
it is sevenfold as existing in the seven stations of consciousness;
it is eightfold as associated with designation-contact, associated with resistance-contact, based on craving, based on renunciation, worldly, unworldly, mundane, and supramundane.
It is ninefold in the nine abodes of sentient beings;
it does not exist as tenfold.
The elevenfold [classification] is as before.
The twelvefold [classification] consists of the twelve types of consciousness:
those of the desire realm that are wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified.
Excluding the three types of unwholesome [states] belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*),
it is likewise for those belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*),
as well as for the supramundane (*lokottara*) states of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Form is of one kind in the sense of being the object of the eye;
it is of two kinds, internal and external;
and it is of three kinds: color, shape, and intimation.
It is fourfold: appearing as a support, appearing as non-support, appearing as pleasure or pain, and existing as an accumulation.
It is fivefold according to the division of the five destinies.

It is sixfold: comprised of the foundation, comprised of the dwelling, comprised of the objects, comprised of what is reckoned as sentient beings, comprised of what is not reckoned as sentient beings, and that which is with discernment and with resistance.
It is sevenfold due to the distinction of seven types of grasping.

It is eightfold with respect to the eight varieties of the world: namely, the variety of ground portions, the variety of mountains, the variety of gardens, groves, lakes, ponds, and so forth; the variety of houses and celestial palaces; the variety of workshops; the variety of paintings; the variety of mosaic work; and the variety of utensils.
It is ninefold: past, future, present, gross, subtle, inferior, superior, distant, or near.
It is tenfold: the ten requisites.
Sound is of one kind by virtue of being the object of the auditory faculty.
It is of two kinds: that which is an articulate sound with a manifest meaning, and that which is an inarticulate sound with an unmanifest meaning.
It is of three kinds: that caused by appropriated primary elements, that caused by non-appropriated primary elements, and that caused by both types of primary elements.
It is fourfold: wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified.
It is fivefold according to the division of the five destinies.

There are six kinds of sounds: the sound of instruction and recitation, the sound of inquiry and counter-inquiry, the sound of the teaching of the Dharma, the sound of definitive discussion, the sound of mutual speech, censure, offenses, and rehabilitation, and the sound of confused clamor.
There are seven kinds of sounds: the sound of women, the sound of men, soft, medium, and intense sounds, the sounds of wild animals, birds, and so forth, and the sounds of wind and trees.
It is eightfold: the four noble modes of discourse and the four ignoble modes of discourse.
To claim to have seen what was not seen, and to claim not to have seen what was seen, is an ignoble mode of discourse.
[Likewise] regarding what was not heard, not thought, and not known...
To claim to have known what was not known, or to claim not to have known what was known, is ignoble conventional usage.
To speak of what was seen as seen, and of what was not seen as not seen, is noble conventional usage.
To speak of what was heard, thought, or cognized as cognized, and of what was not cognized as not cognized, is noble conventional usage.
Furthermore, there are eight wholesome [paths of action] and four unwholesome paths of vocal action;
ninefold, categorized as past, future, and present, up to distant and near;
and tenfold, comprised within the five-fold musical ensemble.
Furthermore, it was accompanied by dancing, singing, and instrumental music; it was accompanied by women and men;
and there were the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, drums, clay drums, and cymbals.
Odor is of one kind in the sense that it is the objective domain of the nose;
it is of two kinds, internal and external;
it is of three kinds: agreeable, disagreeable, and neutral.
And there is that which is the basis for equanimity.
There are four kinds of great fragrances: the fragrance of agarwood, the fragrance of turuṣka resin, the fragrance of camphor, and the fragrance of musk.
There are five kinds of fragrances: root-fragrance, heartwood-fragrance, leaf-fragrance, flower-fragrance, and fruit-fragrance.
There are six kinds of fragrance: the fragrance of food, the fragrance of drink, the fragrance of clothing, the fragrance of ornaments, the fragrance of vehicles, and the fragrance of dwellings.

There are seven kinds of fragrance: the fragrance of bark, the fragrance of leaves, the fragrance of cardamom, the fragrance of sandalwood, the fragrance of the three pungents, the fragrance of incense, and the fragrance of aromatic powder.
It is of eight kinds: innate, non-innate, stable, unstable, conjoined, isolated, intense, and mild.
It is ninefold: past, future, present, and so on, up to distant and near.

It is tenfold: the odor of women, the odor of men, the odor of excrement, the odor of urine, the odor of saliva, the odor of nasal mucus, the odor of fat, lymph, pus, and blood, the odor of flesh, and the odor of mixed filth and mire.
Taste is of one kind in the sense that it is the object of the tongue.
It is of two kinds: internal and external.
It is of three kinds—agreeable, disagreeable, and so forth—as previously described.
There are four kinds of grain juices: barley juice, rice juice, wheat juice, and the juice of inferior grains.
There are five kinds of juice for drinking: alcoholic juice, non-alcoholic juice, vegetable leaf juice, forest fruit juice, and edible food juice.
The sixfold [taste] consists of bitter and the others.
The sevenfold [taste] consists of the juices of ghee, oil, honey, sugarcane products, cow's milk, salt, and meat.
The eightfold [taste] is like that of fragrance.
The ninefold [category] is like that of odor.

The tenfold [category] consists of the taste of food, the taste of drink, the taste of what is to be relished, the taste of what is to be sucked, the medicinal taste that is refining, the medicinal taste that is nourishing, the medicinal taste that is pacifying, the medicinal taste that is purifying, and the medicinal taste that is habitually used.
Tangible objects are of one kind in the sense of being the domain of the body;
they are of two kinds like odors;
and they are of three kinds, such as the agreeable and so forth.
Tangible contact is of four kinds: the contact of touching, the contact of pressing, the contact of striking, and the contact of rubbing.
It is of five kinds according to the distinction of the five destinies (*gati*).
Furthermore, there is contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping reptiles;
it is sixfold: pleasant, painful, neither-painful-nor-pleasant, innate, comprised within the adverse side, and comprised within the remedial side.
It is of seven kinds:
hardness, fluidity, heat, the contact of leaping and falling, the contact of stroking, and the contact of bodily transformation;
for example, smoothness and so forth.

The tactile contact is eightfold: contact with the hand, contact with a clod of earth, contact with a staff, contact with a weapon, contact with cold, contact with heat, contact with hunger, and contact with thirst.
It is ninefold like the [nine types of] odor.
The tactile contact is tenfold: contact with food, contact with drink, contact with clothing, and contact with ornaments.
There is the contact with beds and chairs; the contact with cushions, pillows, and bolsters; the contact with women; the contact with men; and the contact with their service and enjoyment.
In brief, the dharma-realm consists of eighty-seven dharmas, together with the dharmas of designation.
Which, then, are these?
They are the fifty-three mental factors beginning with attention and ending with applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).

[It includes] matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), matter comprised of restraint and non-restraint, and matter that is the domain of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It also includes acquisition (*prāpti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), and matter that is the domain of meditative concentration; the attainment of non-perception, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the state of being without perception (*āsaṃjñika*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character of a group (*nikāyasabhāga*), the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), birth, aging, duration, impermanence, the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), the sets of phrases (*padakāya*), and the sets of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*); as well as activity, determination, conjunction, and velocity.

Sequence, time, place, number, completeness, and incompleteness—these are the eight unconditioned entities (*asaṃskṛta-vastu*). They are: space, non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the suchness (*tathatā*) of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena, the immovable (*aniñja*), and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).
These eight, when considered as equal, become six; and these six, when considered as equal, become eight.
Furthermore, that [dharmadhātu] is of one kind in the sense of being the objective domain of the mind;
it is of two kinds:
that which is comprised within designated phenomena (*prajñaptidharma*) and that which is comprised within non-designated phenomena (*aprajñaptidharma*).
It is threefold: material, immaterial, and conditioned as well as unconditioned.

The fourfold [classification] consists of: that which is material and included among designated phenomena; that which is immaterial and included among mental phenomena; that which is immaterial and included among designations for dissociated factors; and that which is immaterial and included among designations for unconditioned phenomena.
It is fivefold: form, mental factors, phenomena dissociated from mind, the unconditioned, and that which is unwholesome or indeterminate.
It is of six kinds: feeling, perception, formations—both associated and dissociated—form, and the unconditioned.
The sevenfold [unconditioned] consists of feeling, perception, volition, the afflicted, the non-afflicted, form, and the unconditioned.
It is eightfold: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; volition, perception, mental formations, form, and the unconditioned.
It is ninefold through the distinctions of past, future, and so forth.

It is tenfold by way of ten meanings: by way of the meaning of the arising of a consequence; by way of the meaning of experiencing the object; by way of the meaning of grasping the signs of the object; by way of the meaning of the formative activity regarding the object; by way of the meaning of the differentiation of the states of those very phenomena; by way of the meaning of dissociation from the impermanent; by way of the meaning of dissociation from the permanent; by way of the meaning of the non-distortion of the permanent; by way of the meaning of dissociation from pleasure and pain, but not by way of dissociation from feeling, and [also] by way of dissociation from feeling.
These are the six hundred and sixty-sixfold divisions of the internal and external sense bases.
It moves therein; it moves for the sake of seeing inexhaustible forms—thus it is the eye (*cakṣus*).
Sounds are perceived here—thus it is the ear (*śrotra*). It smells odors—thus it is the nose (*ghrāṇa*).
It is called the *jihvā* because it dispels hunger and weakness and issues invitations through familiarity with various forms of speech.

It is called the *kāya* because this body follows the functions of the sense-faculties in their entirety. For a long night, this has been cherished and claimed as "mine" by the foolish, thinking, "This is mine; this is I."
"This is my self.
And in this regard, the world’s designations are: a being, a person, a soul, a creature, a human, a man, and a mind.

Because it is perceived in various places and because it grows, it is called "rūpa" (form); because one speaks while speaking it, and because one recites while reciting it, it is called "śabda" (sound);
because knowledge and discourses rest upon it, it is called "śabda";
and because it goes and runs with the wind, it is called "gandha" (odor).
Because it accumulates diseases and is to be consumed, it is "taste" (*rasa*).
Because it is touched by the body, it is "the tangible" (*spraṣṭavya*).
Because it maintains the state of being an object solely for the mind, it is "phenomenon" (*dharma*). Such are the categories [of the sense objects].

The differentiation of these phenomena (dharmas) should be understood. Regarding this, there is a summary verse: "By way of intrinsic nature, basis, object, assistance, and function, the activity of the mind occurs through five gateways. In this context, it should be understood that skill in the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*) is subsumed by these five factors—belonging to the six groups of consciousness—by way of their intrinsic nature, basis, object, assistance, and function.

Likewise, skill in the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*), skill in the sense-fields (*āyatana-kauśalya*), skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*), and skill in what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*) and skill in the faculties (*indriya-kauśalya*) should also be understood.
It should be understood that the word of the Buddha is also comprised within nine topics.

What are the nine topics? They are: the topic of sentient beings, the topic of enjoyment, the topic of arising, the topic of duration, the topic of affliction and purification, the topic of diversity, the topic of the teacher, the topic of what is taught, and the topic of the assembly.
In this context, the entity of sentient beings consists of the five aggregates of clinging;
the entity of their enjoyment consists of the twelve bases;
and the entity of their arising consists of the twelve-linked dependent origination.
The basis for the persistence of what has arisen consists of the four nutriments;
the basis for affliction and purification consists of the four noble truths;
and the bases for diversity consist of the immeasurable realms.
The entities that are teachers are the Buddhas and their disciples;
the entities that are the teachings are the factors conducive to enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness;
and the entities that are the assemblies are the eight assemblies.
The assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of brahmins, and the assembly of householders.
The assembly of ascetics,
the assembly of the gods of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of brahmins.
This is the summary verse (uddāna).
The aggregate, the collection, the paths, the characteristics, and the conditions;
the classification into wholesome and so forth, and finally, the basis of skillfulness.
The second level, the Mind Level (*manobhūmi*), within the *Yogācārabhūmi*, is completed.
The third stage is that which is without applied thought and possesses only sustained thought; the fourth stage is that which is without applied thought and without sustained thought;
and the fifth stage is likewise without applied thought and without sustained thought.
What is the stage with applied thought and sustained thought?
What is the stage without applied thought and with sustained thought only?
What is the stage without applied thought and sustained thought?
The summary verse:
The elements, characteristics, and the proper method; the improper method, and finally, the afflictions.
Thus, regarding these three stages, there is also [distinction] by way of the establishment of the designation of elements (*dhātu*),
by way of the establishment of the designation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),
and by way of the establishment of the designation of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśomanaskāra*).

The establishment [of this teaching] should be understood also from the perspective of the designation and systematic arrangement of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśomanaskāra*), and [also] from the perspective of the designation and systematic arrangement of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
The summary: enumeration, location, measure, lifespan, and the nature of enjoyment;
birth, the physical body, and the detailed exposition of causes and conditions.
What is the formal establishment of the designation of the elements (*dhātu*)?
It should be understood as having eight aspects,
including the establishment by way of number.
Also by way of the arrangement of different locations, by way of the arrangement of the measure of those very sentient beings,
and by way of the arrangement of the lifespan of those very sentient beings.
It is also [to be understood] through the determination of the enjoyment and utilization of those very beings, through the determination of their arising,
through the determination of their personal existence, and through the determination of their causes and conditions.
In this regard, the determination of their number is as follows:
there are three realms—the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
These are the included realms.
And that cessation of the view of a self-identity, which is unconditioned, accompanied by skillful means, and the untainted realm,
is free from conceptual proliferation.

In that regard, throughout the entire realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), within the first dhyāna—excluding the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) pertaining to meditative attainment and rebirth—the stage is characterized by both applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*).

The intermediate dhyāna, both in terms of meditative attainment and rebirth, is a stage characterized solely by the absence of applied thought and the presence of sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāramātra*);
by cultivating this, a certain individual attains the state of Mahābrahmā.

The remaining portion of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) starting from the second dhyāna, as well as the entire formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), constitute the stage without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ*).
In that context, it is called the stage without applied and sustained thought by virtue of being free from passion for applied and sustained thought;
it is not, however, because they do not manifest at all.
For instance,

even for one who has not yet abandoned desire for the objects of sensual pleasure (*kāma*), there may at times occur a movement of the mind free from applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra*) due to a specific mental attention (*manaskāra*) based on instruction; and even for one who has abandoned desire for them, there may occur the active manifestation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarkavicārasamudācāra*) despite being free from [desire for] them.
That is to say,

for those who have emerged [from meditative attainment] and for those reborn there, that which is the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu) consisting of conditioned states (saṃskṛta) included within meditative attainment (samāpatti).
Therein, the first dhyāna is the stage characterized by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

This is because one takes suchness as the object of focus regarding those phenomena that serve as the basis for applied and sustained thought, through the attainment thereof, and not through the movement of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
The remainder is as previously stated.
[The desire realm:
In this regard, the arrangement of its distinct locations is as follows:
the desire realm consists of thirty-six distinct locations.
There are eight locations of the great hells,
namely: Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṅghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Mahātāpana, and Avīci.
Ten thousand yojanas beyond those very great hells, at a distance of ten thousand yojanas to the side, lie eight locations for cold hells,
namely: Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma.
Thirty-two thousand *yojanas* from here is Saṃjīva; beyond that, the others are to be understood as being separated by intervals of four thousand *yojanas*.
Just as the location of the great hell Saṃjīva is, so too is the location of the first cold hell.
Beyond that, the others are to be understood as being separated by intervals of two thousand *yojanas*.
The realm of hungry ghosts is distinct from the realm of asuras;
however, animals, gods, and humans are merely co-residents [of other realms].
Therefore, no separate distinct realm is established for them.
The four continents are as previously described. There are eight intermediate islands.

There are six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm: the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.
Furthermore, the realm of Māra is included within the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods and is not a distinct location.

The individual hells (*pratyekanaraka*) and the neighboring hells (*sāmantanaraka*) are merely situated around the great hells and the cold hells, and are not distinct locations; they are even found among humans. Some of these are individual hells, as described by the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "I see a being aflame, blazing, burning intensely, become a single mass of fire," and so forth.
Thus, these thirty-six distinct locations are called the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The form realm (*rūpadhātu*) consists of eighteen distinct locations.

The Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā deities [arise] from the first dhyāna being cultivated in its weak, medium, and intense degrees; the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara deities [arise] from the second dhyāna being cultivated in its weak, medium, and intense degrees;
and the Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna deities [arise] from the third dhyāna being cultivated in its weak, medium, and intense degrees.

The Anabhrakas, Puṇyaprasavas, and Bṛhatphalas [are so named] because of the cultivation of the fourth dhyāna in its weak, medium, and superior degrees. The state of non-perception (asaṃjñika) is not a separate location distinct from the Bṛhatphala realm, as it is included within it; furthermore, it is not shared by the Noble Ones (āryas). There are five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsabhūmis): the Abṛhas, Atapas, Sudṛśas, Sudarśanas, and Akaniṣṭhas, which result from the cultivation of the mixed dhyāna in its progressively weaker, medium, superior, more superior, and most superior degrees.

Beyond the fourth dhyāna and transcending the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa), there is the station of Maheśvara, where Bodhisattvas established on the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are born, having been fully cultivated by the tenth stage.
[The formless realm:
The formless realm consists of four stations;
or rather, it does not consist of any distinct location at all.
[The Determination of the Measure of Sentient Beings] In this regard, this is the determination of the measure of sentient beings:
first, for the humans of Jambudvīpa, the measure of the physical basis is indefinite.
At one time it is large, and at another time it is minute;
furthermore, its own hand measures three and a half [yojanas].
Those born in Pūrvavideha have a fixed bodily stature.
They too, with their own hands, are three and a half cubits in height and possess even larger bodies;
just as it is for those of Pūrvavideha, so it is for those of Avaragodānīya and Uttarakuru—they are of even greater stature.
The measurement for the gods of the Four Great Kings is one-quarter of a *krośa*; for the Trāyastriṃśa gods, it is slightly more than a quarter of a *krośa*;
for Śakra, the lord of the gods, it is half a *krośa*; and for the Yāma gods, it is half a *krośa*.
Beyond that, in all other classes of gods, the measurement should be understood to increase by one-quarter *yojana* at each stage:
for the Brahmakāyikas it is half a *yojana*,
and for the Brahmapurohitas it is one *yojana*.
The body size of the Mahābrahmās is two and a half yojanas; that of the Parīttābhas is two yojanas.

Beyond that, for the remaining classes of gods, the measurement of the physical support should be understood as doubling at each stage, with the exception of the Anabhrakas. In that case, however, three yojanas must be subtracted from the calculation.
Regarding the fixed dimensions in the great hells:
for one who has committed and accumulated particularly intense evil and unwholesome karma, a correspondingly larger physical basis is produced;
for others, however, it is otherwise.
Just as it is in the great hells, so it is in the cold hells, the individual hells, and the neighboring hells, as well as among animals and hungry ghosts.
Regarding the asuras, their establishment of physical basis (*āśraya*) should be understood to be like the establishment of the Trayastriṃśa gods.
Furthermore, in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), because they are formless, there is no measurement of size.
[The determination of the lifespan of sentient beings:
In this regard, this is the determination of lifespan.
For the humans of Jambudvīpa, with a month consisting of thirty nights and a year consisting of twelve months, the measure of lifespan is indefinite.
At one time their lifespan is of limited measure; at another time it is eighty thousand years;
and at another time it lasts for as little as ten years.
For the inhabitants of Pūrvavideha, however, the lifespan is fixed at two hundred and fifty years.
The lifespan of those in Aparagodānīya is five hundred years;
the lifespan of those in Uttarakuru is one thousand years.
Furthermore, what constitutes fifty years for humans is a single day and night for the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm.
By that night-and-day reckoning, with thirty such nights making a month and twelve months making a year, the lifespan of the gods is five hundred divine years.
Indeed, one hundred human years constitute a single night-and-day for the Trāyastriṃśa gods;
by that night-and-day reckoning, thirty such days make a month, and so on as before, up to a divine year.
In the other classes of gods, their lifespan increases by double that amount for each successive day and night, continuing up to the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.
Whatever constitutes the full lifespan of the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings is a single day and night in the great Sañjīva hell.
With that day and night, thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year; by this reckoning, the lifespan of the denizens of that hell is five hundred years.

Just as the lifespan of those born in the great Sañjīva hell is measured by the lifespan of the gods of the Four Great Kings, so too is the lifespan of those born in the Kālasūtra hell measured by the lifespan of the Trayastriṃśa gods.

The lifespan of those born in the Saṅghāta hell is equal to the lifespan of the Yāma gods; the lifespan of those born in the Raurava hell is equal to the lifespan of the Tuṣita gods; and the lifespan of those born in the Tapana hell is to be understood as equal to the lifespan of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.
The lifespan of beings born in the Pratāpana hell is half an intermediate kalpa;
the lifespan of beings in the Avīci hell is one intermediate kalpa.
As it is for the Trayastriṃśa gods, so it is for the asuras; the lifespan of animals and hungry ghosts is indefinite.
The lifespan of beings born in the cold hells should be understood as being half that of the beings born in each successive great hell.
For beings born in the individual hells (*pratyekanaraka*), the lifespan is also indefinite.
For beings belonging to the Brahma-realm (*brahmakāyika*), the lifespan is one *kalpa*, where a *kalpa* consists of twenty intermediate *kalpas*.
The lifespan of the beings of the Brahmā-purohita heaven is one kalpa, measured by forty intermediate kalpas.
The lifespan of the Mahābrahmā heaven is one kalpa, measured by sixty intermediate kalpas.
The lifespan of the Parīttābha heaven is two kalpas, measured by eighty intermediate kalpas.

Beyond that, in the other classes of gods, one should establish a lifespan that is double and then double again, with the exception of the Anabhrakas; however, for those three [classes], a lifespan of three *kalpas* should be established. For sentient beings born in the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the lifespan is twenty thousand *kalpas*.
The lifespan of beings born in the sphere of infinite consciousness is forty thousand eons; for those born in the sphere of nothingness, it is sixty thousand eons;
and for those born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the lifespan is eighty thousand eons.
Setting aside the inhabitants of Uttarakuru,
among humans, animals, and hungry ghosts (pretas), there are bodies of residue that remain after death;
however, among the gods and in the hells, non-residual bodies remain together with consciousness itself.
[The establishment of the experience and enjoyment: therein, the establishment of the experience and enjoyment consists in the experiencing of pleasure and pain as well.
Also from the enjoyment of food,
and also from the enjoyment of sexual intercourse.
In those hells, for the most part, sentient beings experience the suffering of being tormented; among animals, the suffering of devouring one another;
among hungry ghosts, the suffering of hunger and thirst;
and among humans, the suffering of the misfortune of seeking.
Among the gods, they experience the suffering associated with falling and passing away.
There, in the great hell Sañjīva, they predominantly experience such forms of suffering through torture.

There, those beings, having come together, engage in mutual slaughter with various weapons produced by the sovereign power of their karma that arise in succession; then, rendered motionless, they fall prostrate upon the ground.
Then a voice issues from the sky, saying, "Alas, let the beings come back to life!
Thereupon, those beings rise up again and once more engage in mutual slaughter in that very same manner;
on account of that, they experience suffering for a long time until that sinful, unwholesome karma is entirely exhausted and brought to an end.
And for that reason, moreover, that hell is called Sañjīva.
In that very Great Hell of Kālasūtra, beings for the most part experience such torturous suffering.
There, those beings are measured with black thread by the executioners belonging to that place;
they are measured as squares, as octagons, and in many various kinds of divisions.
Once they have been measured out, they are likewise dug, carved, and thoroughly hewn;
on account of that, they experience suffering for a long time until that evil, unwholesome karma is entirely exhausted and brought to an end.
For this reason, moreover, that hell is called Kālasūtra (Black Line).
In that great hell of Saṅghāta, beings for the most part experience such forms of suffering caused by torture.

When those beings have been gathered together into one mass and have reached a state of total compression, they are then made to enter a gap between two great iron mountains with the faces of goats by the executioners belonging to that place.
As soon as they have entered, they are crushed by those two mountains.
As they are being crushed, rivers of blood flow and pour forth from all sides.
This occurs with those having the faces of goats, as well as those with the faces of rams, horses, elephants, lions, and tigers.
Again, having been gathered together and cast into great iron machines, they are crushed like the pressing of sugarcane.
As they are being tormented there, rivers of blood flow and stream forth.
