Furthermore, when they have come together in a mass, a great iron boulder falls from above, which cuts, pierces, crushes, and completely shatters those beings upon the iron ground.
As they are being cut, pierced, crushed, and completely shattered here and there, rivers of blood flow and stream forth.
On that account, they experience suffering for a long time until that evil, unwholesome karma has been entirely exhausted and eliminated;
therefore, that hell is called Saṅghāta (the Crushing).
In that great hell, Raurava, beings for the most part experience such suffering caused by torment.
Seeking a place of refuge there, those beings enter an iron house;
once they have entered it, fire is released, whereby they burn, blaze, and are consumed by a fierce conflagration.
There they wail with cries of distress and scream; on that account, they experience suffering for a long time until that sinful, unwholesome karma is entirely exhausted and eliminated.
For this reason, moreover, that hell is called Raurava.
In that great hell, Mahāraurava, this is the distinction: whatever was a cell in Raurava is to be understood as a cell there as well, but it is one with an interior chamber.
And for that reason, moreover, that hell is called Mahāraurava.
There, in the Tāpana great hell, beings for the most part experience such suffering of punishment.

The executioners included therein cast those beings into a cauldron many yojanas in size— boiling, seething, and fully ablaze— and they turn them over and over, heating and scorching them just like fish.
Furthermore, they pierce them from below with iron spikes;
those spikes enter through the small of the back and emerge from the crown of the head, blazing and aflame.
From the mouths, from the pupils of the eyes, from the nostrils, and from all the pores of their skin, flames issue forth.

Furthermore, having placed them upon the iron ground— whether face upwards or head downwards— that is heated, glowing, and blazing, they strike, beat, and crush them with iron hammers that are heated,
glowing, and fully aflame, just like a piece of meat. On account of this,
they experience suffering for a long time, until that sinful, unwholesome karma is entirely exhausted and brought to an end.
And for that reason, moreover, that hell is called Tapana (the Heating).
In that great hell of Pratāpana, this is the distinction:
they cause a trident-stake to emerge from their backs.
And of that [fire], one flame issues forth from one shoulder,
a second from the second [shoulder], and a third from the head;
because of that cause, flames also issue forth from their mouths.

With red-hot, intensely heated, and fully blazing iron plates, they envelop their bodies on all sides; furthermore, those beings are thrown with feet upward and faces downward into a great, vast iron cauldron filled with boiling lye, which is ignited, ablaze, and fully aflame. Once thrown in, they are scorched and tormented as they move both upward and downward.
As they walk, even as they move sideways, their skin, flesh, and blood become so thoroughly mixed that only a skeleton remains;
then, having been repeatedly lifted up and set down upon the iron ground,
once skin, flesh, and blood have grown back again, they are thrown down once more.
The remainder is like that of the Tapana hell;
and on that account, they experience suffering for a long time,
until that sinful, unwholesome karma has been entirely and completely exhausted and brought to an end.
And for that reason, moreover, that hell is called Pratāpana (the Intensely Heating).
There, in that very great hell of Avīci, they experience such suffering caused by torture:

from the eastern direction, the force of a mass of flames comes from the earth, which for many hundreds of yojanas is burning, blazing, and fully aflame; it strikes those beings, piercing through their skin, piercing through their flesh, cutting through their sinews, piercing through their bones, and reaching the marrow within the bones.
Just as with an oil-soaked wick,
so too does it remain pervading the entire basis with flames;
as from the eastern direction, so likewise from the southern, western, and northern directions.
And those beings, on that account, are perceived as being nothing but masses of fire.

When that mass of fire has spread and reached them from the four directions, they find no interval even for a moment from painful sensations; rather, they are recognized as "beings" only by their wailing with cries of distress.
Furthermore, they purify and polish iron coals—blazing and fiercely flaming—with iron winnowing baskets.
Again, they ascend and descend great iron mountains upon an iron ground.
Furthermore, having caused their tongues to emerge from their mouths, the tongues become stretched out by a hundred iron spikes.
It is stretched out so that it is free of wrinkles and free of folds, just like the hide of a bull.

Then, having placed them face upward upon that very same iron ground and having forced open their mouths with an iron wedge, glowing, blazing, and fiercely burning iron balls are thrown into their mouths;
these burn their mouths, and having burned their throats and intestines as well, they emerge again through the lower part of their bodies.
They throw molten copper into their mouths;
having burned the mouth, it burns the throat and the intestines as well, and having burned through the lower parts, it flows out from the lower parts.
The rest is like that of the Pratāpana hell.
On that account, they experience suffering for a long time until that evil, unwholesome karma is entirely exhausted and eliminated.
Furthermore, that hell is called Avīci because it is there that beings who have committed the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) are mostly reborn.
In this regard, these gross causes have been proclaimed;
however, it is not that many other causes of various forms are not found within these great hells.
Furthermore, in the neighboring hells (*sāmantanaraka*), sentient beings experience suffering caused by these very same factors.
All these great hells have four walls and four gates on the four sides, surrounded by iron enclosures.
And there, having gone out through the four gates on the four sides, at each individual gate there are four secondary hells (*utsada*).
It is as follows:
there is a pit of hot ashes reaching up to the knees,
which those beings enter seeking a place of shelter.
They step upon it;

having fallen there, they remain submerged with their heads and feet. And in that corpse, in the mud of excrement, there are insects and living beings which pierce even the skin of those beings, tear through the flesh, and break through the sinews and bones, until they reach the marrow within the bone.
They write.
Immediately adjacent to that corpse and excrement-mud is a path strewn with razor edges, which those beings, seeking a place of refuge, tread upon.
When they set their foot there, their skin, flesh, and blood are cut away;
when the foot is lifted again, the skin, flesh, and blood grow back once more.
Immediately following that path strewn with razor edges is the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana) situated right nearby.
There, those beings, seeking refuge, approach and sit in its shade;
as they sit there beneath it, swords fall from the trees, cutting and piercing the limbs and members of those beings.
When they have fallen there, dogs named Śyāmaśabalā come and, repeatedly tearing out their spinal columns, devour them.

Immediately adjacent to that Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana) is the Forest of Iron Silk-cotton Trees (Ayaḥśālmalīvana). When those beings, seeking a place of refuge, approach and climb it, the thorns turn downward;
when they descend, the thorns turn upward. These thorns pierce and split their major and minor limbs.
And there, iron-beaked crows, having alighted upon the shoulders or the heads of those beings, pierce them and, repeatedly tearing out the eyeballs, devour them.
Immediately adjacent to that forest of iron *śālmalī* trees is the river Vaitaraṇī, filled with boiling alkaline water, into which those beings, seeking a place of refuge, fall.
As they move upward, they are tormented and cooked;
as they move downward and sideways, they too are tormented and cooked.
It is just as if, for example, mung beans, black gram, jujube fruits, or horse gram were thrown into a cauldron filled with water set over a blazing fire.

On both banks of that river, beings stand with staffs in their hands, hooks in their hands, and nets in their hands; they do not even allow those beings to emerge, but rather, having pulled them up with hooks or nets, and having placed them face-up on ground heated by a blazing fire, they ask: "O beings, what do you desire?"
They say this:
"We do not know, nor do we see; however, we are hungry.
Then those beings, having forced open the mouths of those other beings with iron wedges, thrust into their mouths iron balls heated by a fierce fire, as described before.
If, however, they say, "We are thirsty," then they likewise pour molten copper into their mouths;
and on account of that, they experience suffering for a long time.
Until that evil, unwholesome karma to be experienced in hell has been entirely exhausted and eliminated in every respect.

In that regard, the path strewn with razor edges, the forest of sword-leaves, the forest of iron-śālmali trees, and the river Vaitaraṇī—considering these as one supplementary hell, there are four such supplementary hells.
There, sentient beings born in the cold hells experience such cold suffering as this:
those born in the Arbuda hell, touched by the intense cold characteristic of that level, undergo a contraction of their entire physical basis like a water-bubble;
therefore, that hell is called Arbuda.
Thus it is said.
In that regard, this is the distinction concerning Nirarbuda:
an *arbuda* (blister) that has emerged from an *arbuda* undergoes contraction.
And for that reason, the hell is called Nirarbuda.
Among them, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, and Huhuva are designations established for those beings based on their vocal utterances.
Furthermore, in the Utpala cold hell, being touched by the intense cold native to that level, the beings become bluish-black and their skin splits into five or six pieces;
therefore, that hell is called Utpala.
In that lotus, this is the distinction:
having transcended blueness, becoming intensely red, they undergo the bursting of the skin tenfold or even more.
And for that reason, that hell is called Padma.
In that regard, this is the distinction concerning the Great Lotus Hell:
the skin becomes even more intensely blood-red and bursts open into a hundred or more pieces.
And for that reason, that great hell is called Mahāpadma.
Furthermore, beings who have been reborn in each individual hell experience, within their respective individual bodies, suffering brought about by their own karma in such a manner;
just as Maudgalyāyana, when questioned by Lakṣmaṇa, explained in detail exactly according to the sūtra.
And for that reason, that hell is called a "pratyekanaraka" (individual hell).
There, animals engage in mutual slaughter, such as the killing of the weak;
and on that account, they experience suffering.
Lacking independence, they are oppressed, beaten, and driven about;
they become mere instruments for gods and humans,
and on that account, they experience various kinds of suffering.

Furthermore, in brief, hungry ghosts (pretas) are of three kinds: those whose obstruction to food and drink is external, those whose obstruction to food and drink is internal, and those whose obstruction consists of the food and drink itself.
In that regard, who are those hindered by external obstacles concerning food and drink?
They are those beings who, because they have excessively indulged in stinginess, are reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Due to the affliction of hunger and thirst, their skin, flesh, and blood are completely withered; they have the appearance of burnt pillars, with mouths resembling mere strands of hair, faces overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, mouths parched, and tongues constantly lapping.
With bewildered faces, they wander here and there among the springs,

lakes, and ponds; yet there, by other beings with swords in hand, nooses in hand, and spears in hand, they are driven away from those springs, lakes, and ponds, and they see that water as pus and blood.
Therefore, they themselves remain with no desire to emerge;
such are these hungry ghosts (preta), who are externally obstructed from food and drink.
What are those who have internal obstructions regarding food and drink?
They are as follows: those with needle-like mouths, those with firebrand-like mouths, those with goiters on their necks, and those with distended bellies.
For indeed, because they themselves have not had obstructions created by others, even when they obtain food and drink, they are unable to eat or to drink.
These are the kinds of hungry ghosts who are internally obstructed regarding food and drink.
What are the obstructions regarding food and drink?

There are hungry ghosts named Jvālāmālins (Flame-Garlanded), for whom whatever is eaten and whatever is drunk is entirely consumed by fire, so that the suffering of hunger and thirst never departs from them.
And there are pretas known as "scavenger-eaters" who, for the most part, consume impurities and drink urine;
whatever is unclean, foul-smelling, raw-scented, repugnant, or loathsome, that they are able to eat or drink.
Some even cut off their own flesh and eat it;
yet whatever is pure or exquisite, they are unable to consume or drink it.
These are the types of pretas who are said to have obstructions regarding food and drink.
Therein, sentient beings born among humans experience such forms of the suffering of frustration:
first, the innate suffering of frustration caused by hunger and thirst;
and the suffering of frustration caused by unfulfilled desires and poor food.
The suffering of affliction caused by the exhaustion of seeking and so forth; the suffering of change due to the seasons caused by the affliction of cold and heat;
the suffering of obstruction caused by the lack of shelter such as a house;
and the suffering of obstruction caused by the interruption of daily activities through coverings such as darkness.
Likewise, there is the suffering of decay through enjoyment, the suffering of illness, and the suffering of death;
for indeed, in the hells, one even considers death itself to be a pleasure,
and therefore that [death] is not established as a suffering in that context.
Among the gods, there is no cutting of the vital organs,
yet there is the suffering of falling and passing away,
as it has been said:
For a son of the gods who is about to pass away, five portents appear:
his unstained garments become soiled;
his previously unfading garlands wither.
Sweat is released from the armpits,
a foul odor pervades the body,
and neither a god nor a son of a god finds delight in his own seat.
At that time, as he was walking about on the terrace, those apsarases were attending upon him together with other sons of the gods.
Seeing them, he experienced great physical pain and mental distress on that account;
likewise, he also underwent the suffering caused by his state of pregnancy.
For what reason?
Because,
in that case, for whoever is endowed with a more extensive mass of merit, more sublime divine objects of the five sensory pleasures manifest for them.
There, upon seeing other sons of the gods who possess even less merit than himself, a state of dejection arises;
on that account, he experiences extensive suffering and mental distress.
Likewise, he also undergoes the sufferings of being cut, torn apart, exiled, oppressed, and slain.
For what reason?

Because when a battle between the gods and the asuras has arisen, the gods and asuras, being mutually opposed, take up four kinds of weapons made of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli, and they fight in battle.
And there, whether among the gods or the asuras, there occurs the severing of limbs and members,
and even the dissolution of the body;
yet their severed limbs and members grow back once again.
A severed body grows back again;
however, when the head is cut off, then they meet their death.
Thus, at one time the gods are defeated and at another time the asuras, but for the most part, the gods are victorious due to their superior strength.
For those among them who are defeated and have entered their own cities, there is relief;
they do not become accessible to one another again.
Therein, for the sake of the Asura maidens, the gods [were challenged] by the Asuras.
They are in conflict with one another.
The asuras are in conflict with the gods for the sake of the four kinds of ambrosia (*sudhā*).
Furthermore, the asuras should be understood as being included within the destiny of the gods (*devagati*) itself.
But they, being deceptive, having the intention to trick, and abounding in illusion and guile,
are therefore not such vessels for pure dharmas as the gods are;
hence, in certain other sūtras, they are designated separately by the description of a distinct realm of existence.
Although they are indeed *surās*, they do not abide by adopting the nature of a *sura*;
therefore, they are *asurās*.
Furthermore, when a more powerful son of the gods becomes angry, he causes a weaker son of the gods to fall from his own abode and banish him.

Therefore, the gods experience three kinds of suffering: the suffering of falling and being cast down, the suffering of becoming like a vulture (madgu), and the suffering of cutting, piercing, killing, and banishment.
[The beings] belonging to the realms of form and formlessness:
for those beings belonging to the realms of form and formlessness, that suffering does not exist at all;
because those beings are not suitable vessels for painful feeling.
Moreover, they too are afflicted by the suffering of *dauṣṭhulya* because they possess afflictions and obstructions, and because they lack autonomy regarding death or remaining in their state.
The untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), however, is completely severed from all suffering of *dauṣṭhulya*.
Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate truth, that alone is happiness;
everything else should be understood as suffering.
In those four types of hells, there is no experience of pleasure.
As it is in the hells, so it is with the three types of hungry ghosts (pretas).
Among the hungry ghosts of great power and among humans, however, a pleasure derived from external requisites is perceived, though it is interspersed and mingled with suffering.
Among humans, the happiness of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) is foremost, supreme, and sublime.
Furthermore, when a wheel-turning monarch appears in the world, he appears endowed with seven treasures;
such are the seven treasures that belong to him.
Namely: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
What kind of wheel-treasure (cakraratna) appears for him at that time? The manifestation of the seven treasures should be described exactly as it is in the Sūtra.
And there, the city-kings of the four continents come to him of their own accord, saying: "These are the territories of Your Majesty;
may Your Majesty govern them."
"We shall be the attendants of the god.
Thereupon, the wheel-turning monarch commands:
"Therefore, O village chiefs, rule each your own respective territories according to the Dharma, not according to what is not the Dharma."
And let it not please you, who practice unrighteousness and act with partiality, to dwell in this kingdom.
They submit by sending envoys to one who rules over three continents,
but they rise up in rebellion against one who rules over two continents.
And when they have been subdued, they bow down;
the gods, moreover, experience the vast realm of heaven, possessing beauty and abundant delight within their own celestial palaces, remaining there for a long time.
They are pure both internally and externally, free from the stench of impurity.
Those impure substances which belong to them—
namely, dust, dirt, bones, sinews, veins, kidneys, heart, and so forth, as found in human beings—
do not exist [in that state].
And their celestial palaces (vimānas) are of four kinds:
made of gold, made of silver, made of crystal, and made of beryl.

They are variegated with various artistic designs, delightful with gabled chambers, delightful with upper stories, delightful with turrets, delightful with railings, and delightful with latticed windows; they are inlaid with various jewels and radiate light like strung pearls.
They shine forth on all sides.
Likewise, there are food-trees from which the fourfold ambrosial food—
blue, yellow, red, and white— is produced;
and similarly, there are drink-trees from which honeyed wine is produced.
The vehicle-trees, from which various vehicles such as chariots, pairs of horses, palanquins, and so forth, are produced.
From the clothing-trees, various garments—fine and coarse, pure white, of diverse colors, and variegated with gold patterns—manifest.
From the ornament-trees, various ornaments are produced: jewels, armlets, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, hand-ornaments, and foot-ornaments;
such diverse ornaments as these, set with variegated gems, manifest.
There are trees of perfumes, incense, and garlands from which come various scents, diverse incenses, and various garlands; among these,
the *pāriyātraka* and *kovidāra* are the foremost,
most excellent, best, and most sublime.
Its roots extend fifty yojanas deep;
it rises a hundred yojanas high;
and its branches, leaves, and foliage spread out for eighty yojanas as it stands.
The fragrance of that tree when it is in full bloom wafts for a hundred yojanas downwind and fifty yojanas against the wind;
and beneath it, the gods of the Thirty-three play with the five divine qualities of sensual pleasure during the four months of the rainy season.
Likewise, there are trees for laughter, dance, song, and instrumental music, from which various vessels for laughter, dance, song, and instrumental music are produced.

Likewise, there are trees for utensils and implements from which various utensils and implements are produced—namely, utensils and implements for food, utensils and implements for drink, and utensils and implements for bedding and seating; such are the utensils and implements.
For those who desire to enjoy those requisites according to their wish and in accordance with their karma, they appear in their hands.
It should be understood that the enjoyment of the bliss and splendor of celestial palaces similar to those is also experienced by the asuras.
Furthermore, in the northern continent of Uttarakuru, trees of this very kind are called *kalpavṛkṣas* (wish-fulfilling trees).
For from those very trees they take what they need themselves; it does not appear in their hands merely by being thought of.
And there, the rice grows without being ploughed or sown.
And those beings are without "mine-ness," without possessions, and are certain to attain distinction.

And there, belonging to Śakra, the lord of the gods, is the Vaijayanta palace, the most excellent of all, wherein there are twenty-one hundred turrets; in each turret there are a hundred gabled chambers;
and in each gabled chamber there are seven inner apartments.
In every single chamber there are seven apsarases;
for each apsaras there are seven attendant maidservants.
And the entire surface of the ground is like the palm of a god’s hand, without elevations or depressions, and pleasant to the touch;
when the foot is set down, it sinks,
and when the foot is lifted, it rises up.
And it remains perpetually strewn knee-deep with mandāraka flowers; there,
the wind carries away the withered blossoms and brings forth fresh ones.
And on the four sides of that city of the gods, the streets were laid out— exquisite, beautiful to behold,
variegated, and well-proportioned. Furthermore,
four gates were constructed on the four sides, which were exquisite, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and supported by many variegated and handsome wings.
There are four pleasure groves in the four directions, namely:
Caitraratha, Pāruṣyaka, Miśraka, and Nandana-vana.
Beyond those are four beautiful terrestrial realms.

Beautiful and pleasing to behold, to the northeast of the city of the gods is the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods, where the gods enter to deliberate upon, weigh, and examine matters. In its vicinity is the Pāṇḍukambala stone, white, beautiful, lovely, and pleasing to behold.
And those gods are self-luminous.

Signs of night appear to them, whereby it occurs to them: "Night has arrived; the day has passed. These are as follows: laziness, a lack of desire to sport with the five strands of sensual pleasure, and sloth-and-torpor.
And birds do not chirp; such are the types of omens.

Day and night, endowed with absolute happiness and mental well-being, they delighted in the five divine strands of sensual pleasure; being completely under the sway of heedlessness, they were captivated by the sounds of dancing, singing, and instrumental music, by the sounds of actors, dancers, jesters, and performers,
and by various sights that were exceedingly pleasing to the mind and various fragrances that were intensely sweet-smelling.

With their minds captivated by various flavors that are exclusively delicious, by various tactile sensations provided primarily by the apsarases that are exclusively pleasant to the touch, they pass the time;
it is such happiness as this that the gods experience.
Neither disease, nor decay, nor old age is found among them;
nor is there innate suffering caused by the lack of food or drink,
nor any other sufferings as previously described, such as those among human beings.
The gods of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) belonging to the level of the first dhyāna experience the joy and bliss born of seclusion;
those belonging to the level of the second dhyāna experience the joy and bliss born of meditative concentration.
Those belonging to the level of the third dhyāna experience the essence of bliss free from rapture;
those belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna experience the peaceful bliss that is purified by equanimity and mindfulness, which is imperturbable.
[Those belonging to the formless realm:
Those born in the formless realm experience the bliss of peaceful liberation.
Furthermore, indeed, a distinction in suffering or a distinction in bliss should be understood by means of six distinctions.
[This occurs] through a specific measure, a specific delicacy, a specific condition, a specific time, a specific state of mind, and a specific physical basis.
To the extent that the body becomes more delicate, to that same extent there is a specific intensity of suffering;
to the extent that the physical basis becomes more delicate, to that same extent there is a specific intensity of suffering.
To the extent that the conditions become more intense, more abundant, and more diverse, to that same extent there is a particularity of suffering.
To the extent that the duration becomes longer and more continuous, to that same extent there is a particularity of suffering.
To the extent that the mind becomes stronger through the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), to that same extent there is a particularity of suffering.
To the extent that the basis becomes more of a vessel for suffering, to that same extent there arises a particularity of suffering.
Just as there are specific varieties of suffering, so too should the specific varieties of happiness be understood in detail according to their respective applications.
Furthermore, happiness is indeed twofold: that born of ignoble wealth and that born of noble wealth.
Among these, the happiness born of ignoble wealth is that which arises in dependence upon four types of requisites:
the requisite for contentment, the requisite for nourishment, the requisite for purification, and the requisite for maintenance.
In that regard, the requisites for satisfaction are as follows:

vehicles, clothing, ornaments, laughter, dance, song, and instrumental music; perfumes, garlands, and ointments; various excellent utensils and furnishings; light; the attendance of women and men; and the accumulation of a treasury.
In that regard, the equipment for satisfaction is as follows, Ānanda: physical exercise, such as the exercise of the stone discus, the exercise of the mace discus, and other activities of this kind.
In that regard, the implements for purification are as follows:
*darbha* grass, a *śaṅku* peg, a *bilva* fruit, a full water-jar, and items of a similar nature.
In that regard, the requisites for maintenance are food and drink.

In that regard, noble wealth-born happiness is that which arises dependent upon the seven noble riches: the wealth of faith, the wealth of ethical discipline, the wealth of moral shame, the wealth of dread of blame, the wealth of learning, the wealth of relinquishment, and the wealth of wisdom.
In this regard, the happiness born of the noble wealth is distinguished from the happiness born of the non-noble wealth by fifteen aspects.
By which fifteen?
The happiness born of the non-noble wealth leads to the arousal of misconduct.
But that which is born of the noble wealth is not like that.
Furthermore, the happiness born of non-noble wealth is associated with blameworthy pleasure; however, that born of noble wealth is associated with blameless pleasure.
Moreover, the happiness born of non-noble wealth is limited, because it does not pervade its entire basis.
The noble wealth born of the noble is sublime because it pervades the entire basis;
furthermore, that which is born of non-noble [wealth] is not constant, as it is dependent upon external conditions,
whereas that which is born of noble wealth is constant because it is dependent upon internal conditions.
Furthermore, that which arises from non-noble wealth is not universal because it belongs exclusively to the desire realm;
conversely, that which arises from noble wealth is universal, as it is unconditioned by and transcends all three realms.

Furthermore, that which arises from non-noble wealth does not bring about noble or non-noble wealth in the future; however, that which arises from noble wealth does bring about noble and non-noble wealth in the future.
Furthermore, that which is born of the non-noble wealth, while being enjoyed, goes to exhaustion and depletion;
however, that which is born of the noble wealth, when cultivated, goes to great increase and expansion.
Furthermore, that which arises from ignoble wealth is liable to be confiscated by others—whether by kings, thieves, adversaries, fire, or water;
however, that which arises from noble wealth is not liable to confiscation.

Furthermore, that which is born of ignoble wealth is to be taken from here and not brought back; furthermore, that which is born of ignoble wealth is to be taken from here and not brought back; whereas that which is born of noble wealth is to be taken from here and brought back.
Furthermore, that which arises from the non-noble wealth, when indulged in, does not lead to satisfaction;
however, that which arises from the noble wealth, when indulged in, leads to satisfaction through its ultimate consummation.
Furthermore, that which arises from ignoble wealth is accompanied by fear, enmity, calamity, and burning anguish;
it does not lead to the abandonment of suffering in the future.
In that regard, it is "with fear" because it serves as a basis for apprehension regarding the arising of future suffering;
it is "with enmity" because it serves as a basis for quarreling, brawling, strife, and dispute;
and it is "with calamity" because it serves as a basis for the states of disease, old age, and death.

In that regard, it is "accompanied by burning" because, like the itching of a leprosy disease, its pleasure is not fully realized; because it serves as a basis for the state of perversion; and because it serves as a basis for the states of sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
Furthermore, it does not lead to the abandonment of suffering in the future because it serves as a basis for the states of the afflictions and secondary afflictions, such as attachment and the rest.
However, that which arises from noble wealth is fearless, free from enmity, without affliction, and does not cause burning; it leads to the abandonment of suffering in the future.
This should be understood in detail and according to its application as the opposite of that [worldly enjoyment].

Furthermore, there are five ways in which the enjoyment of the Dharma by the Noble Ones who live by wisdom excels the enjoyment of sensual pleasures by outsiders who are driven by desire: because the enjoyment of the Dharma by the Noble One who lives by wisdom is called "supreme living by wisdom," due to the fact that the enjoyment of the Dharma is undefiled, the enjoyment of the Dharma is ultimate, the enjoyment of the Dharma is exclusive, and the enjoyment of the Dharma is... [the text continues].
This is because the enjoyment of the Dharma by others who live by wisdom is common to all;
because the enjoyment of the Dharma consists of perfected bliss; and because it has subdued Māra and all adversaries.

In that regard, for those possessed by desire, sensual pleasure is associated with attachment and serves as a basis for mental joy; it is associated with aversion and serves as a basis for mental grief; and it is associated with non-analytical equanimity and serves as a basis for indifference.
However, the enjoyment of the Dharma by those who live by noble wisdom is not like that.
Furthermore, for those possessed by desire, the prior limit of the enjoyment of sensual pleasures is not known;
through impermanence, they abandon some desires and obtain others,
and at times they do not obtain them at all.

But the enjoyment of the Dharma by those who live by noble wisdom is not like that. Furthermore, for those possessed of desire who are engaged in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, the very same object becomes a basis for mental pleasure for some, while for others it becomes a basis for mental distress;
moreover, after a short time, those same objects become bases for mental pleasure once again.
For a short time these things may be conducive to dejection,
but the enjoyment of the Dharma by those who live by noble wisdom is not like that.

Furthermore, for those outside [this teaching] who have renounced sensual desires and live by wisdom, yet whose minds are firmly grasping and attached to various views— positions of false conviction arisen from their own conceptual constructions— the affliction of desire remains persistently adhered to them. Moreover, even for those who are free from passion, there occurs a relapse.
But the enjoyment of the Dharma by those who live by noble wisdom is not like that.
Furthermore, for those who enjoy the Dharma and for even those worldly persons who are free from passion, there exists the fully accomplished pleasure of sensual desire and the pleasure of seclusion.

Yet that pleasure which follows after Māra and his adversaries— which is like an illusion, like an echo, like a reflection, like a mirage, like a dream, and like ornaments fashioned by magic— is what the fools who enjoy sensual pleasures and the worldly ones who are free from passion pursue, being like those who are insane.
Those who have conquered the battle against Māra enjoy [pleasures] that are compared to a drunkard and the like;
therefore, they remain unperfected and have not vanquished Māra as their adversary.
However, the enjoyment of the Dharma by those who live by noble wisdom is not like that.
Furthermore, how should the basis of sentient beings belonging to the three realms be viewed?
It is, for example, like a boil accompanied by burning pain because it is permeated by *dauṣṭhulya*.
How is the occurrence of a pleasant sensation in that basis to be viewed?
It is, for example, like the occurrence of a cool touch upon a boil that is already inflamed.
How should the occurrence of painful feeling upon that basis be viewed?
It is, for example, like the application of caustic to a boil that is already inflamed. How is it that pleasant-neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling occurs upon this basis?
It should be viewed as follows:
just as in that very same inflamed boil, there is a natural inflammation that has been relieved by cold and alkaline substances.
For this very reason, the Blessed One stated that even pleasant feeling is suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in change;
painful feelings, moreover, are suffering by virtue of the nature of suffering itself;
and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is stated to be suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations.
As for what was also said— that there is joy with worldly attachment (*sāmiṣā*),
and there is joy that is free from worldly attachment (*nirāmiṣā*), more free from worldly attachment, and most free from worldly attachment—
that too should be understood in detail according to the sūtra as falling within two realms.

Furthermore, when the Blessed One established the bliss of the cessation of perception and feeling as the foremost among all forms of bliss, he was referring to the bliss of that meditative dwelling, and not to the bliss of felt sensation.
As for what was also said— that there are three kinds of happiness, namely the fading away of passion, the fading away of hatred, and the fading away of delusion—
these three are found only in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
Therefore, by means of these three kinds of happiness, the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu) is at all times indeed happiness.
[The Enjoyment of Nutriment] In this regard, this is the enjoyment of nutriment:
namely, for those beings born and come into existence who belong to the three realms, their continued existence for as long as their lifespan lasts is sustained by the four kinds of nutriment.
In that regard, the maintenance and subsistence of all sentient beings belonging to the three realms occurs through three types of nutriment: contact, mental volition, and consciousness.

Furthermore, the maintenance and subsistence of only those sentient beings belonging to the desire realm occurs through edible food; even for those sentient beings born in the hells, there blows a subtle wind containing edible food as its essence.
That by which their subsistence occurs is as follows:

the coarse food of animals, hungry ghosts, and humans, which they consume by taking it into mouthfuls; whereas that which is the subtle [food] of beings in the stages of the *kalala* and so forth, and of the gods of the desire realm.
For instance,
as soon as they have consumed the food in morsels, it undergoes decay as it spreads through the entire body and all its limbs;
moreover, no excrement or urine remains in them.
[Regarding sexual enjoyment:
In that regard, this sexual enjoyment does not exist at all for the beings in the hells.
This is because they experience intense, diverse, long-lasting, and uninterrupted suffering.
Consequently, among those men, no desire for women arises in them,
and among the women, no desire for men arises in them;
how much less, then, will they engage in sexual union with one another?
Among animals, hungry ghosts, and humans, because their physical bases are intermingled with both pleasure and pain, there exists the practice of sexual union.
There, females and males, in pairs, engage in copulation and discharge impurity.
Among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is sexual union, yet there is no discharge of impurity;
rather, it is simply the air that exits through the gateway of the sense organ.
In that regard, for those belonging to the assembly of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*), the feverish heat departs through the coupling of pairs.

Just as it is for the gods of the Four Great Kings, so it is for the Trāyastriṃśa gods: their feverish heat subsides merely by mutual embracing; for the Yāma gods, it subsides merely by mutual holding of hands; and for the Nirmāṇarati gods, it subsides merely by mutual laughing together.
Among the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, as soon as they look at one another with their eyes, fixing their gaze upon each other's eyes, their burning fever disappears.
In those three realms, there is the taking of wives, as well as the bringing together of brides and the giving away of daughters in marriage.
Among the continents— namely Jambūdvīpa, Pūrvavideha, and Avaragodānīya— the taking of wives and the practice of marriage are known to exist.
However, among the people of Uttarakuru, because they possess no sense of "mine" and have no sense of possession, there is neither the taking of wives nor the practice of marriage.

As it is in the three continents, so it is in the realms of hungry ghosts (*preta*), in the hells, and among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). With the exception of the gods who Delight in Emanations (*nirmāṇarati*) and those who Wield Power over Others' Creations (*paranirmitavaśavartin*), among the classes of gods in the desire realm, no embryo of an *apsaras* comes to term. Among the gods of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*), a being is born spontaneously (*aupapāduka*) upon the lap or in the embrace of the parents as a five-year-old boy; among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, as a six-year-old; and among the Yāma gods, as a seven-year-old.
Or else, as an eight-year-old among the Tuṣitas, a nine-year-old among the Nirmāṇaratis, or a ten-year-old boy among the Paranirmitavaśavartins, he is born spontaneously upon a shoulder or in a lap.
[This is the formal definition of the designation of rebirth.]
In this regard, the formal establishment of the designation of rebirth is as follows:
there are three types of rebirth in the desire realm.
There are beings for whom desires are present, who exercise mastery and control over those present desires.
Who, then, are they? They are as follows: all human beings, and the gods beginning from those of the Four Great Kings up to those in Tuṣita.
This is the first rebirth resulting from sensual desire.
There are beings whose sensual pleasures are emanated, who, having repeatedly emanated them, exercise mastery and control over their desires.
Who, then, are they? They are, for example, the gods who Delight in Emanations (*nirmāṇarati*).
And for those Nirmāṇarati gods, the creation of objects of desire for their own sake succeeds,
but not that which is caused by another. Therefore, they exercise sovereignty and mastery over the objects of desire created by themselves alone.
This is the second rebirth in the realm of desire.
There are beings whose sensual desires are created by others, who exercise mastery and control even over those desires created by others;
namely, the gods who wield power over the creations of others (*paranirmitavaśavartin*).
For indeed, for those gods, both emanations characterized by their own self and those characterized by another are successfully manifested.
Then, dwelling with little concern for their own creations,
they exercise mastery over the pleasures created by others;
because of this, they are called "Those Who Exercise Mastery over the Creations of Others."
But they do not enjoy only pleasures created by others; rather, they enjoy those created by themselves as well.
This is the third rebirth in the realm of desire.
[The Arising of Happiness] There are these three arisings of happiness.
There are beings who, through the joy and happiness born of seclusion, thoroughly drench their desires.
Namely, the gods belonging to the level of the first dhyāna;
this is the first rebirth in happiness.
There are beings who thoroughly moisten their desires with the joy and bliss born of concentration;
namely, the gods belonging to the level of the second dhyāna. This is the second rebirth in happiness.
There are beings who thoroughly drench themselves with the pleasure that is free from rapture, namely, the gods belonging to the level of the third dhyāna;
this is the third rebirth in happiness.
For what reason are the three rebirths in the desire realm and the three rebirths in happiness established?
[The three searches:
He said: "There are these three searches: the search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for the holy life.
In this regard, whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas fall into the search for sensual pleasures, they all do so for the sake of the three types of rebirths in the realm of desire."
There is nothing higher than this, nor anything further.

In this regard, whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas fall into the pursuit of existence for the sake of pleasure, they all for the most part do so out of a desire for pleasure for the sake of the three types of rebirths in happiness;
those who seek the state that is neither painful nor pleasant are fewer still than those.
They undertake the quest for the sake of a peaceful rebirth;
therefore, no rebirth is established beyond that point.
Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas undertake the pursuit of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), they all do so for the sake of the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*).

Yet some undertake a false pursuit of the holy life for the sake of the imperturbable (*āniñja*), that is, for the sake of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It is for the sake of liberation from the falsely imagined;
and that should be understood as the quest for the holy life with something superior.
Furthermore, the unsurpassed [quest] is for the sake of the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
[The Establishment of the Personal Existence] Therein, the establishment of the personal existence is as follows:
Four acquisitions of personal existence (*ātmabhāva-pratilambha*) for sentient beings are known to exist within the three realms:
there is an acquisition of personal existence wherein one's own volition (*ātma-saṃcetanā*) operates, but not the volition of another. For example:
In the realm of desire, there are gods known as the *krīḍāpramoṣaka* (those who are deluded by play).
At this time, they dwell excessively devoted to play, pleasure, and adornment.
As they dwell in that manner, their mindfulness is lost; through the loss of mindfulness, those beings undergo a fall from that state.
Likewise, there are gods named Manaḥpradūṣika who, at that time, look upon one another by gazing directly from eye to eye.
As they gaze at one another in that manner, their minds become corrupted; through that corruption of mind, those beings undergo a fall from that state.
There is an acquisition of personal existence wherein the volition of another operates, but not one's own volition;
namely, in the case of beings situated in the mother’s womb during the stages of the *kalala*, the *ghana*, the *peśī*, and the *arbuda*.
There is a certain acquisition of personal existence wherein both one's own volition and the volition of others operate;
namely, among those very beings who are born with fully developed faculties and matured faculties.
There is an acquisition of personal existence where neither one's own volition nor the volition of another operates.

This includes beings such as those among the gods of the form and formless realms, those in the hells, those among the pretas who resemble those in hell, the messengers of the Tathāgata, those in their final existence, those who have entered the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpanna*), those who have entered the cessation absorption (*nirodha-samāpanna*), and those in the intermediate state (*antarābhavika*), as well as other beings of this category.
[The Establishment of Cause and Fruit] Regarding that, the establishment of cause and fruit is to be understood through four aspects:
by way of characteristic, basis, classification, and formal establishment.
In this regard, what is the characteristic of a cause?

That which is prior, that upon which something depends, that with which it comes together, and by means of which a phenomenon attains its acquisition, establishment, completion, or activity—that is called its cause.
What is prior, depending on what, coming together with what, does the arising of a phenomenon occur?

Preceded by its own seed, having established a seed-basis— whether that other basis be with form or without form— and depending upon karma, conjoining with an auxiliary and an object, there arises [consciousness] associated with the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm,
or unassociated [with any realm], as is appropriate for each case.
What precedes it, upon what is it established, by coming together with what, and of which dharma is there attainment?

Preceded by the lineages of the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and tathāgata; established upon the power of internal factors; and by coming together with the power of external factors, there is the attainment of nirvāṇa, which is the dissociation from the afflictions.
In this regard, the internal factor-power consists of, for example,
appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) and fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*), among others;
as well as internal wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*), such as being born as a human being (*manuṣyatva*).
Rebirth in a noble realm;
being unimpaired in one's faculties; and having unerring conduct in one's actions.
Clarity directed toward the sense bases—
dharmas such as these are called the power of internal factors.
In this regard, the external auxiliary power is as follows: the arising of Buddhas,
the teaching of the true Dharma,
and the persistence of the taught Dharmas.
The continued engagement of those who are already established,
and compassion toward others—
such qualities as these are called the power of external factors.
In this regard, what precedes it, upon what is it established, by coming together with what, and of which phenomenon is there accomplishment?

Accomplishment of the matter to be proven occurs preceded by conviction regarding the object of knowledge and interest; it is established upon the proposition, the reason, and the example; and it comes about by coming together with an opponent and an assembly that is not hostile.
What is its precursor? Upon what is it established? By coming together with what does the accomplishment of which dharma occur?

It has knowledge of the craft as its precursor; it is established upon an effort that follows from that, and by means of the tools and equipment belonging to that particular field of craft, the successful completion of that specific craft occurs.

[What is its precursor? Upon what does it depend? By uniting with what does the persistence of which phenomenon occur? It has craving as its precursor; depending upon the basis of sustenance and maintenance, and by uniting with the four kinds of nutriment, there occurs the persistence, maintenance, and nourishment of existing sentient beings.
What precedes it, what does it rely upon, what does it come together with, and of what phenomenon is its activity?

Its own activity is discerned as the performance of its own function by a phenomenon that possesses action, based on its arising preceded by its own seed, relying on [the body], and coming together with the conditions for its arising. For example, the seeing of the eye;
in the same way, the respective functions of the remaining sense-faculties should be understood.
Likewise, the earth supports,
the waters moisten,
and fire burns.
One should understand that each of the external phenomena also has its own specific function, such as wind causing desiccation, and so forth.
[The basis of the fruit of causes and conditions:
What is the basis of the fruit of causes and conditions?
There are these fifteen bases of the cause.
Namely: speech and experience.
Latent predisposition (*vāsanā*),
which is the seed accompanied by its natural outflow (*sābhiniṣyanda*),
is the closely associated cessation (*śliṣṭanirodha*).
The object, the sense faculty, and the action.
Human effort,
the vision of reality,
and conformity.
The diversity of capacities, the causal complex, and the obstacles.
And there is no obstacle.
What is the differentiation of causes, conditions, and fruits?
There are ten causes and four conditions.
There are five fruits.
What are the ten causes? They are:
the cause of conventional designation, the cause of dependence, and so forth.
The projecting cause,
the productive cause,
the appropriating cause, and the inducing cause.
The cause of specific determination,
the auxiliary cause,
and the cause of opposition.
And the reason of non-contradiction.
What are the four conditions? The causal condition, the immediately preceding condition, [the object condition, and the dominant condition].
The object-condition and the dominant condition.
What are the five fruits?
The fruit of ripening,
the fruit of outflow, and so forth.
The fruit of dissociation, the fruit of human effort,
and the dominant fruit.
[The Determination of Causes and Conditions] What is the determination of causes and conditions?
In that regard, based upon speech as the locus of the cause, the cause for subsequent conventional expression is discerned.
For what reason? Because,

with respect to phenomena associated with the desire realm, those associated with the form realm, those associated with the formless realm, and those that are unassociated, perception proceeds preceded by the establishment of names.
Speech proceeds preceded by perception;
through speech, one communicates according to what has been seen, heard, thought, and cognized.
Therefore, based upon speech, the cause for communication is designated.
In that regard, having established the basis consisting of the cause of experience, the expectant cause is designated.
Why is that?
Because it is as follows:
One who desires pleasure associated with sensual desire seeks the acquisition of those sensual desires, or seeks their accumulation or their enjoyment, depending upon that [desire].
One who desires the pleasure associated with the realm of form or the formless realm seeks, in dependence upon that [pleasure], either the acquisition or the cultivation of its conditions.
Or, one who desires the pleasure associated with the [desire] realm seeks, in dependence upon that, either the acquisition or the cultivation of its conditions.
Furthermore, one who does not desire suffering seeks, in dependence upon that, the avoidance of its conditions, or the acquisition or the cultivation of the conditions for its abandonment.
Therefore, based upon experience, the projecting cause is designated.
In that regard, based upon the basis of the cause consisting of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), the projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*) is designated.
For what reason?
Because it is as follows:

Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), permeated by wholesome and unwholesome karma, project desirable and undesirable personal existences (*ātmabhāva*) within the three realms across desirable and undesirable destinies.
Furthermore, by that very same sovereign influence, there is the success or failure of external entities.
Therefore, based upon the latencies (*vāsanā*) of wholesome and unwholesome karma within conditioned phenomena, the "expectation cause" (*apekṣāhetu*) is designated.
In that regard, based upon the seed together with its moisture as the causal basis, the cause of production is designated.
Why is that? Because:
Phenomena associated with the desire realm, as well as those associated with the form and formless realms, arise from their respective seeds.
Furthermore, craving is called the "moistening of the seed.
Thus, the seed moistened by that [craving] serves for the production of the personal existences (ātmabhāva) projected [by karma]. As it has been said:
Karma is the cause for rebirth;
craving is the cause for actualization.
Therefore, based upon the seed accompanied by moisture, the cause of actualization is designated.

In that regard, based upon the causal basis consisting of the conjoined cessation, and likewise based upon the causal basis consisting of the object, the sense faculty, the activity, human effort, and the vision of reality, the "appropriating cause" is designated. For what reason?
For it is thus:
regarding phenomena associated with the desire realm, the activity of conditioned formations occurs as being grasped by immediate cessation,
and as being grasped by objects, grasped by faculties, grasped by actions, and grasped by human effort.

Just as it is for those factors associated with the desire realm, so too do the factors associated with the form realm, the formless realm, or those other factors not associated with any realm— whether they are embraced by the vision of reality or otherwise— come into operation. Therefore,
based upon the remaining cessation, the object, the sense faculty, the activity, human effort, and the vision of reality, the "appropriating cause" (parigraha-hetu) is designated.
Therein, based upon the basis of the conformable cause, the producing cause is designated.
For what reason?
Because:
Wholesome factors associated with the desire realm bring about superior wholesome factors associated with the desire realm.
Likewise, wholesome factors associated with the desire realm bring about wholesome factors associated with the form realm, the formless realm, and those that are unassociated [with any realm].

Because they are conducive to them, just as it is for those associated with the desire realm, so too for those associated with the form realm: wholesome factors associated with the form realm bring about superior wholesome factors associated with the form realm, the formless realm, and those that are unassociated.

Just as those associated with the form realm (rūpadhātu) are so, likewise those associated with the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) bring about wholesome dharmas associated with the formless realm, as well as superior wholesome dharmas associated [with other realms] and wholesome dharmas that are unassociated.
Just as those associated with the formless realm are so, likewise those that are unassociated bring about wholesome dharmas that are unassociated;
they even directly bring about the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) form.
Likewise, wholesome dharmas bring about unwholesome dharmas that are specifically distinguished;
namely, sensual desire brings about hatred, delusion, pride, views, doubt, misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
Just as it is with sensual desire, so too should hatred, delusion, pride, views, and doubt be understood according to their respective applications.
In this way, indeterminate factors bring about wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate factors;
that is to say, they bring about the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which contains the seeds of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Likewise, determinate factors bring about specific indeterminate factors.
For example, edible food brings about the maintenance, the subsistence, and the nourishment of vigor, strength, and growth for beings who have come into existence, by way of being conducive to them.
Therefore, based upon the cause of conduciveness, the bringing-about cause is designated.
In that regard, the cause of specific determination is designated by depending upon the basis of causes, which is the diversity of capacities.
For what reason?
Because it is as follows:
Phenomena associated with the desire realm arise from a variety of intrinsic natures, from a variety of specific intrinsic natures, and from a variety of potencies.
Just as it is with those associated with the desire realm, so it is with those associated with the form realm, those associated with the formless realm, and those that are unassociated.
Therefore, based upon this variety of potencies, the cause of specific determination is designated.
In that regard, based upon the basis of the cause consisting of the totality of conditions (*sāmagrīhetu*), the cooperative cause (*sahakārihetu*) is designated.
For what reason?
Because it is as follows:
Depending upon its own causal complex for arising (*utpatti-sāmagrī*), there occurs the production of phenomena associated with the desire realm (*kāma-pratisaṃyukta*).

Just as it is for those associated with the desire realm, so it is for those associated with the form realm (*rūpa-pratisaṃyukta*), those associated with the formless realm (*ārūpya-pratisaṃyukta*), and those that are unassociated (*apratisaṃyukta*).

Just as it is with the causal complex for arising, so it is with the causal complex for acquisition (*prāpti-sāmagrī*), the causal complex for accomplishment (*siddhi-sāmagrī*), the causal complex for completion (*niṣpatti-sāmagrī*), and the causal complex for activity (*kriyā-sāmagrī*).
Therefore, based upon the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*), the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-hetu*) is designated.
Therein, based upon the basis for the cause of obstruction, the cause of contradiction is designated.
For what reason?
Because it is as follows:
If an obstacle arises for the arising of phenomena associated with the desire realm, they do not arise.
Just as it is for those associated with the desire realm, so it is for those associated with the form realm, those associated with the formless realm, and those that are unassociated.
Just as it is for their arising, so it is for their attainment, their accomplishment, their completion, and their performance.
Therefore, based upon an obstacle, the cause of contradiction is designated.
In that regard, based upon the basis of the cause that is free from obstacles, the cause of non-contradiction is designated.
For what reason?
Because it is as follows:

For the arising of phenomena associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), if there is no obstacle present, their arising occurs. Just as it is for those associated with the desire realm, so it is for those associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): in this same way, there is attainment (*prāpti*), accomplishment (*siddhi*), completion (*niṣpatti*), and activity (*kriyā*).
Therefore, based on the absence of obstacles, the cause of non-contradiction is designated.
In that regard, based upon the seed as the locus of conditions, the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) is designated.
Based upon the basis of conditions consisting of contiguous cessation, the immediately preceding condition is designated.
The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is designated by means of establishing the objective field as the basis for the condition.
Based upon other bases of conditions, the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya) is designated.

In this regard, based upon the conformity of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) and based upon the basis of causes (*hetvadhiṣṭhāna*) and the basis of conditions (*pratyayādhiṣṭhāna*), the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*) are designated.
Based upon the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*) and based upon the basis of causes and the basis of conditions, the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*) is designated.
Based upon human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and based upon the basis of causes and the basis of conditions, the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) is designated.
Based upon the remaining bases of causes and the bases of conditions, the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala) is designated.
In this context, "cause" has the sense of benefit;
"condition" has the sense of support;
and "fruit" has the sense of accomplishment.
Furthermore, the establishment of causes occurs by way of five aspects, namely:
the producing cause (*janaka-hetu*) and the instrumental cause (*upāya-hetu*).
The co-existent cause is that which has ceased immediately prior,
as well as that which has ceased long ago.
In that regard, the producer is the cause of actualization;
the remaining [causes] are the causes of means, existing as co-existent factors.
For example:
One is the cause of appropriation (*parigraha-hetu*);
for example, the eye [is the cause] of visual consciousness.
Likewise, the ear and so forth are the causes of their respective other consciousnesses, as is that which has just ceased (*anantaraniruddha*).
Namely:
the cause of production [which has long since ceased].
For example:
the cause has been introduced.
Furthermore, the establishment of the cause occurs through another five aspects.
Namely:
the desirable cause and the undesirable cause.
The cause of view,
the cause of engagement, and the cause of cessation.
Furthermore, the establishment of causes occurs through another seven aspects.
Namely: the cause is impermanent;
no permanent phenomenon can be the cause of anything.
Whether it be the cause of arising, the cause of attainment, the cause of establishment,
or the cause of completion.
Or it is the cause of stability;
or it is the cause of activity;
and even an impermanent dharma [serves as the cause] for that which is impermanent.
Being a cause, it becomes the cause of another nature and of its subsequent intrinsic nature;
however, it does not become the cause of that which is momentary, nor of another subsequent intrinsic nature.
It is arisen and unceased, not unarisen and unceased.
Even that which has arisen and ceased becomes [a cause] when it obtains another condition, but not when it does not obtain one;
and even having obtained another condition, it undergoes transformation while becoming, but not without undergoing transformation.

Even when undergoing transformation, you arise from that which is endowed with power, not from that which is devoid of power; and even arising from that which is endowed with power, you arise from that which is appropriate and favorable, not from that which is inappropriate and unfavorable— it should be understood that the establishment [of this process] according to the cause occurs through these seven aspects as applicable.
In that regard, what is the formal establishment of the designation of characteristics? It should be understood as being sevenfold: by way of its body, and so forth.
Also by way of object,
by way of aspect, by way of origination,
and by way of classification.
Also from the perspective of definitive determination,
and also from the perspective of occurrence.

In this regard, the summary verse (uddāna) is as follows: Briefly stated, the characteristics [of the aggregates] consist of the body, the object, the aspect, the origination, the classification, the determination, and the activity.
What is the nature of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*)?
When there is no deliberation regarding an object, applied thought and sustained thought have volition (*cetanā*) as their nature;
furthermore, when there is deliberation regarding an object, it should be understood that applied thought and sustained thought have knowledge (*jñāna*) as their nature.
In that regard, what is the object of vitarka and vicāra?
The object is the meaning based upon the sets of names (nāmakāya), the sets of phrases (padakāya), and the sets of phonemes (vyañjanakāya).
What is the aspect of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*)?
Applied thought has the aspect of directing [the mind] toward or not directing it toward that very same object.
Furthermore, in that very same context, investigation is the mode of examining.
From what do applied thought and sustained thought arise?
They arise from speech.
What is the classification of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*)?
There are seven kinds of classification:
that which is based on signs (*naimittika*), as previously described, up to that which is undefiled (*akliṣṭa*).
What is the determination regarding applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*)?
Whatever is applied thought and sustained thought is also conceptualization (*vikalpa*);
whatever is conceptualization is also applied thought and sustained thought.
That which is applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) is indeed conceptualization (*vikalpa*). However, there may be conceptualization that is not applied or sustained thought.

With respect to supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*), all other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) belonging to the three realms are conceptualization, yet they are not applied or sustained thought.

What is the activity of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*)? How do the applied and sustained thoughts of hell-beings proceed; what is their aspect (*ākāra*), what is their contact (*sparśa*), by what are they aroused (*samudīrita*), with what are they associated (*samprayukta*), what is their longing (*prārthanā*), and what is their function (*karmaka*)?

Just as it is for hell-beings, so too for animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as well as the gods belonging to the level of the first dhyāna—what is the aspect of their applied and sustained thoughts, and what is their contact?
By what are they aroused, with what are they associated, by what are they characterized as aspirations, and what is their function?

In that regard, the applied and sustained thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*) of hell-beings proceed exclusively in a dejected form; they are aroused by undesirable objects, associated with mental distress (*daurmanasya*), characterized by the aspiration for liberation from suffering, and have the function of agitating the mind.

Just as it is for those in the hells, so it is for suffering *pretas*, animals, and humans who share the destiny of *pretas*: their thoughts and investigations (*vitarka-vicāra*) are for the most part of a dejected nature and only slightly joyful;
they consist mostly of contact with undesirable objects and only rarely of contact with desirable objects;
and they are for the most part aroused by suffering and only slightly aroused by pleasure.
For the most part, they are associated with mental distress and only slight joy;
for the most part, they proceed with a longing for liberation from suffering and a longing for the attainment of little happiness, and they function to agitate the mind.
For the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) are for the most part of a joyful nature and only slightly of a miserable nature;
they are for the most part contact with desirable objects and only slightly contact with undesirable objects;
they are for the most part aroused by pleasure and only slightly aroused by pain.
For the most part, they are associated with mental pleasure and only rarely associated with mental pain;
for the most part, they involve the aspiration for the attainment of happiness and only rarely the aspiration for liberation from suffering, and they function as causes for the agitation of the mind.
For the gods belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, applied thought and sustained thought are exclusively of a joyful nature;
they are exclusively internal contacts with desirable objects;
and they are exclusively aroused by pleasure.
They are exclusively associated with mental joy;
they consist of the longing for never being separated from happiness, and their function is the agitation of thought.
[The Designation of Proper Mental Attention] In that regard, what is the establishment of the designation of proper mental attention?
It should be understood as having eight aspects.
Also by way of the basis,
also by way of the entity,
and also by way of investigation.
Also from the perspective of enjoyment, from the perspective of correct practice,
and from the perspective of the application of the equipment for the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Also from the application of the equipment for the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas;
and also from the application of the accomplishment of the perfections.
In this regard, the summary verse (uddāna) is as follows:
The basis, the object, the seeking, the enjoyment, the practice, the two types of awakening, and likewise the perfections.
What is the basis for the applied thoughts and discursive investigations of those engaged in appropriate mental attention?
There are six bases, namely:
The time of certainty;
the time of cessation;
the time of action.
The time for mundane detachment,
the time for supramundane detachment,
and the time for benefiting sentient beings.

What is the object associated with wise attention? There are eight objects: the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving; [the basis of meritorious action consisting in ethical discipline; the basis of meritorious action consisting in mental cultivation; the basis of meritorious action consisting in the ripening of others; the basis of meritorious action consisting in the service of the Sangha; the basis of meritorious action consisting in the service of stūpas; the basis of meritorious action consisting in the service of parents; and the basis of meritorious action consisting in the service of teachers and preceptors. These are the eight objects. The basis of meritorious action consisting in giving...
That consisting of ethical discipline, that consisting of cultivation, and that consisting of learning.
That which consists of reflection,
that which consists of cultivation other than that,
and that which consists of analytical discernment.
And it consists of the benefit of sentient beings.
What is the investigation of applied and sustained thought by those engaged in appropriate mental attention?
It is when, for example, a certain person here seeks wealth through righteous and non-coercive means, and not through unrighteous or coercive means.
What is enjoyment?

It is when one, having thus sought out enjoyments, partakes of them without being stained by passion, without attachment, without greed, without being bound, without infatuation, without obsession, and without falling into a state of fixation;
rather, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of renunciation, one partakes of them as if they were medicine.

What is right practice? It is when, for example, a certain person here is respectful toward his mother, respectful toward his father, respectful toward ascetics, respectful toward brahmins, reverent toward the elders of the family,
one who performs what is beneficial, one who performs what is duty-bound, and one who perceives the fault in this world and the next.
He gives gifts,
performs meritorious deeds,
and observes the fast.
Having undertaken ethical discipline, one abides in it.
I shall explain the application of the equipment for the śrāvakas in detail in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*;
I shall explain the application of the equipment for the pratyekabuddhas in detail in the *Pratyekabuddhabhūmi*;
and I shall explain the application for the accomplishment of the perfections in detail in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Furthermore, there are four characteristics of a donor: desire, impartiality, the removal of distress, and [the granting of] gifts.
And right knowledge.
There are four characteristics of ethical discipline (*śīla*): aspiration, the construction of a bridge, non-transgression, and non-occurrence.
And right knowledge.
There are four characteristics of the practitioner:
purity of intention,
purity of application, and purity of resolute conviction and meditative attainment.
And there is the purification of knowledge.
There are six kinds of alms-food: alms-food by formal undertaking and alms-food for the sake of livelihood.
Alms from one who has fallen [from the community], alms from one who has renounced [the community],
and alms from one who remains in a state of deficiency regarding the [monastic] domain.
And greed for alms-food.
There are eight kinds of affliction:
the affliction of hunger and the affliction of thirst.
The affliction of hunger,
the affliction of fatigue,
and the affliction of cold.
Affliction by heat,
affliction by non-obstruction,
and affliction by obstruction.
Furthermore, there are six kinds of affliction:
that which is innate and that which obstructs one's desires.
That which is caused by external injury,
that which results from the transformation of the seasons,
and that which arises from outflows.
And it brings about the cessation of worldly discourse.
There are six kinds of assistance:
assistance by means of support,
and assistance by means of non-injury through medical treatment.
The favor of concealment,
the favor of anointing with perfumes and garlands, and the favor of living together.
There are four characteristics of a non-friend: not relinquishing an intention to cause anger,
persisting in obstructing what is desired, [and so forth].
The infliction of what is undesirable, and the infliction of what is unwholesome.
By the reversal of these [faults], the four characteristics of a friend are to be understood.
There are three kinds of assistance:
assistance with material requisites,
and assistance with joy and happiness.
The withdrawal from the bliss that is free from rapture.
Furthermore, there are these four ways of conforming and following:
namely, conforming to and following guests.
The commitment to follow one's attendants,
the commitment to follow one's elders, and the commitment to follow one's refined companions.
Indeed, regarding these four ways of following and approaching, one should understand five kinds of results by determining four points:
namely, favoring and non-harming.
Worship,
conformity with one's peers,
and these— having determined them— constitute great wealth.
Fame in all directions and intermediate directions; freedom from affliction;
and the attainment of nirvana.
And there is the going to a happy rebirth.
Furthermore, this fivefold fruit is produced.
These three are the characteristics of a wise person.
The undertaking of wholesome qualities,
the exclusivity toward the wholesome,
and firmness in the wholesome.
Furthermore, there are three:
the undertaking of higher ethical discipline,
and the undertaking of higher mind.
And the undertaking of higher wisdom.
[The designation of improper mental attention.
In that regard, what is the establishment of the designation of improper mental attention?
Herein is the summary verse:
The manifestation of the effect in the cause, the existence of the past and the future,
the self, eternal karma, and the denial of Īśvara and so forth.
The finite and the infinite, distraction, causelessness, annihilationism, non-existence,
the supreme, purity, auspiciousness, and the sixteen heterodox doctrines.
[The Sixteen Opposing Views] These sixteen are the opposing views;
namely:
The doctrine that cause and fruit exist;
the doctrine of manifestation;
and the doctrine that the past and future exist as substantial entities.
The doctrine of self; the doctrine of eternalism;
and the doctrine that there is a real cause consisting of past actions.
The doctrine that God and others are the creator; the doctrine that violence is dharma;
and the doctrine of finitude and infinity.
The doctrine of the immortality of the soul,
the doctrine of non-causality,
and the doctrine of annihilationism.
The doctrine of preeminence, the doctrine of purity,
and the doctrine of auspiciousness through curiosity.
[The Doctrine of the Existence of Cause and Effect] What is the doctrine of the existence of cause and effect?
