It is when a certain ascetic or brahmin here holds such a view and speaks thus: "At all times, eternally, constantly, and perpetually, the effect exists within the cause," such as, for example, Vārṣagaṇya.
Furthermore, for what reason do they perceive, establish, and elucidate the fruit within the cause?
Namely, through scripture and through reasoning.

What is scripture (āgama)? It is that which has come down to them through the transmission of the scriptural collections (piṭaka) via a continuous lineage of oral tradition related thereto, [namely]: "The fruit indeed exists within the cause."
What is reasoning (*yukti*)?

It is as follows: suppose that very same ascetic or brahmin is a dialectician (*tārkika*) and an investigator (*mīmāṃsaka*), established on a level encompassed by reasoning, characterized by personal intuition, pertaining to ordinary persons, and pursued through investigation.
It occurs to him thus:
Those entities from which other entities arise are established and designated as their causes,
and not others;
and for the sake of that fruit, those seeking the fruit also take up those [causes], and not others.
And it is precisely those [factors] that are employed in their respective functions, not others;
and from those alone does that fruit arise, not from others.
Therefore, that fruit belongs to this or that [specific factor].
Otherwise, indeed, everything would be established as the cause of everything;
everything would be appropriated;
and everything would be employed in every task.
Everything would arise from everything.
They perceive the fruit in the cause at all times by way of designation, by way of appropriation, by way of the application of function, and by way of arising.

He should be addressed as follows: "Do you maintain that the characteristic of the cause and the characteristic of the effect, or the characteristic of the effect of a cause, have identical characteristics or different characteristics?
If they have identical characteristics, then there is no fixed determination of the cause."

Regarding the "determination of the fruit": because cause and fruit are indistinguishable, it is not logical to say that the fruit exists within the cause. If [the fruit] were of a different characteristic, would you then maintain that it has the characteristic of being unarisen or the characteristic of being arisen?

If it has the characteristic of being unarisen, then it must have either the characteristic of a cause or the characteristic of an arisen thing. If it has the characteristic of being unarisen, then it is not tenable to say that the fruit exists unarisen within the cause.
If it has the characteristic of being already arisen,
then it is not logical that the effect arises within the cause;
therefore, the effect does not exist within the cause.
But when the cause exists, it arises in dependence upon conditions.
In that regard, a phenomenon characterized by existence should be understood as having five aspects of characteristics with respect to a phenomenon characterized by existence:
it is perceived in its location;
For example,
water in a jar is perceived in its support.
For example, visual consciousness [is perceived] in the eye;
or likewise, it is apprehended by its own characteristic.
For example, a cause is not something to be inferred.
It performs its own function,
and when the cause undergoes transformation, it too undergoes transformation, either through that change itself or through conditions for change.
Therefore, it is also illogical to claim that the effect exists eternally and permanently within the cause.
By this reasoning as well, this doctrine is indeed improperly formulated, whether from the perspective of its general characteristic, its specific characteristic,
or even its characteristic of non-arising.
It is also not tenable from the perspective of having the characteristic of being produced.
[The Theory of Manifestation: What is the theory of manifestation? It is when a certain ascetic or brahmin here holds such a view and speaks thus:
Existing entities alone are manifested; they do not arise anew.
This is just like that same proponent of the real existence of cause and effect who also maintains the theory of the defining characteristics of sound.
For what reason does the proponent of the existence of cause and effect perceive the manifestation of an effect that already exists within the cause?
It is through scripture (*āgama*) and through reasoning (*yukti*).
The scripture is to be understood as previously explained.
What is reasoning (*yukti*)?
It is when someone here becomes a rationalist (*tārkika*) or an investigator (*mīmāṃsaka*) by themselves;
the details are as before.
It occurs to him:
"Indeed, it is not logical for a fruit that already exists in its cause to arise;
yet, effort is not lacking for the production of the fruit."
And for what purpose is that [manifestation] produced?
It is solely for the sake of manifestation.
Thus, having made such a conceptual construction, he becomes a proponent of manifestation (*abhivyaktivādin*).
In this regard, one who asserts the manifestation of cause and effect should be asked this:
do you maintain that obscuration exists when the cause of obscuration is absent, or when it is present?
If [you say] when it is absent:
If the cause of obscuration does not exist, it is illogical to say that something is obscured.
If it does exist, why is it not logical for it to be connected to the fruit? If it exists, why does it not obscure the cause that is connected to the fruit?
Even if it exists,
that is not tenable;
just as darkness, by obscuring the water in a bowl, also obscures the bowl itself.
Furthermore, if the cause were also obscured by an obscuring factor,
then the effect, though existing within that cause, would be manifested;
[it is not tenable to say that the cause is not [obscured]].
He should be addressed as follows:
Is it the cause that obstructs existence, or is it the cause that obstructs the fruit?
If it is the cause that obstructs existence, then it is not logical that there is no manifestation at all times for that which exists, since the cause itself also exists.
If it is a fruit,
then that very same cause becomes the fruit of something else;
for example, a sprout is the fruit of a seed and the cause of the stalk and so forth.
Therefore, it is not logical to say that the very same thing is both manifested and unmanifested.
Therefore, he should be asked as follows:
"Do you maintain that manifestation from that dharma is non-different [or different] from it?
If it is non-different,"
It is not logical to say that a dharma which is eternally manifest is being manifested;
for if it were manifested by something else, that [cause] would have to be either with cause or without cause.
If it were causeless,
then manifestation without a cause would not be logical;
if, on the other hand, it were caused...
Therefore, manifestation as a result [of that] is not logical, because it would entail the manifestation of what was previously unmanifested.
Therefore, it is because of the non-existence of the causes of obscuration,
because of the existence of the causes of obscuration,
and because of the characteristic of being presently existing.
Also by way of the characteristic of the fruit; also by way of manifestation and other than manifestation,
and even by way of that which is other than manifestation.
It is not tenable.
Therefore, whatever entity does not exist, it simply does not exist, characterized by that [non-existence];
whatever entity exists, it simply exists, characterized by that [existence].
The non-manifestation of the non-existent is simply its non-existence;
the manifestation of the existent is simply its existence.
I shall now state the characteristics of how an existent object is perceived according to its mode of apprehension;
furthermore, there is non-apprehension of an existent object due to distance.
It occurs because it is obscured by four causes of obscuration,
and also because of even subtle distraction of the mind.
Also because of the impairment of the cessation and delight of the faculties,
and also because of the non-attainment of the knowledge associated with them.
Just as the theory of the manifestation of cause and effect is untenable, so too should the theory of the manifestation of sound be regarded as untenable;
however, there is this distinction between them.
The proponent of sound perceives that the characteristic of sound is fixed exactly as it has been designated.

Furthermore, he perceives that its manifestation occurs through the repeated utterance by means of expression of that which is thus fixed; because of this, he concludes that "sound is eternal. Therefore, even the theory of manifestation is improperly formulated.
[The Doctrine of the Real Existence of Past and Future Entities:
What is the doctrine of the real existence of past and future entities?
It is when a certain ascetic or brahmin here—whether following this Dharma or not—possesses such a view and speaks thus based on improper reflection.
The past exists;
the future exists;
it is fully established by way of its characteristic.
Just as the present [dharma] is substantially existent (dravyasat),
it is not nominally existent (prajñaptisat).
For what reason does he hold such a view and speak thus?
It is because of both scripture and reasoning.
[It is established] through scripture and through reasoning. What is scripture?
It should be understood as previously described.
Furthermore, in this context, one who follows the Dharma may incorrectly conceptualize the discourses (sūtrāntas).
For example:
"Everything exists" refers to the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*). The twelve sense bases exist by way of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇataḥ*).
For example, it was said by the Blessed One: "There is past karma.
For example: "There is past form, there is future [form], and so on up to consciousness."
What is reasoning (*yukti*)?
It is as follows: here, a certain person is a dialectician (*tārkika*) or an investigator (*mīmāṃsaka*), as described previously;
it occurs to him as follows:
Whatever phenomenon is established by whatever characteristic, it is perfected by that [characteristic]. If it were not future, it would then lack its own unappropriated characteristic;
if it were not past, it would then have lost its own characteristic.
In that case, it would have a self-characteristic that is fully established;
therefore, it is not tenable to say that it has a self-characteristic that is not fully established.
It is by virtue of this [view] that one holds such a view and speaks thus: "The past exists."
"There is also that which is future."
He should be asked this:
do you maintain that the characteristics of the past and the future are either non-different in characteristic from the characteristic of the present, or are they different in characteristic?
If they are non-different in characteristic, [then...]
The threefold establishment of the characteristic is not tenable;
if it were a distinct characteristic, the perfected characteristic would not be tenable.
He should be addressed as follows:
"Do you maintain that a phenomenon not included within the three times has the characteristic of permanence or the characteristic of impermanence?
If it has the characteristic of permanence, then it is not logical for it to be included within the three times."
If it were characterized by impermanence,
then it would not be logical for it to exist in that same way throughout the three times.
He should be asked this:
"Do you perceive the present time-path or the arrival of that which has not yet come? Or do you perceive its passing away or its rebirth, while it remains thus in the future?"
Depending on that, there is the arising of the present;
or the state of being transitive for that which is intransitive;
or the state of having complete characteristics for that which has incomplete characteristics; or [the state of] having distinct characteristics.
Or, if the future entity, having a distinct characteristic, comes into the state of the present,
then by that it becomes situated in space.
And it is not logical that he be eternal while remaining indistinguishable from the present;
for if he were to pass away and be reborn, then he would neither be future nor already arisen.
It is not tenable that what was previously unarisen becomes arisen, or that what was unarisen falls away;
for if it were to arise dependently while remaining exactly as it was [there], [it would be contradictory].
It is not eternal; nor is it that something previously non-existent has arisen;
nor is it tenable to say that what was future has arisen.

If, having been without action (*akarmaka*), it becomes possessed of action (*sakarmaka*), then because it comes into being from what was previously non-existent, the aforementioned faults would apply to that very same [entity]; thus, it is not tenable. Furthermore, do you maintain that this action has a characteristic distinct from [the entity] or a characteristic non-distinct from it?
If it has distinct characteristics,
it is not tenable that it lacks the characteristic of the future;
if it has non-distinct characteristics, [it is likewise untenable].
Therefore, it is not logical to say that having been without an object, it subsequently comes to have an object.
Just as it is with its own karma, so too should it be understood as having complete characteristics, distinct characteristics, and the characteristics of future existence;
in this regard, the distinction is that the fault of the confusion of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) is not applicable.

Just as the future and the present are [faulty], so too the present and the past should be seen as endowed with faults, as appropriate, by these very same reasons and by this very subsequent method— both in terms of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*),
and their sequence (*āgatita*).
Also from the perspective of death and rebirth,
also from the perspective of dependent origination,
and also from the perspective of karma.

The doctrine that past and future entities exist substantially is [refuted] by way of their being complete in characteristics, by way of their having distinct characteristics, and by way of their non-existence in the future.
It is not tenable.
Furthermore, when this has been thus explained,
if one were to say further: "If the past and the future do not exist,
how can cognition proceed with a non-existent object?"
Furthermore, that [consciousness] continues to proceed. How, then, is there no contradiction with the scripture which states that "all" refers only to the twelve sense-bases?
He should be addressed as follows:
"Do you maintain that the cognition apprehending 'it does not exist' either does not occur or does occur in the world?"
If [it refers to] non-occurrence,
then it is not tenable that there is no cognition whatsoever which apprehends selflessness or apprehends things such as a rabbit’s horn or the son of a barren woman.
Furthermore, as for what was said— that "everything exists" to the extent of the twelve bases— that too was said with reference to the existence of the characteristic of being existent.
And there is the existence of the characteristic of non-existence;
for even those phenomena that possess the characteristic of existence maintain the characteristic of existence,
and even those phenomena that possess the characteristic of non-existence maintain the characteristic of non-existence.
Therefore, they are called "dharmas.

Otherwise, because of the knowledge of what exists and the non-knowledge of what does not exist, the yogin would not have an uninterrupted investigation of the dharmas to be known; thus, [the other view] is not tenable.

As for what was said— that there exists past karma because sentient beings experience affliction and the results of affliction— even in that case, it was stated with the intention of applying the designation "existence" to its latent impression (*vāsanā*).

That specific continuum of formations (*saṃskāra-santati*) which proceeds by means of that cause and that condition— namely, whatever wholesome or unwholesome karma has arisen and ceased within those formations— is called the "latent impression."
It is not tenable that the desirable or undesirable fruit is produced from that [action] which has fallen into the continuum;
therefore, there is no fault even on that account.
As for what was also said— that "past form exists, future form exists, and present form exists, and so on up to consciousness"—
that too was stated with reference to the threefold characteristic of conditioned phenomena:
the characteristic of the cause, the specific characteristic, and the characteristic of the fruit.
With reference to the characteristic of cause, it was said that "the future exists";
with reference to the existence of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it was said that "the present exists";
and with reference to the characteristic of fruit, it was said that "the past exists."
For this reason as well, there is no fault.
Moreover, when it is not being applied [to the present], the future characteristic should be understood as having twelve aspects, even though it is substantially characterized by the past and future;
it is manifested by its cause.
It has an unarisen body, depends upon conditions,
belongs to the class of the arisen,
and is also subject to the nature of arising.
It is without the arising of affliction, without the arising of purification,
and yet it is worthy of aspiration.
It is neither to be sought nor not to be sought; it is both to be examined and not to be examined;
it is precisely the present characteristic in its twelve aspects.
Manifested by its fruit;
having arisen as a body;
with conditions present.
Of the nature of having arisen,
momentary,
and subject to non-arising.
That which is accompanied by affliction, that which is accompanied by purification,
that which is conducive to dependence, and that which is not conducive to dependence.

It should be understood that the past characteristic is also to be examined and not to be examined; it is also to be examined and not to be examined as a point of reference; and it possesses twelve aspects.
It has past causes, past conditions, and past fruits.
Its body is destroyed;
its intrinsic nature has ceased;
it is of a nature that does not arise.
With afflictions thoroughly stilled, with purification thoroughly stilled,
it is a state that serves as a basis for dependence.
[That which is] like a state of indifference,
that which is to be examined, and that which is not to be examined.
[The Theory of Self] What is the theory of self?
It is when a certain ascetic or brahmin here possesses such a view and speaks thus:
For example:

an outsider, a non-Buddhist, [asserts] that from the perspective of reality and from the perspective of its abiding nature, there exists a self, or a sentient being, or a living soul, or a nourisher, or a person, and so forth.
Why does he hold such a view and speak thus? It is both through scriptural authority and through reasoning.
In this regard, the scriptural authority (*āgama*) is as before.
What is the reasoning (*yukti*)?
It is as follows: for instance, there is here a certain person who is a dialectician (*tārkika*) or an investigator (*mīmāṃsaka*), and so forth, as described previously.
It is due to two reasons:

because, even when there is no prior conscious intent, the engagement of the notion of a sentient being is observed; and because, when there is prior conscious intent, purposeful movement is observed.
It occurs to him as follows:
"If the self did not exist, then upon seeing the five kinds of objects through the five modes, the notion of a self would not arise.
Upon seeing a form, only the cognition of 'form' would arise, and not the cognition of a 'sentient being'."

Having seen a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskāra) that is neither rent asunder by pleasure nor by pain, only the cognition of "perception" (saṃjñā) would arise, not the cognition of a being as low or high;
only the cognition of "feeling" (vedanā), and so forth, would arise,
not the cognition of a being as low or high.
Upon seeing a formation associated with a name, there would arise only the cognition of the name;
there would not be the cognition of a sentient being, such as "a kṣatriya," "a brāhmaṇa," "a vaiśya," "a śūdra," "Brahmadatta," or "Guṇamitra.
Upon seeing a formation associated with auspicious or inauspicious activities, there would arise only the cognition of the formation.
There is no cognition of beings as either fools or wise;
rather, having observed the conformity of consciousness to its objects, it is only the cognition of the mind that proceeds,
such as the cognition of beings [expressed as] "I do not see," and so forth.
And since, in these five bases, the notion of a "sentient being" alone arises without prior reflection— rather than the notion of "formative forces"—
therefore, first of all, having seen this without prior reflection, it occurs to him simply from the perception of the notion of a sentient being that "the self exists."
It occurs to him thus:
"If there were no self, then no volitional activity preceded by cognition would be observed regarding the formative forces (saṃskāra), such as:
'I shall see forms with the eye,' 'I am seeing them,' or 'I have seen them.'"
Nor does one act preceded by the volitional formation (abhisaṃskāra) thinking, "I shall not see.
Just as it is with seeing, so it should be understood regarding hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the mind.

Likewise, this applies to the performance of wholesome karma and the manifestation of wholesome karma, as well as the performance of unwholesome karma and the manifestation of unwholesome karma, and so forth.
Volitional activity preceded by cognition would not be perceived;
nor is such activity compatible with a mere formation (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, it occurs thus: "The self exists."
He should be asked this:
Do you maintain that the notion of a sentient being arises with respect to exactly what one perceives,
or rather that one perceives one thing while the notion of a sentient being arises with respect to another?

If it were in that very [self], then because of the misconception that there is a "being" in form and so forth, the claim that "the self exists" would be untenable. If, on the other hand, it were elsewhere, [then the self would not be perceived].
Therefore, it is not tenable that the self possesses form;
nor is it tenable that the self is something that falls or rises, or is a kṣatriya and so forth, or is a fool or a wise man, or is the grasper of objects such as visible forms.

Do you maintain that the arising of cognition regarding a phenomenon occurs solely from its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or also from the intrinsic nature of another? If it were solely from its own intrinsic nature, then by that [reasoning], the cognition would be inverted with respect to exactly that which it perceives; thus, a cognition of a self (*ātman*) would not be tenable.
If it were from another [cause] as well, it would not be logical that all objects serve as the causes for the cognition of all objects.

Do you maintain that there arises, or does not arise, the cognition of a being in what is reckoned as a non-being, or the cognition of a non-being in what is reckoned as a being, or furthermore, the cognition of one being reckoned as such-and-such in what is reckoned as another being?
If it arises, then even a non-sentient being would become a sentient being, and a sentient being would also become another sentient being; this is not tenable.
If it does not arise, [then it is not tenable].
It is not tenable to claim that the means of valid cognition known as direct perception (pratyakṣa-pramāṇa) is thereby rejected.
Do you maintain that this cognition of a "sentient being" (sattva-buddhi) apprehends an object of direct perception or an object of inference?
If it apprehends an object of direct perception,
then it is not tenable, because in that case the aggregates (skandhas), such as form (rūpa) and so forth, would be the directly perceived objects, and not a "sentient being."
If it were a grasper of objects apprehended through inference, then it would not be logical for it to function impulsively even in infants who have not yet engaged in such inferential deliberation.
He should be addressed as follows:
"Do you maintain that [the self] is caused by cognition or caused by sentient beings?
If he says it is caused by cognition, [then...]
It is not tenable that the self acts;
if it were caused by the self,
it is not tenable that action is preceded by intelligence.
Do you wish that the cause of movement is impermanent or permanent?
If it were impermanent,
it would not be tenable for the self, being subject to change, to move.
If it were eternal and unchanging,
then it would not be logical for that which is unchanging to engage in activity.
Do you wish that the being acts with a resolute nature, or without a resolute nature? If it is with a resolute nature:
In that case, it is not logical to say that what was previously inactive acts again.
If it were of the nature of non-determination,
then it would not be logical for that which is of the nature of non-determination to act.
Do you maintain that a sentient being acts with a cause or acts without a cause?
If it is with a cause,
then it is not tenable that there is another who impels the sentient being to act.
If it were without cause, it would follow that everything would always and at all times be active; this is not tenable.
Do you hold that a sentient being acts independently or dependently?
If it were independent,
it would not be logical for it to exert itself toward its own sickness, old age, death, suffering, and affliction.
If it were dependent on another,
it would not be logical to say that the self acts of its own accord.
He should be addressed as follows:

"Do you maintain that the designation 'sentient being' applies to the mere aggregates, or to something within the aggregates, or to something other than the aggregates? If it is the former, then the being is not distinct from the aggregates."
Therefore, it is not tenable that there exists a self as a reality established apart from the aggregates; nor,
if [it were] within the aggregates, would it be distinct from them.
It must be either eternal or non-eternal. If it were eternal,
then for that which is eternal, benefit by pleasure or injury by suffering would not be possible.

Furthermore, in the absence of benefit or harm, the operation of merit and demerit is not tenable. If the operation of merit and demerit does not exist, there would be the absolute non-arising of bodies.
And if there were no effort, it would not be tenable that the self is eternally liberated.
If it were impermanent,
it would not be tenable, because it would not be perceived as distinct from conditioned phenomena due to its occurrence as a continuous succession of destruction and arising.
Moreover, in this case, it would not be logical for that which has perished here to undergo the fault of "attaining what was not done" elsewhere.
If [the being] were other than the aggregates,
then it would not be logical for the being to be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If it were separate from the aggregates, then because of the lack of connection, it would not be logical for the self to be eternally defiled by them.
Do you maintain that [the self] is characterized by being a seer and so forth, or that it has characteristics other than those?
If it is characterized by being a seer and so forth,
is it characterized as a seer by applying the metaphorical designation of "seer-ness" to the acts of seeing and so on, or is it distinct from them?
If there is a metaphorical designation [of "self"] with respect to seeing and so forth, then it is not tenable that seeing and so forth themselves are the seers, nor that the self is the seer;
for the self would be indistinguishable from seeing and so forth.
If, on the other hand, it were something other than those, [it would follow that it could exist even without them].
Therefore, that seeing and so forth must be either the action (karman) or the instrument (karaṇa) of the self;
if it were the action,
it would be like a seed.
Therefore, because it is impermanent, it is not tenable;
for example, like a person engaged in conventional activities such as a potter.
Consequently, it is neither tenable that it is impermanent nor that it is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*).
It is not logical that he should act according to his own will in all matters;
for if he were like the earth, he would therefore be impermanent.
Nor is it incorrect to say that its action is not as manifest as that of the earth; for the action of the earth is clearly perceived,
in that, by virtue of it, [the body] does not fall downward.
If it were like space,
then it would not be tenable to define space as the mere absence of form;
moreover, even though it exists only as a designation, its activity is clearly perceived.
However, it is not tenable to say that [the self] does not [possess action].
For indeed, the action of space is clearly perceived, by virtue of which actions such as coming, going, contracting, and expanding proceed.
Therefore, it is not tenable to claim that [space] lacks action.

If it were an instrument, like a sickle or similar tools, then just as there is no action such as cutting other than the sickle itself, so too no other act of seeing could be perceived apart from the seeing [itself]; thus, [the position] is not tenable.
If, on the other hand, it were like fire...
Therefore, the postulation of a useless fire is not tenable;
for in that case, fire would burn by itself even without a burner. If it were distinct from that which is characterized as the seer and so forth, [it would follow that it burns independently].
Therefore, it is not tenable that the self is devoid of all means of valid cognition.
He should be addressed as follows:
"Do you maintain that what is endowed with the characteristics of affliction and purification is either afflicted or purified,
or rather that which is not endowed with those characteristics?"
If something endowed with the characteristics of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) is either afflicted or purified,

then those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in which calamities, misfortunes, and obstacles are found, as well as their cessation and benefits, are endowed with the characteristics of affliction and purification.
Therefore, in the absence of a self (*ātman*), it is not logical that they themselves are afflicted or purified.
For example, just as external entities and internal bodies—
if that [self] were devoid of their characteristics,
then being free from the characteristics of affliction and purification, it would be illogical for it to be afflicted, purified, or to be called "self."
He should be addressed as follows:
"Do you maintain that whatever is endowed with the characteristic of being active both proceeds and ceases,
or rather that it is not endowed with that characteristic?"
If it is endowed with such characteristics, then within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the characteristic of the fivefold activator (*pravartaka-lakṣaṇa*) is perceived;
for it is as follows:

That which has the nature of arising from causes, the nature of passing away, proceeding through mutual succession, and being subject to change— that is the characteristic of that which sets [phenomena] in motion.
And this is observed among conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*),
such as in the body, a sprout, a river, a lamp, and the current of a vehicle.
Therefore, it is not logical that it is the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) alone that proceed and cease in the absence of a self;
for if that were the case,
it would follow that a self devoid of the characteristic of being an agent proceeds and ceases, which is likewise not logical.
He should be addressed as follows:
"Do you maintain that one who undergoes transformation through pleasure and pain produced by sense objects is the same as one who undergoes transformation through volition?"
And he who undergoes transformation through the primary and secondary afflictions is either the enjoyer, the agent, or the liberator; or else,
he who does not undergo transformation [is so].
If it undergoes transformation,
then it is not tenable that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) alone are the experiencers, the agents, and the liberators, nor that the self (*ātman*) is impermanent.
If, on the other hand, it does not undergo transformation, [then it is likewise untenable].
Therefore, it is not logical to claim that the self—which is the enjoyer, the agent, and the liberator—is free from change.
He should be addressed as follows:
"Do you maintain that the metaphorical designation of 'agent' applies only to the self, or also to something other than the self?
If it applies only to the self,"
It is not tenable to say that fire burns and produces light.

If [the agent] is also elsewhere, then the metaphorical designation of an "agent" with respect to the sense faculties such as sight is merely a useless conceptualization of a self; thus, it is not tenable.
He should be asked this:
"Do you intend the metaphorical designation 'self' to apply only to the self itself, or also to something else?
If he says it applies only to the self itself, [then...]
Therefore, conventional designations such as "Guṇamitra" or "Buddhadatta" applied to a human body would not be tenable;
nor would they be tenable if [the designation] were applied elsewhere.

Consequently, since the metaphorical designation of a "self" applies to nothing more than the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), the conceptualization of a self is useless and is therefore untenable.
For in this way, it is in common usage that the person alone is designated here by the term "sentient being" (sattva);
he is so designated both by himself and by others.
He should be addressed as follows:
"Do you maintain that this view of self is wholesome or unwholesome?
If it is wholesome..."
Therefore, it arises even more intensely in those who are more deluded;
it arises even without application;
and because it causes terror regarding liberation and nourishes faults, it is not tenable [to claim that such a view is the path].
If it were unwholesome, then, in that case,
it would not be appropriate to say it is non-erroneous;
and if there were such an error, it would not be appropriate to say "the self exists."
Do you maintain that the view of selflessness is wholesome or unwholesome?
If it is wholesome,
then it is not logical to claim that the view of selflessness— which exists as a reality, abides as a reality, and pertains to a real self— is wholesome and non-erroneous.
If it were unwholesome,
then it would not be logical that it was taught by the Omniscient One, produced through application, non-terrifying toward liberation, possessing white fruit, and serving as the antidote to faults.
Do you maintain that it is the self itself which thinks "the self exists," or that this is a view of self?
If it were the self itself, then the cognition that "the self never does not exist" would arise; therefore, [your position] is not tenable.

If it is the view of a self, then even though no self exists, because of the power of the vision of a self, one thinks "the self exists" with respect to what is merely conditioned formations; thus, it is not tenable. [Therefore, it is not tenable that the self exists.]

Thus, by way of the establishment of characteristics, the establishment of affliction and purification, and the establishment of engagement and cessation—even by way of the designation of an enjoyer, an agent, a knower, and a seer—it is not tenable that a self exists.
Rather, I shall explain the ultimate characteristic of the self:
it is the designation of a self with respect to phenomena (*dharmas*).
It cannot be described as either different or non-different from them,
lest it possess substantial existence (*dravyasattva*),
or else those phenomena (*dharmas*) themselves would possess the characteristic of a self (*ātman*). Furthermore, its characteristic is impermanence (*anitya*).
It has the characteristic of instability;
it has the characteristic of being unreliable; it has the characteristic of being untrustworthy;
it has the characteristic of transformation; and it has the characteristic of being subject to birth.
It has the characteristic of being subject to old age, sickness, and death;
it has the characteristic of being merely phenomena (dharma);
it has the characteristic of being merely suffering (duḥkha).
For thus it was said by the Blessed One:
"In this way, monks, these phenomena are the self;
that self of yours, monks, is impermanent, unstable, and unreliable."
"O monk, 'self' is of a nature subject to change," and so forth.

Furthermore, the designation of a "sentient being" with respect to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) should be understood as being for four reasons: for the sake of ease of communication, for the sake of conforming to worldly convention, for the sake of abandoning fear that the entity of a sentient being does not exist in any way whatsoever, and [for the sake of... [Note: The source text appears to be truncated here].
It is for the purpose of designating [distinctions] between self and other, and for the sake of producing the conviction regarding the existence of qualities and the existence of defects;
therefore, even the doctrine of a self is established through improper application.
[The Doctrine of Eternalism] What is the doctrine of eternalism?
It is as follows: here, a certain ascetic or brahmin—as before.
The self and the world are eternal;
they are uncreated, not produced by a creator, and unmanifested.
Not created by transformation, he is indestructible;
he remains as immovable as a pillar, standing firm like a shaft.
For example:

Those who maintain the doctrine of eternalism, those who maintain partial eternalism, and those who speculate about the past or the future— including those who maintain the doctrine of perception, the doctrine of non-perception,
and the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
as well as certain others who maintain the doctrine of eternalism.
For what reason does one hold such a view and speak thus:
"The self and the world are eternal"?
That reason should be understood exactly as it is in the sūtra and according to the appropriate application.

In this regard, for those who speculate about the past (*pūrvāntakalpaka*), who— relying on weak, medium, or intense meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and possessing skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)— speculate about the past limit (*pūrvānta*) through the recollection of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), there arises that [false] view for them as they correctly perceive and understand with mindfulness alone regarding past conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

Or again, for those who speculate about the past limit of the present time by relying on the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), [there arises that view] regarding the momentary destruction and continuous succession of conditioned phenomena.
This view arises for those who do not understand things as they truly are, perceiving a continuous stream of consciousness that passes from this world to the next;
or for one who perceives the fulfillment of Brahmā’s own desire, and perceives the transformation of the primary elements and the transformation of consciousness.

Furthermore, when one perceives the diversity of perception and feeling in the future limit (*aparānta*), yet does not perceive a diversity of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the following view does not arise:
"The self and the world are eternal."
Furthermore, those who grasp at the permanence of atoms, relying on mundane meditative concentration (*laukikadhyāna*), perceive things in this way:

they fail to understand dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as it truly is; instead, they imagine that the arising of the accumulation of effects among entities is preceded by existence, and their destruction is preceded by non-existence, whereby such a view occurs to them.
A gross substance is produced from atoms;
and when a gross substance is divided, it remains in the state of atoms.
Therefore, a gross substance is impermanent.
"Atoms are eternal.

In this regard, because the doctrine of eternalism held by those who speculate about the past and those who speculate about the future is subsumed under specific characteristics, when the doctrine of a self has been refuted within the theory of a self, the doctrine of the specific characteristics of a self is also thereby refuted.
Furthermore, he should be asked this:
"Do you maintain that the recollection of past lives grasps at the aggregates (*skandha*) or grasps at a self (*ātman*)? If it grasps at the aggregates,"
It is not tenable that the self and the world are eternal;
if there were such grasping at a self,
then those [beings] would have been named "so-and-so."
It is not tenable to state in detail, "In that place where I existed, I had such a name, such a birth," and so forth.

Do you maintain that when visual consciousness, which has form as its objective support, has become manifest and the object of form alone is present while other objects are absent, there is either the cessation or the arising of the other consciousnesses?
If [you say] there is cessation:
It is not logical that consciousness is the cause of its own opposition;
for if it were an active process,
then by means of that single object, the activity of all consciousnesses would occur at all times, which is not logical.
Do you maintain that there is a modification of the self produced by perception or produced by feeling, or not? If [you say] it exists, then it is not tenable that the self and the world are eternal;
if it does not exist, [then the same follows].

Therefore, it is not logical that one who has become possessed of the perception of unity should subsequently possess the perception of diversity, the perception of the limited, or the perception of the immeasurable.
That one becomes exclusively happy, exclusively miserable, both happy and miserable, or neither miserable nor happy is not tenable.
[The doctrine of the soul being identical with the body:

In that regard, whoever perceives that the living being is the same as the body perceives the self as possessing form; whereas he who perceives that the living being is one thing and the body another [perceives the self as formless].
He [who perceives] the formless;

he who perceives the self as both entirely, non-dual, and complete— both the formed and the formless, and their opposites— clinging to this very same meaning through different words and syllables, sees the self as formed and not as formless.
If, moreover, he perceives it as either material or immaterial, or as limited, he perceives it as finite.
If he sees it as immeasurable, he sees it as infinite;
if he sees it as a whole.
By way of the form-aspect it is limited, and by way of the formless-aspect it is immeasurable; or by way of the formless-aspect it is limited, and by way of the form-aspect it is immeasurable.
He perceives it as both finite and infinite.

Or, through the antidote to that, while not adhering to a diversity of meaning, he perceives a diversity of expression; thus he perceives it as neither finite nor infinite, or else, being liberated, he perceives the non-dual.
[The Doctrine of the Permanence of Atoms:
Furthermore, the proponent of the permanence of atoms should be asked this:
Do you maintain that the permanence of the atom is unexamined, or is it examined?
If it is unexamined,
then it is not logical to determine its permanence without such examination.
If it has been examined,
then it is not tenable [to claim] that it contradicts all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Do you assert that atoms are eternal because of their subtlety, or because they possess characteristics distinct from gross, effect-producing substances?
If it is because of their subtlety,
then since that which is diminished is weaker, it is not logical for it to be eternal.
If [it is argued that it arises] because of having a different characteristic,
then by that [reasoning], having transcended the characteristics of earth, water, fire, and air, the production of an effect with a characteristic of a dissimilar kind is also not tenable;
furthermore, another characteristic is also not possible, and thus it is not tenable.
Do you maintain that a gross substance is of non-different characteristics from its atoms, or of different characteristics?
If it is of non-different characteristics, then,
being indistinguishable from the cause, it would likewise be eternal.
Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that there is neither a fixed law of causes nor a fixed law of results.
If it has an undifferentiated characteristic,
do you then maintain that it is produced from atoms that are separated or from those that are joined?
If [you say] from those that are separated:
Therefore, it is not logical that all effects should arise at all times, nor that there should be no determination of cause or determination of effect.
If [you say it arises] from those that are conjoined,
then do you maintain that its form and substance are non-distinct from them, or that its form and substance are distinct?
If [you say] its form and substance are non-distinct;
That which is produced from the substance of its form is not [identical] to the form itself;
for if the form were not distinct from its configuration,
then, because an atom lacks parts, there would be no division.
It is not tenable that even a gross substance is eternal;
furthermore, it is not tenable that an atom is eternal when a previously non-existent atom comes into being.
Do you maintain that atoms initiate gross substances like seeds and so forth, or like potters and the like?
If it is like seeds and so forth,
then it is not tenable to say that [the self] is impermanent like a seed.
If [the atom] were like a potter and so forth,
then it would not be logical for the atom to be conscious.
If it is not like a seed and so forth, then it is not like a potter and so forth either.
Therefore, it is not logical to say that no illustrative example can be found.
Do you maintain that the production of external phenomena is caused by sentient beings or not? If it is caused by sentient beings,
then gross matter must be caused by sentient beings.
It is not logical that the subtle substance which serves as their basis is not caused by sentient beings;
for by what could its capacity be prevented?
If it were not caused by sentient beings, then the manifestation of external entities would be purposeless, which is also illogical.
Thus, it is [the case] even from the recollection of the aggregates and sentient beings;
even from the fact that the stream of all consciousnesses proceeds by means of a single object;
and even from the presence of change and the absence of change due to perceptions and feelings.
For those who speculate about the past and those who speculate about the future, the doctrine of eternalism is not tenable.
Also by way of examination and re-examination,
also by way of the general characteristic,
and also by way of the fundamental characteristic.
Even from the perspective of its inception and even from the perspective of its fundamental purpose,
there is the doctrine of the permanence of atoms.
This is not tenable;
therefore, this doctrine as well is established through improper reasoning.
Furthermore, I shall explain the characteristic of the eternal: that which is at all times characterized by the absence of change,
and in every way characterized by the absence of change.
It is characterized by being itself changeless,
and characterized by being changeless from another perspective, as well as being unborn;
this should be understood as the characteristic of permanence.
[The doctrine of past deeds as the cause:
What is the doctrine of past deeds as the cause?
It is as follows: "There is here a certain ascetic or brahmin," and so on in detail, as in the Sūtra.
Whatever this person experiences is generally designated as "suffering. The phrase "caused by previous actions" means it is caused by evil deeds.
The phrase "by the exhaustion of past karma through austerity" means by means of hardship in the present life. And [the exhaustion] of new [karma]...
The intention is that this is due to the complete eradication of the non-performance of unwholesome actions;
thus, it is "without outflows" (anāsrava) in the future.
Exclusively wholesome states are called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) in the future.
Because of being outflow-free, there is the exhaustion of karma; the intention here is that this refers to evil.

Because of the exhaustion of karma, there is the exhaustion of suffering; the intention here is that this refers both to that which has previously been caused by past actions and to that which arises from present conditions in this very life.

The statement that "from the destruction of suffering, there comes an end to suffering" refers to that which pertains to the continuity of future births; this is the intention [of the teaching], as for example among the Nirgranthas.
For what reason does one have such a view and speak thus?
It is because of both scripture and reasoning.

The scriptural authority (*āgama*) is as before. What is the reasoning (*yukti*)? It is as follows: for instance, there is here a certain person who is a dialectician (*tārkika*), and so forth, as described previously.
Because in the present life, one observes the failure of human effort;
for instance, he sees that in the world suffering arises even for those who possess correct application.
Even for those who engage in wrong practice, when pleasure arises,
it occurs to them: "If this were caused by human effort (*puruṣakāra*),
then it would be the opposite of this [i.e., it would not arise]."
Because that [result] arises for me from the reversal of that [cause], therefore this has a prior cause; one who holds such a view is a proponent of such a doctrine.
He should be addressed as follows:
"Do you maintain that this suffering which arises from present conditions is caused by past actions, or is it caused by present conditions?
If it is caused by past actions..."

Therefore, it is not logically consistent [to claim] that there is no outflow in the future because of the exhaustion of past karmas through asceticism (*tapas*), or because of the eradication of the performance of present ones;
this would apply only if [the suffering] were caused by an onset in the present life.

That whatever this person experiences is entirely caused by past actions is not tenable; thus, it is not tenable that even the suffering resulting from external assault has either past action as its cause or human effort as its cause.
Therefore, this doctrine too is improperly formulated.
Moreover, there is suffering that is caused exclusively by past actions;
for instance, here some person, through the sovereign power of their own karma, is born in the miserable realms, or in low, wretched families.
There is also suffering caused by a mixture of factors.
For example, it is like the fruitless suffering that comes from serving a king in a wrongful manner;
as one serves a king, so too [is it].
For one engaged in the activities of commerce, agricultural labor, or theft,
or for one intent upon harming others,
human effort succeeds when it is meritorious, but becomes fruitless when it is demeritorious.
It is caused exclusively by human effort (*puruṣakāra*), such as: karma that projects a new existence;
for one who hears the true Dharma, realizes the dharmas face-to-face, adopts a [specific] posture, or trains in the various arts and crafts.
Such are the factors that have human effort as their cause.
[The Doctrine of a Creator such as Īśvara] What is the doctrine of a creator such as Īśvara? It is as follows: "There is, for instance, a certain ascetic or brahmin," and so on in detail as before.
Whatever this person experiences, all that is caused by the creation of Īśvara, or caused by the creation of another person, and so forth—
such as those who propound an unequal cause such as Īśvara and the like.
For what reason does one hold such a view and speak in such a manner?
From scripture and from reasoning.
Scripture is as previously described.
What is reasoning?
For example, as previously stated, there is someone here who is a dialectician;
this is because one observes the occurrence of acting according to one's own will with respect to both causes and results. To illustrate:
And at the time of the cause, thinking "we shall proceed toward what is wholesome," sentient beings, against their own will, proceed even toward evil;
and at the time of the fruit, thinking "we shall be reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world among the gods," they are reborn in the miserable states.

Thinking, "We shall enjoy happiness," they instead experience only suffering, because of which it occurs to them: "There exists some agent, creator, fashioner, or father of beings—whether he be Īśvara or someone else."
He should be addressed as follows: [This is] the summary verse:
because of the impossibility of capacity, due to the absence of inclusion and the contradiction of non-existence, even though it is purposeless.
Because faults would arise if [the self] were the cause.
Regarding that power of creation belonging to the Lord, do you maintain that it has karma-yoga as its cause or that it is causeless?
If it has karma-yoga as its cause, then it is not tenable to say that the world has karma-yoga as its cause [independently of the Lord].
If it were causeless,
then it would not be logical to say that this world is causeless.
Do you maintain that the Lord is included within the world or not?
If he is included, [then...]
It is not logical that one who possesses the same attributes as the world should create the world.
If he is not included [within the world],
then it is not logical that he creates the world once he is liberated from it.
Furthermore, do you maintain that he creates for a purpose, or without a purpose?
If he possesses a purpose, then it is not logical that the Lord of the World is not sovereign with respect to that purpose.
If it were purposeless,
then since there would be no purpose, it is not logical that he creates [the world].
Do you maintain that creation has God as its cause, or that it has some other material cause?
If it has God alone as its cause, then whenever God exists, there must be creation.
Since the creation is the Lord himself, it is not tenable to say that the creation has the Lord as its cause.

If that [rebirth] has as its cause the appropriation of something other than that, then it must either have desire as its cause, or— setting aside desire— it must have the appropriation of something other than that as its cause. If it has desire as its cause:
Furthermore, is that desire caused solely by Īśvara, or is it caused by a material cause other than him?
If it were caused solely by Īśvara, then whenever there is Īśvara there would be desire, and whenever there is desire there would be Īśvara; thus, creation would have to occur eternally.
If it were caused by another material cause,
that [cause] is not perceived; and since he is not present there, it is not tenable to say that Īśvara is the Lord of the world.
Thus, also by way of capacity;
also by way of inclusion and non-inclusion;
and also by way of being purposeful and being purposeless.
It is also not tenable from the perspective of its being a cause;
therefore, this doctrine as well is improperly formulated.
[The doctrine of violence as dharma:
What is the doctrine of violence as dharma?
It is, for example, as when someone here [holds such a view], and so on in detail as previously described.
In sacrifices, there is the taking of life preceded by the ritual application of mantras;

and it is for the sake of the heavenly rebirth of all of them—the one who offers the oblation, the one to whom it is offered, and those who are their assistants—that such a view arises and such a doctrine is held.
For what reason does he have this view and speak thus?
This is a doctrine established on the fringes, fabricated by the crafty and not set forth after considering logical reasoning.
It was devised by Brahmins when the Kali age had arrived, who, desiring to eat meat, transgressed the ancient dharma of the Brahmins.
Furthermore, he should be asked this: "Do you maintain that this ritual procedure for mantras is of the nature of dharma or of the nature of non-dharma?
If it is of the nature of dharma..."
Even without that [intention], one does not accomplish what is desired by oneself through the taking of life;
therefore, it is not logical to say that one performs non-dharma or dharma [merely through the act].
If it were of the nature of non-dharma,
then it would not be logical that a dharma which is itself undesirable in its result could turn away another dharma that is undesirable in its result.
And if, when this has been refuted, he should further say:
"Just as poison, when held under the control of a mantra-ritual, does not cause death,
so too should the mantra-ritual be understood in this case."
He should be addressed as follows:
"Do you maintain that just as the ritual of mantras pacifies external poison, so too does it pacify the internal poison of passion, hatred, and delusion?
If he maintains that it pacifies them in exactly that way, [then one should respond accordingly].
Furthermore, since that tranquility is not perceived in any place, at any time, or in anyone in such a manner, it is not tenable.
If it does not pacify [the afflictions],
then it is not logical that unwholesome states (adharma) should pacify them in the same way that the ritual procedures for mantras pacify external poison.
Do you maintain that the ritual procedure for mantras is universal or non-universal?
If it is universal, [then...]
It is not logical that one's own beloved kinsman, who was cherished from the beginning, should not be offered as a victim.
Now, as for [the reason] being "pervasive" (sarvatraga):
it is not tenable [to claim] that its capacity is subject to deviation because of that.

Do you maintain that the ritual procedure of the mantra is capable of turning back only the cause, or even the result as well? If it turns back only the cause, then by that same logic it must turn back the result as well.
If it turns back only the cause, then it follows that it is devoid of the power to affect the result; thus, your position is untenable.
If even the fruit [were to perish],
then it would not be logical that even an animal, having abandoned its animal body, takes on a divine body.
Do you maintain that the author of those mantras is capable or compassionate;
or that he is capable but lacks compassion?
If he were capable and compassionate,
then it would not be logical that he leads the entire world to heaven without [the act of] taking life.
If he were incapable and lacking in compassion,
it would not be logical that the mantra would succeed for him.
Thus, indeed, [it is refuted] by way of the reason, by way of the example, by way of deviation,
and also by way of the loss of the power of the fruit.
Nor is it tenable [that the Veda originated] from the author of the mantra;
therefore, this doctrine as well is established through improper reasoning.
And I shall state the characteristic of that which does not conduce to the Dharma:
whatever action harms others and for which no remedy for the fault is observed—that, at least, does not conduce to the Dharma;
as does that which, among all heretics, is established as having undesirable results.
Furthermore, that which has been declared categorically as unwholesome by the Omniscient Ones, that which is not desired by oneself,
that which is produced by a defiled mind,
and that which is devoid of auspicious factors such as the *vidyā* mantras— that too does not lead to the Dharma.
[The Doctrine of Finitude and Infinity] What is the doctrine of finitude and infinity?

It is as follows: here, a certain ascetic or brahmin, relying on mundane dhyāna, dwells perceiving the world as finite, or perceiving it as infinite, or perceiving it as both finite and infinite, or perceiving it as neither finite nor infinite.
In detail, it is exactly as stated in the Sūtra:
one holds such a view and speaks thus: "The world is finite," up to "it is neither finite nor infinite.
In this regard, the reason should be understood as being of the same nature as that which has already been explained.
And the person as well.

In that regard, when one seeking the end of the world searches from the perspective of its ultimate destruction, and recollects the eon of dissolution (*saṃvartakalpa*), then one forms the notion of "an end. When one recollects the eon of evolution (*vivartakalpa*), then one forms the notion of "no end. Alternatively, searching from the perspective of the ultimate extent of space, when [one looks] downward as far as the Avīci hell...
One does not perceive [it] beyond;
nor does one perceive it above the fourth dhyāna.
But horizontally, one perceives it everywhere beyond.
Above that and below that, there is the perception of finitude; across [the horizontal], there is the perception of infinitude.

Alternatively, by way of its opposite, there is an adherence to specific phonetic forms, but not an adherence to the meaning; thus, one neither has the perception of finitude nor the perception of infinitude.
He should be asked this:
"Do you maintain that there is the activity of the world prior to that eon of dissolution, or not?
If you say there is,"
It is not tenable that the world is finite.
If that does not exist,
then it is not logical to say that one, while remaining in the world, recollects the end of the world.
Thus, even from the perspective of being posterior,
this is not tenable;
therefore, this doctrine is also established as irrational.
[The doctrine of evasive speech by the immortals:
What is the doctrine of evasive speech by the immortals?
It is as when someone here [speaks thus].
...he is indeed dull-witted.
Among them, the first, being afraid of falsehood and afraid of ignorance, does not answer clearly, saying, "I do not know."
The second, fearing cross-examination, fearing false speech, and fearing wrong view, does not clearly declare, "I have attained realization.
The third, fearing wrong view and fearing cross-examination, does not clearly declare, "I have attained realization.
Even in that situation, they resort to verbal evasion by deflecting one point with another.

The fourth person, being terrified of the fear of being cross-examined, does not clearly explain that "this is the path to all prosperity and the path to the highest good" in every respect, even though he is skilled in mere words; rather, being utterly bewildered, he says, "I am confused," and asks back the very same question.
Or, by following after that, one falls into distraction through speech.
The cause of those arguments is also of the form already described; the person and the reply are likewise exactly as stated in the Sūtra.
For they dwell elsewhere out of fear of that very thing; however,
when it occurs to them that "when the opponent has arrived in this manner, one must proceed with deceit," [they resort to it].
This is the point of view to be understood here;
therefore, this doctrine as well is improperly formulated.
[The doctrine of no-cause:
What is the doctrine of no-cause?
It should be understood as being of two kinds—based on meditative absorption and based on speculative reasoning—just as it is described in the sūtra.
For what reason does one, relying on mere reasoning (*tarka*), see that the self and the world have arisen without cause? Briefly stated:

having perceived the immeasurable variety of internal and external entities as occurring without prior intention, and having perceived at times the variety of causes—for instance, that at one time winds blow and at another time they do not—one concludes that they arise without cause.
Suddenly, at one time, rivers flow and at another time they do not flow;
suddenly, some trees flower and bear fruit and at another time they neither flower nor bear fruit—and so forth.
He should be addressed as follows:
"Do you recollect non-existence or do you recollect a self?
If it is non-existence,"
And it is not logical that you should recollect something that is non-existent, unfamiliar, and unpracticed.
If it were the self,
then it would not be logical to say, "I did not exist previously, but later arose."

Thus, it is not tenable [to conceive of a self] either through the recollection of non-existence, or through the recollection of a self, or by way of the causeless variety of internal and external phenomena, or even by way of their variety having a cause.
Therefore, this doctrine as well is improperly formulated.
[The doctrine of annihilationism:
What is the doctrine of annihilationism?

It is when a certain ascetic or brahmin here possesses such a view and speaks thus: "As long as the self—material, gross, and composed of the four great elements—remains, persists, and continues, so long is it subject to disease."
It is accompanied by swelling, accompanied by arrows, accompanied by fever, and accompanied by torment;
and because the self is cut off, perishes, and ceases to exist after death, the self is thereby completely annihilated.

Thus, there is the divine [being] belonging to the desire realm, the divine belonging to the form realm, and those belonging to the formless realms, from the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
the details are exactly as in the Sūtra.
For example, the seven proponents of annihilationism.
For what reason does one have such a view and speak thus?
It is because of scripture and reasoning.
Scripture is as previously stated.
What is reasoning? It is as follows: here, a certain person is a dialectician, as previously described; it occurs to him thus:
If the self were to exist after death, there would be the fault of the arrival of what was not done regarding karmic actions;
if the self were to cease to exist in every respect, then there would likewise be no experience [of the results].

There would be no [connection] between actions and their fruits. Seeing that both [views] are untenable, one holds such a view and speaks thus: "The self is cut off, it perishes, and it does not exist after death," just as, for example, shards that have been broken become disconnected.
Just as a stone, once split, cannot be rejoined,
so too should this principle be understood in this case.
He should be asked this:
"Do you maintain that the aggregates are annihilated, or that the self is annihilated?"
If the aggregates were real,
then it would not be logical that the aggregates— which are impermanent and proceed as a succession of causes and effects— are utterly cut off.

If the self were to be annihilated— whether it be the coarse material form composed of the four great elements, accompanied by disease, swelling, thorns, fever, and torment; or whether it be divine, belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*), or divine, belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), ranging from those who have reached the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) up to those who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)—
then [it would be so] even by way of the annihilation of the aggregates (*skandha*).
This is not tenable.
Therefore, this doctrine as well is improperly formulated.
[Nihilism] What is nihilism?
It is when a certain person here— whether a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa— holds such a view and speaks thus:
"There is no giving, there is no sacrifice," and so on in detail, up to "there is no Arhat in the world.
Such is his view, such is his doctrine:
that everything does not exist in any way whatsoever.
For what reason does one have such a view and such a doctrine?
It is because of scripture and reasoning.
Scripture is as previously described.
What is reasoning (*yukti*)?
It is as follows: here, a certain person is a dialectician (*tārkika*), as described previously;
relying upon worldly meditative absorption (*laukika-dhyāna*), he perceives a certain donor throughout his entire life.
And he sees him, having passed away and died, being reborn into low families— among those who are poor, wretched, and destitute. To him, it occurs thus:
There is no gift; there is no sacrifice; there is no oblation.
Again, he sees a certain person who has practiced either good conduct or bad conduct;
he sees that person, having passed away and died, being reborn in a state of deprivation, a miserable destination, a downfall, or in the hells;
or else being reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world among the gods.
It occurs to him: "There is no good conduct;
there is no misconduct."
There is no fruit or ripening of the karmas of good conduct and bad conduct.
Again, he sees a certain kṣatriya being reborn in the brahmin caste,
or in the vaiśya caste, or in the śūdra caste;
or a brahmin being reborn in the kṣatriya caste, or in the vaiśya caste, or in the śūdra caste.
The same applies to a Vaiśya or a Śūdra.
It occurs to him:
"There is no such thing as this world [arising] from the next world for those who are Kṣatriyas and so forth, in order for them to remain Kṣatriyas and so forth."

"There is no world beyond this world for those who are Kṣatriyas and so forth, because they remain as Kṣatriyas and so forth. Furthermore, he sees one who is free from passion being reborn in a lower realm.
Or again, one sees one's mother being reborn as a daughter;
or a daughter being reborn as a mother;
or a father being reborn as a son.
Or again, one may regard even a son as being in the state of a father;
having observed the lack of fixed status regarding mother and father, it occurs to him: "There is no mother;
there is no father."
Or, while investigating the rebirth of a certain individual, he does not perceive it;
that individual has either been reborn among the non-percipient beings or in the formless realms.
Or, having entered final nirvana, it occurs to him:
"There is no spontaneously born being for one who does not recognize that state," or again, one who is conceited regarding the state of an Arhat sees his own rebirth while passing away.
It occurs to him thus:
"There are no Arhats in the world," and so forth in detail.
For what reason does one hold such a view and speak thus, saying that "everything is non-existent in every respect"?
It is because they do not understand otherwise those discourses spoken by the Tathāgata— which are profound, appearing profound, and concerning the ineffable nature of phenomena.
Furthermore, for one who establishes the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) in an improper manner (*ayoniśas*), the view of non-existence (*nāstidṛṣṭi*) arises;
by which [view] it occurs to him: "Everything does not exist in its entirety according to its characteristics."
He should be asked this:

"Do you maintain that there is karma to be experienced upon rebirth [and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives], or do you maintain that everything is exclusively to be experienced upon rebirth?"
If that exists, then by that [very fact], there is no giving, no sacrifice, and no offering.
There is no good conduct;
there is no misconduct;
there is no ripening of the fruit of actions consisting of good and bad conduct.
It is logical to say that "this world does not exist" and "the other world does not exist," provided that karma to be experienced in a subsequent life does not exist.
Therefore, it is not logical that another formation of wholesome or unwholesome karma would experience the ripening of those wholesome and unwholesome karmas immediately upon being reborn.
Do you maintain that she who gives birth to one is his mother or not?
Or that he who arises from another's seed is his father or not?
Whether it be the mother or the father—
"It is not tenable to say that there is no mother and no father;
for if there were neither mother nor father, then by what would one be born?
And from what seed would one come into being?"
And that father produces him; he arises from that seed; yet it is not logical for him to be both mother and father.
When one is a mother, then one is neither daughter nor son;
when one is a daughter or a son, then one is neither mother nor father.
Do you maintain that there exists such a sphere where a being being reborn is not seen by the divine eye, or that it does not exist?
If it exists,
then it is not tenable to say that there is no spontaneously born being (*upapāduka*).
If it does not exist, then it would follow that detachment from perception, detachment from form, and detachment from the three realms have been excluded; therefore, this is not tenable.
Do you maintain that there is someone who falsely conceives themselves to have attained arhatship, or not?
If there is such a person, then there are no arhats in the world.
Thus, it is not logical. If [an Arhat] does not exist,
then even anyone who has acted improperly and conceives erroneously would be an Arhat.
It is not tenable.
He should be addressed as follows:

"Do you maintain that there exists a phenomenon characterized by the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*), or that it does not exist?
If it exists..."
Therefore, it is not tenable to say that everything does not exist in every respect.
If that does not exist,
then it is illogical to say that there is no perversion, no affliction, and no purification.
Thus, [it is established] also by way of being experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*), by way of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*),
and by way of the existence of the place of rebirth (*upapattyāyatana-sadbhāva*).
It is not tenable [to say that it exists] either because of the existence of conceit or because of its possessing the three characteristics.
Therefore, this doctrine as well is improperly formulated.
[Extremist View] What is an extremist view? It is when a certain person here— a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa— holds such a view and speaks thus:
The Brahmin is the foremost caste; other castes are inferior. The Brahmin is the white caste; other castes are black.

Brahmins are purified, not non-Brahmins. Brahmins are the legitimate sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth; they are born of Brahmā, emerged from Brahmā, and are the attendants of Brahmā—just like the Brahmins of the Kali age.
For what reason does one hold such a view and speak thus?
It is due to both scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*).
Scripture is as previously stated.
What is reasoning (*yukti*)? It is as follows:
"In this case, there is a certain person who is a dialectician," and so forth;
having observed the natural morality of those who are Brahmins by birth, and having taken into account their acquisition of gain and honor.
He should be addressed as follows:
"Do you maintain that only those other castes are born of a mother and produced from a womb,
or do you include the Brahmin caste as well?"

If it were otherwise, then by that very fact of being born from a womb and originating from a mother—which is directly perceived—the claim that the Brahmin caste is [divinely] produced would be refuted; therefore, this is not tenable.
If even the brahmin caste were such [as to be subject to birth], then it would not be logical to say that the brahmins are the highest caste and other castes are inferior.

Just as that which is born from a womb arises from a mother, so too does one who performs unwholesome deeds and one who performs wholesome deeds— whether they have engaged in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, or engaged in good conduct of body, speech, and mind— experience their undesirable or desirable results in this very life, or again in the future life. Whether being reborn in the states of woe, or being reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world among the gods, or due to the manifestation of three conditions, or being reborn from the mother’s womb, [one encounters] the worldly arts and crafts and the stations of work.

Whether it be wholesome or unwholesome; whether it be a king or his servant; whether one who is skillful and endowed with diligence, or one favored by the king, or one not so favored; whether subject to illness, subject to old age, or subject to death; whether one who, having cultivated the Brahma-abodes, is being reborn in the Brahma-world; or one who is cultivating the factors conducive to enlightenment, or not cultivating them; or one who is awakening to the enlightenment of a Śrāvaka, the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha, or unsurpassed perfect complete enlightenment, or not awakening to them—such [beings] as these.
"Do you maintain that one who is superior by birth alone is the best, or rather one who is so through learning or moral conduct?
If it is by birth alone,
then it would not be logical to accept as authoritative in a sacrifice one who is preeminent in learning or preeminent in moral conduct."
If, by virtue of learning or moral conduct, the Brahmins were the highest caste and other castes were inferior, that would not be logical.
Thus, [it is distinguished] by way of its source, by way of its karma, by way of its rebirth,
and by way of its craft and occupation.
Also by way of sovereignty, by way of its appropriation,
and by way of the divine abodes.
It is not tenable [that it is a cause] either through the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment or through the attainment of enlightenment.
Therefore, this doctrine as well is not established by reason.
[The Doctrine of Purity] What is the doctrine of purity?

It is when a certain ascetic or brahmin here possesses such a view and speaks thus: "Since the self has attained liberation and mastery over the mind, and has attained mastery over yoga, by means of the five divine [powers]..."
Endowed with and fully possessed of the qualities of sensual pleasure, he plays, delights, and amuses himself.

He becomes pure through the purity of attaining nirvāṇa in this very life. And because he dwells having attained the first dhyāna—which is secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and born of seclusion, characterized by joy and happiness—[he is purified].

He dwells having attained and entered up to the fourth dhyāna; he becomes pure through the purity of attaining Nirvāṇa in this very life. For instance, he holds such a view and speaks thus: "Whoever bathes in the river Sundarikā is cleansed of all evils."
Just as with the Sundarikā, so too with the Bāhudā, the Gayā, the Sarasvatī river, and the Gaṅgā;
he considers himself purified there by bathing in their waters.

Likewise, some here consider purification to come through the dog-vow, the cow-vow, the mongoose-vow, the naked-vow, the ash-vow, the austerity-vow, the asceticism-vow, and other such undertakings of vows.
One considers it pure,
just as those who propound nirvana in this very life (dṛṣṭadharmavādin) and those who propound purification by water and so forth do.
For what reason does he hold such a view and speak thus?
