It is on account of scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*). Scripture is as previously described.
What is reasoning? It is as follows: for instance, here a certain person is a dialectician, and so forth in detail.
Having attained mastery and sovereignty over all things, he becomes a lord of desires and a lord of yoga;
yet he does not understand that mastery and sovereignty as they truly are.
For instance, there is one here who, through self-restraint, perceives his own liberation from evil, or like one who has committed an offense, perceives his liberation from that offense.
He should be asked this:
"Do you maintain that he who sports with the five strands of sensual pleasure is one who has abandoned passion for sensual pleasures, or one who has not abandoned it?"
If he is free from passion, it is not tenable that he plays, enjoys himself, and amuses himself;
if he is not free from passion, it is not tenable that he is liberated and pure.
Do you maintain that one who dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna is either entirely free from passion (*sarvavītarāga*) or not entirely free from passion?
If he were entirely free from passion, it would not be tenable to say that he dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna.
If he were not free from all passion,
it would not be tenable to say that he is liberated and pure.
He should be asked this:
"Is purity internal or external?
If it is internal, [the following should be addressed].
Therefore, it is not logical that one is purified by bathing at sacred fords;
for if they were external,
one would remain just as full of passion, hatred, and delusion as before.
The external impurity is purified by means of removal.
"Do you maintain that purity comes from taking up pure things, or from taking up impure things?
If it is from taking up pure things,
then dogs and the like would be considered impure."
Regarding the world, purification through the appropriation of that [world] is not tenable;
if it were due to the appropriation of impure things, then it would not be tenable that a thing which is pure by nature could lead to purification.

Do you maintain that, when one undertakes the vows of the dog-ascetics and so forth, it is either wrong practice such as bodily misconduct that leads to purification, or right practice such as good bodily conduct?
If it is wrong practice,
then it is not logical that one both practices wrongly and is purified thereby.
If it were right practice, then the dog-vow and so forth would be purposeless; therefore, it is not logical that purification is achieved through them.
Thus, whether from the perspective of one free from passion or not free from passion,
and whether internally or externally.
It is also not tenable [to speak of a self] from the perspective of grasping at the impure as pure, nor from the perspective of erroneous or correct practice.
Therefore, this doctrine as well is improperly formulated.
[The Discourse on Auspicious Rites and Blessings:
What is the discourse on auspicious rites and blessings?

It is as follows: here, a certain ascetic or brahmin holds such a view and speaks thus: "Through the unfavorable influence of the sun, moon, planets, and lunar days, one's desires fail to be fulfilled."
And in accordance with that, his desires are fulfilled.
For that purpose, he performs worship of the sun and other deities;
he provides offerings such as fire-oblations, recitations, full water-jars, bilva fruits, conch shells, and so forth.
For example, the mathematicians.
For what reason does such a view and such a doctrine arise?
From scripture and from reasoning.
The scripture (*āgama*) is as before. What is the reasoning (*yukti*)? It is as follows: for instance, there is here a certain person who is a dialectician (*tārkika*), and so forth, as before.
He becomes an attainer of worldly meditative absorptions (*laukika-dhyāna*) and is regarded as an Arhat by the great multitude of people.

When questioned regarding his own prosperity and success by those desiring such things, he— failing to understand the course of karma as it has arisen through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpanna*) as it truly is— relies instead on the movements of the sun, moon, planets, constellations, and lunar days.
He perceives the ripening of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karmas among sentient beings;
he illuminates and establishes that very [ripening] for those sentient beings who desire it.
He should be addressed as follows:
"Do you maintain that prosperity or adversity is caused by the sun, the moon, the planets, the constellations, and the lunar days, or rather that it is caused by wholesome and unwholesome karma?"
If it were produced by the sun and so forth,
then it would not be logical that prosperity and misfortune, which persist for as long as one lives, are seen to follow from meritorious and non-meritorious actions respectively.
If, on the other hand, they were produced by good and evil karma...
Therefore, it is not logical that it was created by the sun and other such [deities].
Thus, even that which is ordained by the Sun and so forth,
or even that which is ordained by auspicious and inauspicious factors,
is not tenable.
Therefore, this doctrine as well is improperly established.
Thus, these sixteen opposing doctrines, when examined through their formulation and scrutinized by means of reasoning, are in every respect untenable.
[The Designation of Defilement] In this regard, what is the formal establishment of the designation of defilement?
It should be understood by means of three types of defilement.
What, then, are they? They are the affliction of defilements (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the affliction of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the affliction of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*).
What is the affliction of defilements? Here is the summary verse (*uddāna*):
Its intrinsic nature, its classifications, its causes, its stages, its gateways, its gravity, its objects, its errors, its synonyms, and its faults.
The intrinsic nature of the afflictive obscuration (kleśasaṃkleśa) should be understood, as well as its classifications, its cause, and its stages.
The entrance,
the intensity,
and the inclusion of the perversions.
The synonyms as well as the disadvantages are to be understood.

What is the intrinsic nature of the afflictions? It is that phenomenon which, as it arises, arises with an inherently unpeaceful characteristic, and by the very arising of that [phenomenon], the continuity of conditioned formations proceeds.
This should be understood as the complete nature of affliction.
What is the classification of the afflictions (*kleśa*)?
There may be a single type of affliction in the sense of being a defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
There may be two types: those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

It may be threefold: associated with the desire realm, associated with the form realm, and associated with the formless realm. It may also be fourfold: associated with the desire realm, and both determinate and indeterminate.
It is associated with the realm of form and is indeterminate, and it is associated with the formless realm and is indeterminate.

It may be of five kinds: that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin, that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path, and that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.
There may be six kinds: attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt.

It may be sevenfold: the seven underlying tendencies (anuśayas), namely, the underlying tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāga-anuśaya), the underlying tendency of aversion (pratigha-anuśaya), the underlying tendency of attachment to existence (bhavarāga-anuśaya), the underlying tendency of pride (māna-anuśaya), the underlying tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya), the underlying tendency of views (dṛṣṭi-anuśaya), and the underlying tendency of doubt (vicikitsā-anuśaya).
Attachment may be of eight kinds: attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, doubt, views, and the two types of misapprehension.
It may be ninefold, consisting of the nine fetters:

the fetter of attachment, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of pride, the fetter of ignorance, the fetter of views, the fetter of grasping, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of avarice.

It may be of ten kinds: the view of a self-identity, the view of grasping at extremes, false view, adherence to views, adherence to rites and rituals, attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, and doubt.
There may be one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions (*kleśa*) based on the establishment of twelve modes of erroneous engagement with the truths for these very ten afflictions.
What are the twelve modes of the truth?
They are the truth of suffering and the truth of origin pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
The truth of suffering and the truth of origin pertaining to the form realm; the truth of suffering and the truth of origin pertaining to the formless realm;
the truth of cessation and the truth of the path which are the fruit of that full comprehension predominant over the desire realm and are manifested by that full comprehension;
and the truth of cessation and the truth of the path which are the fruit of that full comprehension predominant over the form realm and are manifested by that full comprehension.
The truth of cessation and the truth of the path are the fruit of that full comprehension which has the formless realm as its predominant object, and they are manifested by that full comprehension.

In that regard, with respect to the truth of suffering and the truth of origin pertaining to the desire realm, and with respect to the truth of cessation and the truth of the path governed by the desire realm, all ten afflictions are erroneously directed toward them.

With respect to the truth of suffering and the truth of origin pertaining to the form realm, and with respect to the truth of cessation and the truth of the path governed by those [realms], those same ten afflictions—excluding hostility—are erroneously directed toward them.
As it is for the form realm, so it is for the formless realm.
In the cultivation of the antidote to the desire realm, six afflictions are erroneously directed toward it, excluding false view, adherence to views, adherence to rites and rituals, and doubt.

Regarding the cultivation of the antidote to the realm of form (rūpāvacara), five afflictions are erroneously directed toward it, derived from these same six [afflictions] with the exception of hostility (pratigha).
As it is with the counteragent to the realm of form, so it is with the counteragent to the formless realm.
As it is with those who have fallen into error, so it is with the obscurations therein.
Among these, what is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?

It is that afflicted wisdom— whether determinate or indeterminate— which, having come about through associating with unworthy persons, hearing false doctrines, improper mental attention, or natural loss of mindfulness, regards the five aggregates of clinging as either a self or belonging to a self.
What is the view of grasping at extremes? It is that which—

based on association with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, improper mental attention, or natural loss of mindfulness— is the determined or undetermined perception of the five aggregates of clinging, which have been grasped as a self, as either eternal or as annihilated.
Or it is afflicted wisdom.

What is wrong view? It is that afflicted wisdom which, based on association with unwholesome persons, hearing false teachings, and improper mental attention, either denies the cause, the fruit, or the efficacy of action, or destroys an existing reality; it is wisdom that is definitively determined [as such].

What is adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)? It is that afflicted wisdom which is definitively determined, arising from associating with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, and improper mental attention; it occurs when one, having compared one's own view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—along with their bases, objects, causes, and co-arising associations—with another's view, regards it as foremost, supreme, distinguished, and preeminent.

What is the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)? It is that which, having relied upon association with unwholesome persons, hearing false teachings, and improper mental attention,

regards that very view and the morality or observance accompanying that view— along with its basis, its object, its cause, and its co-arising and associated factors— as being purity, liberation, and the means of deliverance.
It is that very afflicted wisdom which has been definitively determined.
What is attachment (*rāga*)?

It is the fixation upon a desirable object—whether determined or undetermined, whether external or internal—resulting from associating with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, improper mental attention (*ayoniśo manaskāra*), or natural loss of mindfulness (*smṛtisampramoṣa*).

What is aversion (*pratigha*)? It is the hostility toward undesirable objects, whether external or internal, determined or undetermined, which arises through associating with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, improper mental attention, or natural loss of mindfulness.
What is pride (*māna*)? It is that which,
based on associating with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, improper mental attention (*ayoniśo manaskāra*),
or natural loss of mindfulness (*smṛtisampramoṣa*), is directed either outwardly or inwardly, and is either specifically determined or undetermined.
Pride consists in haughtiness regarding high and low status, and regarding inferiority and superiority.
What is ignorance?

It is that afflicted lack of knowledge regarding an object of cognition—whether determined or undetermined—which arises from associating with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, improper mental attention, or from an innate lapse of mindfulness.
What is doubt?
It is a state of indecision that is definitively fixed regarding an object of knowledge itself, arising from associating with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, and improper mental attention.
What is the cause of the afflictions?
There are six causes:
affliction arises from the basis as well as from the object.
Through association, through teaching, and through practice.
Also from mental attention.
Therein, [affliction arises] from the basis (*āśraya*) when it arises from a latent tendency (*anuśaya*);
from the object (*ālambana*) when the object conducive to affliction has come into view;
and from association (*saṃsarga*) when one follows the example of unwholesome persons.
Therein, [the cause] from teaching is that which arises from hearing the false dharma;

therein, [the cause] from habituation is that which arises from the reinforcement of the power of previous familiarity; therein, [the cause] from mental attention is that which arises from improper reflection (ayoniśas).
It arises for one who attends to it mentally.
How many states of the afflictions are there? In brief, there are seven:

the state of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the state of active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), the state of the imagined (*parikalpita*), the state of the innate (*sahaja*), the weak state, the medium state, and the intense state.
In that regard, the latent tendency of the afflictions persists due to two causes:
by way of the persistence of the seed and by way of its dominant object.
By how many aspects do the afflictions defile? In brief, by two aspects:
by way of the outbursts (paryavasthāna) and by way of the latent tendencies (anuśaya).
How is it by way of the outbursts?
In five ways:
through dwelling in a state of lack of tranquility, and through the obstruction of the wholesome.
Because it gives rise to misconduct leading to the miserable states of existence, because it entails birth in the present life, and because it brings about the suffering of birth and so forth.
How does it defile by way of the latent dispositions? By providing a basis for the outbursts and by bringing about the suffering of birth and so forth.
Furthermore, it should be understood that all afflictions act as obstacles and hindrances to both vision and cultivation through seven aspects:

namely, by way of wrong comprehension, non-comprehension, both comprehension and non-comprehension, practice based on wrong comprehension, the basis and ground for those [afflictions], the production of fear regarding them, and their natural manifestation.

How is an affliction (kleśa) to be understood as having the characteristics of being excessive, intense, or heavy? In brief, it is to be understood through six aspects: by way of transgression, by way of rebirth, by way of the mental continuum, by way of the object, by way of the origination of action, and by way of its limit.
In that context, [the classification] by way of transgression refers to that obsession with afflictions (*kleśaparyavasthāna*) by which one incurs a transgression without remainder.
Therein, [the classification] by way of rebirth refers to one who belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) or is subject to the states of woe (*āpāyika*).

Therein, [the classification] by way of the continuum (*santāna*) refers to those whose conduct is dominated by passion and so forth, whose faculties are matured, who are young, and who do not possess the nature of attaining parinirvāṇa in this very life.

In that regard, [unwholesome action] is defined by way of its basis (*vastu*) as that which has for its object a field of teachers (*gurukṣetra*), a field of qualities (*guṇakṣetra*), or a field of those who should not be approached (*agamyakṣetra*).

It is defined by way of the origination of the action (*karmasamutthāna*) as that by which one, being overcome and possessed by a particular obsession of the afflictions (*kleśaparyavasthāna*), originates bodily and vocal action.
And it is defined by way of its limit (*paryanta*) as that which is comprised of an inherently superior degree (*adhimātraprakāra*).
Therein, first of all, the inversion is abandoned by means of a weak counteragent.
These inversions are seven.
Namely:

perversion of perception, perversion of view, and perversion of mind; the perversion of [perceiving] the impermanent as permanent, the perversion of [perceiving] suffering as happiness, and [the perversion of perceiving] the impure...
"Purity" is the inversion [of perceiving the impure as pure]; "self in what is not-self" is the inversion [of perceiving a self in the non-self].
What is the inversion of perception?
It is the conceptual construction of perception that takes the impermanent to be permanent, suffering to be happiness, the impure to be pure, and the non-self to be self.
What is the perversion of view? It is the acceptance, preference, establishment, and adherence toward that very thing which has been thus conceptualized through perception.
What is the perversion of mind?
It is the affliction of passion and so forth toward that very [object] which has been thus adhered to.
In this regard, the afflictions are to be understood through three aspects:
there is an affliction that is the root of error,
and there is error itself.
There is that which is the outflow of perversion.
In this context, ignorance is the root of error.

Error consists of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), a portion of the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhaka-dṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and attachment (*rāga*).
The outflow of error consists of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), a portion of the view of grasping at extremes, hostility (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
In this context, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the inversion that perceives a self in what is not-self;
a portion of the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is the inversion that perceives permanence in what is impermanent.
Adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is the misapprehension of the impure as pure.

Adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is the inversion of perceiving suffering as happiness. Attachment (*rāga*) is likewise [an inversion] in both ways, namely, the inversion of perceiving the impure as pure.
Furthermore, the inversion of perceiving suffering as happiness is a misconception.
[Synonyms:
What are the synonyms for the afflictions?
There are many synonyms.

Namely: fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, outbursts, floods, yokes, clingings, knots, hindrances, barrenness, stains, obstructions, arrows, possessions, roots, misconducts, outflows, vexations, fevers, despair, strifes, fires, plagues, and entanglements— such are the synonyms for the afflictions (*kleśa*).
In this context, they are called *saṃyojana* (fetters) because they yoke one to suffering;
they are called *bandhana* (bonds) because they prevent one from acting according to one's will in virtuous conduct;
and they are called *anuśaya* (latent tendencies) because they follow along with the seeds of all worldly excellence.
They are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) because they afflict the mind through the distortions (*viparyāsa*).
They are called outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) because they manifest repeatedly. They are called floods (*ogha*) because they are difficult to fathom and because they carry one away with the current.
They are called *yogas* because they are the means for wrong practice;
they are called *upādānas* because they cause the appropriation of the continuity of personal existence; and they are called *granthas* because they are difficult to untie.
They are called *nīvaraṇas* (hindrances) because they obscure the true meaning;
they are called *khilas* (barrennesses) because they act as a fallow field for the flowers of wholesome qualities; and they are called *malas* (stains) because their very nature is defiled.
They are called "strikes" (*nigha*) because they constantly strike;
they are "darts" (*śalya*) because their characteristic is lack of peace and because they follow one from afar; they are "roots" (*mūla*) because they cause the grasping of acquisitions (*upadhi*);
and they are "misconducts" (*duścarita*) because their intrinsic nature is wrong practice.
They are called *āsravas* because they cause distraction of the mind;
they are called *vighātas* because they bring about dissatisfaction with enjoyments;
they are called *paridāhas* because they cause the frustration of one's desires.
They are called *upāyāsas* (afflictions) because they bring about misfortune; they are called *raṇas* (strifes) because they serve as the cause for quarreling, reviling, conflict, and dispute;
and they are called *agnayas* (fires) because they burn the fuel of the fruits of accumulated roots of merit.
They are called "fevers" because they have become great diseases;
"forests" because they destroy the trees that are various forms of personal existence;
and "obstructions" because they cause attachment to the qualities of sensual desire and act as obstacles to the supramundane Dharma.
These are synonyms for all the afflictions;
however, because of their predominance, the Blessed One established those various afflictions under this or that specific synonym.
"Fetters" refers to the nine fetters;
the fetter of attachment (anunaya-saṃyojana) is explained in detail as before.
"Bonds" refers to the three bonds: attachment, aversion, and delusion.
"Latent dispositions" refers to the seven latent dispositions (*anuśaya*):
the latent disposition of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānuśaya*), and so forth, as detailed previously.
Regarding "secondary afflictions" (upakleśa): there are three secondary afflictions, namely attachment, aversion, and delusion.
The "envelopments" (paryavasthāna) refer to the eight envelopments:
lack of shame (āhrīkya), lack of dread (anapatrāpya), lethargy and drowsiness (styāna-middha), restlessness (auddhatya), remorse (kaukṛtya), envy (īrṣyā), and avarice (mātsarya).
The floods (*ogha*) are the four floods: the flood of sensual desire (*kāmaugha*), the flood of existence (*bhavaugha*), the flood of views (*dṛṣṭyaugha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avidyaugha*).
As it is with floods, so it is with the bonds.
"Graspings" refers to the four graspings:
grasping at sensual pleasures, grasping at views, grasping at rules and observances, and grasping at the doctrine of self.
"Knots" refers to the four knots:

the bodily knot of covetousness, the bodily knot of ill will, the bodily knot of adherence to rules and observances, and the bodily knot of dogmatic adherence to the conviction that "this alone is the truth."
"Obstructions" refers to the five obstructions:
the obstruction of sensual desire,
the obstruction of ill will, the obstruction of sloth and torpor, the obstruction of restlessness and remorse, and the obstruction of doubt.
"Obstacles" refers to the three obstacles: passion, hatred, and delusion.
As it is with the barren soils, so it is with the stains, the obstructions, the arrows, the possessions, and the misdeeds.
"Roots" refers to the three roots:
greed is an unwholesome root;
hatred and delusion are unwholesome roots.
The outflows (āsravas) are the three outflows:
the outflow of sensual desire (kāmāsrava), the outflow of existence (bhavāsrava), and the outflow of ignorance (avidyāsrava).
"Obstructions" refers to the three obstructions: passion, hatred, and delusion.

Just as with the afflictions (*vighāta*), so it is with the burnings (*paridāha*), the desperations (*upāyāsa*), the conflicts (*raṇa*), the fires (*agni*), the fevers (*jvara*), the forests (*vanasa*), and the fetters (*vinibandha*).
There are five fetters: dependence on the body, dependence on sensual pleasures, dwelling in lack of association, deficiency in conformable discourse, and contentment with merely a small amount.
What is the disadvantage of the afflictions?
It should be understood that their disadvantage is of many kinds.
For example, as an affliction arises, it first of all defiles the mind and produces a perversion regarding the object of perception.
It sets in motion a flow of conditioned formations that is of the nature of outflow;
it leads to one's own affliction,
to the affliction of others, and to the affliction of both.

It produces fault pertaining to the present life, fault pertaining to future lives, and fault pertaining to both the present and future lives. One experiences the mental suffering and dejection born thereof;
it brings about the suffering of birth and so forth, and distances one from nirvāṇa.
He causes his continuum to fall away from wholesome states; he undergoes the loss of wealth; and he becomes dejected and lacking in joy.
Confident, he approaches the assembly;
yet, in all directions and intermediate points, evil reports, dispraise, and ill-famed verses circulate.
He becomes censurable by the virtuous; he dies with remorse;
and at the breaking up of the body, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a miserable destination, a downfall, in the hells; and he does not attain his own true welfare.
[The defilement of karma:
What is the defilement of karma? The summary verse (uddāna) says: Its intrinsic nature, its classifications, and also by way of causes, stages, and gateways.
Heaviness, as well as perversion, synonym, and indeed fault.
The intrinsic nature of actions, their classification, their cause, their stages, their gateway, their intensity, and their perversion should also be understood.
The synonyms as well as the disadvantages are to be understood.
What is the intrinsic nature of action (*karmasvabhāva*)?

It is that phenomenon which, when arising, arises with the characteristic of volitional formation (*abhisaṃskāra*); and through its arising, the bodily formation or the vocal formation proceeds at a subsequent time.
This is called the intrinsic nature of action.
What is the classification of karma?
It is to be understood through two aspects:
by way of the classification of the characteristics of persons.
And by way of the differentiation of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇaprabheda*),
there are those ten unwholesome and wholesome paths of action (*karmapatha*):
namely, taking life and abstaining from taking life.
Taking what is not given and abstaining from taking what is not given; sexual misconduct and abstaining from sexual misconduct;
false speech and abstaining from false speech.
Slander and abstention from slander;
harsh speech and abstention from harsh speech;
frivolous chatter and abstention from frivolous chatter.
Covetousness and the abstention from covetousness; ill-will and the abstention from ill-will;
and wrong view and the abstention from wrong view.

In that regard, the establishment of the characteristics of the person (*pudgala*) is as previously stated, in detail according to the Sūtra: "Therein, one indeed becomes a killer of living beings. This phrase, "one indeed becomes a killer of living beings," is the introductory statement (*uddeśapada*).
He is "fierce" (*raudra*) because of the presence of a mind intent on slaughter and violence.
He is "blood-handed" (*rudhirapāṇi*) because he brings about that killing, thereby undergoing a physical transformation.

He is intent on striking and killing, depriving others of life and dismembering them limb by limb for the sake of making a livelihood; he is devoid of shame because he produces faults in himself, and he has fallen into a state of lack of compassion because he brings about what is undesirable for others.
There are renunciants called Nirgranthas who say this:
"Regarding those living beings within a hundred yojanas, are they restrained or unrestrained?"
As an antidote to that, they say "toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, those same people say that external entities such as trees are living beings;
as an antidote to that, they say "toward those who are living beings."
Thus, both the counteragent to the cessation of true merit and the counteragent to the cessation of false merit are proclaimed.
By these aforementioned terms, the destruction of conditioned beings is illuminated, down to even a single living creature such as an ant;
by that term, killing without exception is fully elucidated.

"He does not abstain from taking life" means that when a condition exists, there is the possibility of rising [from the restraint]; the summarized meaning is that as long as one has not abstained, for that long one is a "taker of life."

Furthermore, by all these terms, there is fully elucidated the characteristic of taking life, the act of taking life, the cause of taking life, and the classification of the acts regarding the object of taking life.
Another summary of the meaning:
what one is like when committing the destruction of life,
and how one causes a living being to be killed.
And that which constitutes the state of being a killer for one who causes a living being to be killed has been fully explained here;
this explains the characteristics of a person who is a killer, not the characteristics of the act of killing itself.
"One who takes what is not given" is the general heading.
"Of others" refers to property such as wealth, grain, and so forth, which has been taken possession of by another;
that very same thing, whether it is placed in a village, moved about, or located in the forest.
Whatever is grown in the wilderness, or gathered, or carried away—that alone is reckoned as theft.
One who takes what is not given, which has not been relinquished or released, thinking "I shall take it," appropriates it;
such a person is a thief of what is not given, whether due to a lack of necessary resources or through the act of appropriation itself.

"Delighting in what is not given" refers to engaging in the act of theft by having undertaken it. "Desiring what is not given, not relinquished, and not released" refers to the longing to appropriate what has been taken from another.
In this context, that which was not previously given by the giver—the owner—by way of a gift is called "not given."
That which has not been relinquished by the owner toward the recipient is said to be "unrelinquished" (*atyakta*).

That which has not been released by the owner for all people to take up and enjoy according to their desire is said to be "unreleased" (*amukta*). Furthermore, one avoids being a thief by virtue of not taking what is not given and because of the state of desiring what is not given.
One avoids that which is greedy by not desiring what has not been given, not relinquished, or not released; one avoids that which is impure due to the impurity of losing a legal case;
and one avoids that which is unclean because of the stain of that fault even for one who has not been defeated.
One avoids what is blameworthy by not undertaking causes that result in undesirable fruits in this life or in future lives.
One abstains from taking what is not given; the analysis of this should be understood as being the same as that for the destruction of life.
This is the summary meaning regarding the other paths of action as well.

Furthermore, because one is a taker of what is not given, wherever it is located and by whatever means it is taken as it truly is, from that act of taking one incurs a fault; this is the summarized meaning.
This too should be understood as the characteristic of one who takes what is not given, rather than the characteristic of the act of taking what is not given;
the same applies to the remaining [unwholesome actions] as well.
"Indeed, one who engages in sexual misconduct" is the heading.
Regarding the phrase "those protected by mother, father, and so forth":
for example, when parents protect their own daughter from sexual intercourse with anyone other than her husband for the sake of her marriage, they guard her and watch over her from time to time.
Or again, when he has passed away, she is protected by a relative, such as a brother or a sister;
in his absence, she is protected by her kin;
and in their absence, she herself [thinks], "This is unbecoming for our family."
Having understood this, she protects herself;
or she is protected by her mother-in-law and father-in-law for the sake of their own son.
She is subject to punishment, because she is protected by the punishments of the royal officials and the families [of the king].
It is "enclosed" because it is guarded by gatekeepers.

Indeed, this threefold protection for one who has been wedded is thus elucidated in brief: protection through the gaze of elders and affectionate kin, protection through the royal officials and noble families, and protection through the gatekeepers.
She is another's wife; that is, she is one who has been married and taken possession of by another, or even one who,
though not married, is protected.
With these three, he protects those of such a form; "suddenly" means having produced delusion.
"By force" means that while all—mother, father, and others—are looking on, one forcibly overcomes her against her will;
"by way of assault" means that they steal her while those who are looking on do not see her as being unwilling.
"He engages in conduct regarding sensual pleasures" (kāmeṣu cāritram āpadyate): here, "sensual pleasure" (kāma) is intended to mean the union of two by two.

"He incurs misconduct" means that those acts which are blameworthy even toward one's own wife when performed outside the appropriate parts, at inappropriate places, or at inappropriate times—this is the summarized meaning.
Furthermore, this explains how sexual misconduct occurs both for one who goes [to another's wife] and for one who approaches her as she comes.
"Indeed, he is a liar" is the introductory statement (*uddeśapada*).
A non-diverse assembly (*apṛthagjanā pariṣad*) and the gathering of those people—the body of persons from the four quarters—possess a knowledge experienced through three modes of discourse:
that which is experienced through what was seen is indeed "seen."
"Out of self-interest," or "out of fear," or "out of a desire for some small gain.
As it is with self-interest, so it is with the interest of others, or with both interests.
Regarding "out of fear": it is from the fear of execution, imprisonment, loss, censure, and so forth.

"Because of some small material gain" means that one speaks false words for the sake of wealth, grain, gold, and so forth; this is because one speaks while having set aside one's true inclination and view.
Furthermore, the summarized meaning is that false speech should be understood by way of its basis, its manner of speaking, its cause, and its dispute over perception.
"Indeed, he is a slanderer" is the general heading; he is a "divider" because of his intent to cause division,
hearing [something] from these people, he reports it to those others, or hearing it from those others, he reports it to these people.
Speech that conforms to the distinctions as they have been heard makes one a divider of those who are united by producing discord;
and for those who are already divided, pleasure arises from providing further incitement.
Through concealment, one takes delight in discord due to a defiled mind that produces displeasure;

one delights in discord due to a defiled mind that destroys the arising of joy; or one utters discordant speech due to a defiled mind that destroys [harmony], or speaks discordant words either without having heard [the truth] or for the sake of another's purpose.

Furthermore, the summarized meaning elucidates the intention regarding distinctions, the application of non-distinct distinctions, the application of distinct distinctions, the state of a mind afflicted by distinctions, and the purpose of others.
"Indeed, he becomes one who speaks harshly" is the introductory heading.
In this context, speech is called "gentle" because it is embraced by the factors of ethical discipline (*śīlāṅga*);
it is "pleasant to the ear" because its words and syllables are sweet and smooth.
Because it is impelled by resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), because it is uncontrived, and because it is not impaired by deceit, it is said to be "heart-reaching" (*hṛdayaṅgamā*).

Because it is free from superimposition and because it is connected with the meaning appropriate to the occasion, it is "affectionate" (*premaṇī*). Because it is directed toward the city of Nirvāṇa, it is "urbane" (*paurī*).
It is "melodious" because its words and syllables are sweet;
it is "clear" because its words and syllables are well-explained;
it is "comprehensible" because it is intelligible.
It is worth hearing because it is in accordance with the Dharma;
it is independent because it is free from worldly motives;
it is not disagreeable because it is well-measured.
Because it is continuous and because it is lucid, it is inexhaustible.
Indeed, this [faith] should be understood as threefold, beginning from the "unblinking" (nelā) up to that which is "inexhaustible.
It is "harmonious" (saṃmodikā) in one aspect, being comprised within the restraint of ethical discipline (śīlasaṃvara);
furthermore, the latter is "endowed with its objective" (adhikārasampannā) by means of the first aspect.
It should be understood that it is endowed with excellence of expression through two [factors], and endowed with excellence of application through the remaining [factors].
It is "lovely" because it is intended for the future time.
Because it was desired with reference to the past time, it is "lovely" (*kāntā*); because it was desired with reference to the past time, it is "dear" (*priyā*).
Because it is desired both in reality and through experience with reference to the present time, it should be understood as "dear" and "agreeable" (*manāpā*).
She who is sociable is beloved, desired, dear, and pleasing to many people;
she who teaches the Dharma is concentrated;
and she who is embraced by the factors of ethical discipline leads, through the gradual sequence of freedom from remorse, to meditative concentration.
In that regard, speech is "biting" (*adaśā*) because it emits the poison of hatred by seeking to harm others;
it is "harsh" (*karkaśā*) because it is pungent toward others due to its contact with suffering. The remainder should be understood by way of the opposite of the white side (*śuklapakṣa*).
"One who engages in frivolous chatter" is the general heading.
There are five kinds of accusation:
namely, false accusation, whether at the proper time or the improper time.
Because he speaks at the wrong time, he is one who speaks untimely; because he speaks what is unreal, he is one who speaks untruthfully;
because he speaks what is not connected with the goal, he is one who speaks what is meaningless.
One who speaks harshly is a speaker of unrighteousness;
one who speaks with internal hatred is a speaker of what is merely heard;
and one who does not reflect at the time of teaching false dharma is likewise.
Having reflected correctly and having understood through the teaching, the speech has been spoken.

Teaching is given to those who listen with contempt; it is not delivered at the proper time, but at a later hour. It is incoherent, because its meaning is disconnected between what precedes and what follows. It is without logical foundation, because the reasons presented fall outside of sound reasoning. It is without illustrative examples, because the application of the analogies is inconsistent.
At times of play such as laughter, singing, and the like, or at times of watching actors, dancers, jesters, and performers of the arts, it is fraught with harm.
Furthermore, the summarized meaning is that, throughout the three times as previously specified, only frivolous speech (saṃbhinnapralāpa) has been fully elucidated.

"Covetous" is the subject term. It refers to an intense passion arising from the cultivation of a resolve to appropriate the property of others, having made greed for that which belongs to another its dominant influence. "Wealth" refers to the various kinds of assets used in worldly transactions.
The requisites that are for one's own enjoyment—both of these taken together should be understood as follows:
"May what belongs to others be mine"—this is explained as the mode of activity of covetousness; thus, in brief, the intrinsic nature of covetousness is revealed.
It should be understood by way of its object and its aspect.
"He has a mind of ill-will" is the summary statement (*uddeśapada*).
It refers to one whose mental resolve is corrupted by making malice toward other beings the dominant factor, through the persistence of the arising of a determination to cause harm.
"Let them be killed" expresses the desire for their destruction, whether of their physical basis (*āśraya*) or their bonds.
"May they be killed" is the desire for the destruction of their physical basis;
"may they live" is the desire for the ruin of another's enjoyments;
"may they meet with calamity through misconduct" is the desire for the ruin of one's own enjoyments.
The summarized meaning should be understood as before.
"Indeed, he possesses false view" is the general heading.
"Having such a view" is an elucidation of one's own acceptance of and inclination toward the intended meaning.
"Speaking thus" is an elucidation of causing others to grasp the intended meaning.

Because he denies the threefold intention of giving—namely, the intention for enjoyment, the intention for purification, and the intention for the worship of deities—he says, "There is no gift, there is no sacrifice, there is no oblation.
Here, "oblation" (huta) should be understood as referring to the intention for the worship of the deity Agni.

Furthermore, this constitutes a denial of wholesome states consisting of ethical discipline and meditative cultivation, along with their opposites and antidotes, as well as the opposite of that which consists of giving.
He says, "There is no good conduct, there is no bad conduct.
Because he denies that threefold wholesome [action] along with its adversaries and antidotes, he says, "There is no ripening of the fruit of well-done or ill-done deeds.
Because he denies the conditions for the basis of engagement, he says, "This world does not exist, the next world does not exist."
Because he denies the causal condition of those states and denies the causal condition of their seeds, he says, "There is no mother; there is no father.

Because he denies the person who undergoes transmigration, he says, "There is no spontaneously born being. Because he denies the cessation that serves as the antidote to transmigration, he says, "There are no Arhats in the world."
Thus he spoke in detail.
In that regard, they have "gone rightly" because of the complete removal of afflictions within themselves;
they are "rightly practicing" because their practice toward sentient beings is free from wrong conduct.
"The time of the cause" refers to this present time;
"the time of the fruit" refers to a future time;
and "by oneself" means having personally realized it through one's own human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
"Having realized by means of the sixth [ground]" refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

"Having accomplished by means of the path of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*) means that they announce their own attainment through their own knowledge and by instilling it in others; the analysis of this, beginning with "Birth is exhausted for me," should be understood as previously explained.
In this regard, the summarized meaning is as follows:
the denial of cause, the denial of effect, the denial of activity, and the denial of existing entities have been elucidated.
In that regard, activity consists of the activity of depositing the seed, the activity of maintaining it, the activity of coming and going, and the activity of karma that brings about rebirth.

"Improper action" refers to the performance of actions that lead to rebirth. Furthermore, there is another summary of the meaning: it elucidates the denial of the process of worldly existence—which, together with its causes and fruits, proceeds through conditions and agents—as well as the denial of the cessation that serves as its antidote.

In that regard, regarding the denial of activity (*pravṛtti*), it should be understood as a denial of the cause (*hetu*), not a denial of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, regarding the denial of cessation (*nivṛtti*), it should be understood as a denial of qualities (*guṇa*), not a denial of the person (*pudgala*).
In that regard, everything concerning the white side (*śuklapakṣa*) should be understood as the opposite of this;
however, I shall state the specific distinction.
Taking sexual misconduct as the basis, "practicing celibacy" (*brahmacārī*) is the term of reference (*uddeśapada*).
This should be understood as purified by three purifications:

purification of time, purification through the confidence of others, and purification of practice; because of practicing throughout one's life, one becomes a practitioner who dwells at a distance from faults.
And this is the purity of time:
he is pure through the purification of legal disputes and clean through non-transgression.
And this is the purity of being esteemed by others.
In this regard, there is a fourfold logical alternative (catuṣkoṭika) concerning one who is pure but not clean:
therein, the first alternative is victory in a legal proceeding for one who has committed an offense;
the second alternative is defeat in a legal proceeding for one who has not committed an offense.
The third alternative is victory in the legal proceeding for one who has not committed an offense;
the fourth alternative is defeat in the legal proceeding for one who has committed an offense.
In that regard, he is free from the odor of raw flesh because he does not consent to physical contact with women;

he abstains from sexual intercourse because he avoids the union of a couple; and he abstains from the village dharma because he does not discharge semen through other means such as manual contact, and because he has undertaken the practice of celibacy without making any worldly aspiration for it.
And this is called the perfection of practice.
The meaning of the compound should be understood as being included within this very [context].
Beginning with the avoidance of false speech, he becomes trustworthy because he is reliable;

he is reliable through being dependable, and thus, by virtue of his authoritative character in various matters, he is established as such. Furthermore, because he does not deceive and does not act with malice toward those who have placed their trust in him, he is non-deceptive.
In brief, three kinds of assistance are illuminated:
assistance through intention, assistance through application, and assistance through action.
[The Establishment of the Characteristics of Dharmas:
Therein, regarding the establishment of the characteristics of dharmas:
what is the taking of life?

It is the bodily action of one who intends to kill, possesses an afflicted mind, and has reached the culmination of the act of killing toward another living being through that very application of killing.
What is taking what is not given?

It is the bodily action of one who intends to steal, with a defiled mind, regarding an object possessed by another, consisting in the application toward that very object and the completion of the theft therein.
What is sexual misconduct?

It is the bodily action that constitutes the preliminary application of sexual misconduct, as well as its completion, by one who intends to engage in it with a defiled mind toward those who are unapproachable, improper parts of the body, or at an inappropriate place or time.

What is false speech? It is the vocal action of one who, having set aside their true perception, desires to speak with a defiled mind toward another being, both in the application of a false witness and in the completion of that false witness.
What is malicious speech?

What is harsh speech? It is the vocal action of one who, with an afflicted mind and the intention to cause division, applies divisive speech toward other beings and brings that divisive speech to its conclusion. What is harshness? It is the vocal action of one who, with an afflicted mind and the desire to speak harshly, applies harsh words toward other beings and brings those harsh words to their conclusion.
What is frivolous speech (*saṃbhinna-pralāpa*)?
It is the vocal action of one who desires to chatter, with a defiled mind, during the preparation for incoherent speech and at the completion of incoherent speech.
What is covetousness?

It is the mental action that occurs when one with a defiled mind and the intention to appropriate the property of another makes a firm resolve and application toward that appropriation, and reaches its completion.
What is ill-will?
It is the mental action of one who possesses a defiled mind and the intention to harm another, occurring during the application of that intention to harm another and at its completion.

What is wrong view? It is the mental action that occurs during the preparation for, and the completion of, the determination to deny [the truth], by one whose intention is to deny and whose mind is afflicted.
What is the abstention from taking life?
It is the bodily action of one who, with a wholesome mind and the intention to see the danger in taking life, engages in its restraint and brings that restraint to completion.

Just as with the abstention from taking life, so too should the abstentions from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slander, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view be understood.
In this regard, the distinction is as follows:

it is the mental action involved in the application of restraint and the completion of that restraint by one who possesses a wholesome mind and intends to perceive the disadvantages of taking what is not given, up to and including intending to perceive the disadvantages of wrong view.
In that regard, there are three things that become ten;
namely, bodily action, vocal action, and mental action.
There are also three things that become ten.
Bodily action and mental action—these three become ten [when subdivided]. What is the cause of actions?

It should be understood as having twelve aspects: greed, hatred, delusion; regarding oneself, others, and compliance with others; for the sake of gain, fear, and the motive of retaliation; for the sake of play, pleasure, and the notion that it is the Dharma; and false view.
What is the state of karma?
In brief, it should be understood as having five aspects:
the weak state, the middling state, the intense state, the state of arising, and the state of latent impression.
In that regard, through weak wholesome karma one is reborn among animals; through middling [wholesome karma], among hungry ghosts;
and through superior [wholesome karma], in the hells.

Through mild wholesome [karma], one is reborn among humans; through middling, among the gods of the desire realm; and through superior, among the gods of the form and formless realms. What is weak-stage unwholesome karma?

That which has mild greed, hatred, and delusion as its cause is the middling state; that which has middling greed, hatred, and delusion as its cause is the intense state; and that which has intense greed, hatred, and delusion as its cause is the highest state.
Furthermore, wholesome [states] should likewise be understood according to their respective causes, such as non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
The state of arising is that which has arisen but not yet ceased, being present before one.
The state of latent impression is that which has arisen and ceased, having turned away from presence.
What is the gateway of karmas?
Briefly stated, it is twofold:
the gateway of yielding fruit, and the gateway of harm and benefit.
What is the gateway of the giving of fruits?
It should be understood as being fivefold:
by way of the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), and the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
By way of the fruit in the present life and by way of the sovereign fruit of another.

In that regard, from the perspective of the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*): when the taking of life is cultivated and frequently practiced within one's own mind, its maturation ripens in the hells.
As it is with the taking of life, so it is with the remaining unwholesome paths of action. This is their fruit of maturation.
In that regard, by way of the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*),
if one is born into the commonality of human beings, one becomes short-lived;
[one is deprived of enjoyments].
He has unguarded sense-doors;
he becomes subject to much slander;
and his friends become divided.
One hears unpleasant sounds;
one's speech becomes unconvincing;
and one suffers from severe illness.
There arises intense hatred;
there arises intense delusion.
This is their outflow fruit (niṣyandaphala).
In that regard, by way of the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*):

because unwholesome actions have been practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed, through that dominance external things become possessed of little vitality; they have imperfect fruits, putrid fruits, transformed fruits, withered fruits, tasteless fruits, non-seasonal fruits, meager fruits, unwholesome fruits, and even no fruits at all.
Virtuous action should be understood as the opposite of this.
In that regard, from the perspective of having its fruit in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*),
karma— whether unwholesome or wholesome— becomes one whose fruit is seen through two causes:
by way of intention (*āśaya*) and by way of the object (*vastu*).
In this regard, intention should be understood as having eight aspects,

namely: the intention of expectation, the intention of non-expectation, the intention of malice, the intention of compassion, the intention of hostility, the intention of serene confidence, the intention of ingratitude, and the intention of gratitude.
In that regard, through intention based on expectation as well,
unwholesome karma may be experienced in the present life;
for example, as when a certain person here [in this world] possesses an excessive [degree of such intention].
He cultivates indifference toward the body, indifference toward enjoyments, and indifference toward existence.
In that regard, even through an intention free from expectation, an action becomes wholesome and to be experienced in the present life;
as when, for example, a certain person here [in this world] possesses an intense...
He cultivates disregard for the body, disregard for enjoyments, and disregard for existence.
In that regard, even through an intention to cause harm,
unwholesome karma becomes to be experienced in the present life;
as when someone here forms an excessively harmful intention toward other beings or other persons.
In that regard, even through an intention of compassion,
an action becomes wholesome and to be experienced in the present life;
for example, when someone here cultivates an exceedingly great intention of compassion toward other beings and other persons.
In that regard, even through an intention of malice, unwholesome karma may become to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).

For example, as when a certain person here forms an excessively intense intention of malice or an intention of hostility toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or any other object occupying a position of reverence.
In that regard, even through an intention of serene confidence (*prasādāśaya*),
karma becomes wholesome and to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
For example, here a certain person forms an intense intention of serene confidence or an intention of resolute conviction toward the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha.
In that regard, even from an intention of ingratitude, unwholesome karma may become something to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
For example, as when a certain person here forms an excessive intention of ingratitude, an intention of malice, or a fierce intention toward his mother, his father, or some other object of benefit.
In that regard, even through an attitude of gratitude, wholesome karma becomes to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
For example, as when a certain person here cultivates an intense attitude of gratitude toward his mother, father, or some other benefactor, and an intense attitude of wishing to repay that kindness.
In that regard, an unwholesome action that is substantial in nature becomes experienced in the present life when committed among the immediate [sins] or in conditions conducive to the immediate;
these are the five actions of immediate retribution.
Namely: matricide, patricide, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, and maliciously drawing blood from the body of a Tathāgata.
Furthermore, those actions similar to the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-sabhāga*) are as follows:
for instance, when someone here has sexual intercourse with an Arhat or with his mother.
Or he strikes a Bodhisattva in his final existence;
or he carries out the slaughter of animals in temples, at crossroads, or at junctions of three roads;
or he betrays, deceives, or causes the exile of a trusted friend, a close companion, or a playmate who has attained the highest degree of trust.
Furthermore, having taken in one who is suffering, destitute, helpless, and without refuge—one who has come for protection—by providing assistance, he later betrays him and acts to cause him harm;
or he seizes the gateway of the Saṅgha; or he causes the destruction of a shrine (caitya).
Action of this kind is called "associated with immediate retribution."
Furthermore, a wholesome [action] may be experienced in the present life by way of its object (*vastu*).
For example, here a certain person encourages, disciplines, settles, and establishes his mother—who lacks faith—in the perfection of faith;
and just as one who lacks faith is established in the perfection of faith, so too is one who is immoral established in the perfection of ethical discipline.

One should treat one who is stingy regarding the perfection of yoga as one would a mother lacking wisdom regarding the perfection of wisdom; likewise, one should treat a father who has emerged from the meditative attainment of loving-kindness by providing him with alms-food.
Or he employs services;

likewise, he provides food and performs services for one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the fruit of stream-entry (*srota-āpattiphala*), or even the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*).
In the same way, he performs services directly toward the Buddha, the Blessed One.
As it is with respect to the Buddha, the Blessed One, so it is with respect to the Saṅgha of those in training and those beyond training.
Furthermore, with respect to these very same objects, unwholesome karma may also be experienced in the present life when it is performed as a result of malice; this is the opposite case.
In that regard, through the sovereign fruit of another, an action becomes to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
For example, in whatever village or field the Tathāgata dwells, there no calamities, disturbances, or misfortunes arise.
The multitude of people dwelt in comfort, free from calamity, affliction, and misfortune;
that is to say, through the majestic power of the Buddha.
Just as it is with the Buddhas, so it is with universal monarchs and with bodhisattvas who dwell in loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Likewise, a bodhisattva whose intention is compassion, having beheld beings who are impoverished, suffering, or struck by fate, satisfies them with food, drink, wealth, grain, and treasuries;
and they, through that condition, dwell in a state of pleasant contact.
This too should be understood as a similar type of action governed by another, which is to be experienced in the present life.
In that regard, there is harm and benefit.
The ten unwholesome paths of action are established with respect to sentient beings by way of eight modes of harm.
What are the eight modes of harm?

The injury of life, the injury of possessions, the injury of one’s spouse, the injury of false testimony, the injury of associates, the injury of proclaiming faults, the injury of withdrawing favor, and the injury of instilling fear.
The gateways to the wholesome paths of action should be understood as the opposite of these.
What is the intensity, vehemence, and gravity of actions?
It is to be understood through six aspects:
by way of volitional formation...

[It is] by way of habituation, by way of intrinsic nature, by way of the entity, by way of being exclusively adverse, and by way of the destruction of the adverse. Among these, "by way of volitional formation" refers to how, for instance,
a certain person here initiates an action through an intense obsession with greed, hatred, and delusion, and through an intense volitional formation of greed, hatred, and delusion.
In that regard, [it occurs] through habituation:
as when, in this world, a certain person has for a long time practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed either wholesome or unwholesome karma.
In that regard, by way of intrinsic nature:
for example, harsh speech is more blameworthy than frivolous chatter; slander is more blameworthy than harsh speech;
and false speech is more blameworthy than slander.
[Compared to false speech, sexual misconduct is more blameworthy; compared to sexual misconduct, taking what is not given is more blameworthy;
compared to taking what is not given, killing is more blameworthy;
and compared to covetousness, malice is more blameworthy.]

False view is a greater fault than malice; that which consists of morality is less blameworthy than that which consists of giving; that which consists of cultivation is less blameworthy than that which consists of morality; and that which consists of reflection is less blameworthy than that which consists of hearing.
In that regard, from the perspective of the actual fact:

just as here, a certain person applies either harm or benefit—each of which is a matter of great weight—toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or toward any other object that occupies the position of a teacher.
In that regard, it is "exclusive" with respect to its opposite:
as when someone here, for their entire life, undertakes and persists solely in unwholesome action,
but never at any time in wholesome action.
In that regard, [it is so] by way of destroying the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*):
as when someone here, having abandoned unwholesome karma which constitutes an adverse factor, purifies wholesome karma.
[The perversion of actions:
What is the perversion of actions?
It should be understood as being threefold.
These are the perversion of action, the perversion of grasping, and the perversion of delight.
In that regard, there is a perversion of action:
as when someone here intends the killing of another living being.
One causes another to kill;

in that case, although there is the act of taking life (*prāṇātipāta*), there is no fault (*avadya*) of taking life itself, but rather one produces a fault that belongs to the same class as taking life, similar to taking life, and concordant with it.
Or, if one does not cause another living being to be killed, but having struck at an object that is not a living being, thinks, "I have killed a living being."

In that case, there is no taking of life, nor is there the fault of one who takes life; nevertheless, one produces a fault that belongs to the same category as taking life, is similar to taking life, and is of the same nature as taking life.

Just as it is with the path of action of taking life, so too should the inversion of action regarding the other paths of action, such as taking what is not given, be understood according to the appropriate case.
In that regard, there is the perversion of grasping (*grāhaviparyāsa*).
For example, here someone has such a view and speaks thus:
"There is no giving, there is no sacrifice," and so forth; this should be explained in detail as wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
It occurs to him:
"For one who kills or causes to kill, who takes what is not given, who engages in sexual misconduct, who speaks falsehoods, who practices slander, or who utters harsh speech;

or for one who indulges in idle chatter, who fails to give gifts, who observes the fast, who performs meritorious deeds, or who lives having undertaken the precepts—there is no evil or merit resulting from such a cause."
For example, here there is a certain person who holds such a view and speaks thus: "Those who hate Brahmins, those who hate Brahmā, and those who hate the gods must be killed;
and having killed them, on that account, there is only merit and no evil."
And among those, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, lying, slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter lead only to merit, not to demerit.
In that regard, there is a perversion of delight:
as when someone here, having undertaken unwholesome courses of action, persists in them to the utmost degree.
He delights,
and through them he engages in the nature of play.
What is the classification of actions?
There is action that has been performed and action that has not been performed; there is action that has been accumulated and action that has not been accumulated.
There is that which is intentional and there is that which is unintentional;
likewise, there is that with determinate ripening and that with indeterminate ripening; there is that whose ripening has matured and that whose ripening has not matured.
It is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral;
it is comprised within restraint, comprised within non-restraint,
or comprised within neither restraint nor non-restraint.
[It is] consisting of giving, consisting of ethical discipline, and consisting of cultivation; meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable;

to be experienced as pleasure, to be experienced as pain, and to be experienced as neither-pain-nor-pleasure; to be experienced in the present life, to be experienced upon rebirth, and to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Past, future, and present;
associated with the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm;
pertaining to those in training and those beyond training.
Neither that of one in training nor that of one beyond training;
to be abandoned by vision, to be abandoned by cultivation, or not to be abandoned;
black, with black maturation.
White karma has white ripening;
black-and-white karma has black-and-white ripening;
and karma that is neither black nor white has neither black nor white ripening.
Action conduces to the destruction of action;
it is fivefold: crooked action, faulty action, turbid action, pure action, and the action of a sage.
What is performed action?
That which is intended, and having intended it, is further initiated by body or speech.
What is unperformed action? That which is not intended, and not having intended it, is not further initiated by body or speech.
What is accumulated karma?
It is karma excluding ten types.

Namely: that performed in a dream, that performed through ignorance, that performed unintentionally, that performed without intense or sharp motivation, that performed under delusion, that performed through loss of mindfulness, that performed against one's will, that which is neutral by nature, and that which is destroyed by remorse.
And that which is impaired by its counteragent—
setting aside these ten kinds of action, whatever other action there may be.
Unaccumulated karma is of ten kinds, exactly as previously specified.
Volitional action is that which is performed intentionally, whether it has been accumulated or not.
Non-intentional karma is that which is performed without prior reflection.
Karma that is definitely to be experienced is that which has been performed intentionally and accumulated.
Karma of indefinite experience is that which is performed intentionally but not accumulated.
Karma that has ripened is that which has already yielded its fruit.
Karma with unripened fruition is that which has not yet yielded its fruit.
Wholesome karma is that which has non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion as its cause.
Unwholesome karma is that which has greed, hatred, and delusion as its cause.
Indeterminate action is that which has neither greed, hatred, and delusion as its cause, nor non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion as its cause.

Action comprised within restraint is that which is comprised within the Prātimokṣa restraint, or comprised within the restraint of meditative attainment and abandonment, or comprised within the untainted (anāsrava) restraint.
Action comprised within non-restraint is that which exists among the twelve groups of those who live by non-restraint.
The twelve groups of those who live by non-restraint are as follows:
Shepherds, poultry-keepers, pig-breeders, dog-trappers, bird-catchers, rabbit-hunters, thieves, executioners, jailers, informers, those who inflict torture, elephant-tamers, and snake-charmers.
Karma comprised within neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint is threefold:

setting aside the three types of restraint and setting aside the karma belonging to the class of those in non-restraint, it refers to whatever other karma— whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral— belongs to other classes, consisting of giving by way of its cause,
its motivation, its intrinsic nature, and its basis.
It should be understood that,
in this regard, from the perspective of its cause (*nidāna*), it has non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion as its causes.

In terms of origination (*samutthāna*), it is the volition (*cetanā*) that originates bodily and vocal actions for the purpose of relinquishing the object to be given, accompanied by non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
In terms of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is the bodily and vocal action originated by that [volition] which constitutes the relinquishment of the object to be given.
In this context, the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*) consists of both the object to be given and the recipient.
Just as it is for that which consists of giving, so too should that which consists of ethical discipline and that which consists of cultivation be understood accordingly.
In that regard, the cause and the origination of that which consists of morality are the same [as those of giving].
Its intrinsic nature is bodily and vocal action comprised within restraint.
Its basis is an object categorized as either sentient or non-sentient.
The cause of that which consists of cultivation is the cause of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), arising from non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion.

Its concomitant is meditative concentration; its intrinsic nature is the volition that brings about accomplishment; its basis is the realm of sentient beings who experience neither-pain-nor-pleasure in the ten directions.

All the characteristics of a donor, the characteristics of one possessing ethical discipline, and the characteristics of one who cultivates [the path] are to be understood in their entirety as previously described.

Meritorious action (*puṇyakarma*) is that which has a pleasant rebirth as its maturation (*sugativaipākya*), being wholesome (*kuśala*) and to be experienced within the five realms of existence (*pañcagativedanīya*).

Non-meritorious action (*apuṇyakarma*) is that which has an unfortunate rebirth as its maturation (*apāyavaipākya*), being unwholesome (*akuśala*) and to be experienced within the five realms of existence.

Imperturbable action (*āniñjyakarma*) is wholesome action that has the form and formless realms as its maturation (*rūpārūpyavaipākya*) and is to be experienced in the form and formless realms (*rūpyārūpyavedanīya*).
Karma to be experienced as pleasure is that which is meritorious and that immovable karma to be experienced through meditative absorption;
karma to be experienced as suffering is that which is non-meritorious;
and karma to be experienced as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is that karma which everywhere results in the maturation of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
Above the fourth dhyāna is the immovable [karma].
Karma to be experienced in the present life is that which has its fruit in the present life.
Karma to be experienced upon rebirth is that which has its fruit in the immediately following birth.
Karma to be experienced in a subsequent life is that which has its fruit in a future birth.
Past karma is that which exists in the state of latent impressions, whether it has already yielded its fruit or not yet yielded its fruit.
Future karma is that which has not yet come into being. Present karma is that which has been performed and accumulated, and which has not yet ceased.
Karma associated with the desire realm is that which has its maturation in the desire realm and is included within the desire realm.

Karma associated with the form realm is that which has its maturation in the form realm and is included within the form realm. Karma associated with the formless realm is that which has its maturation in the formless realm and is included within the formless realm.
Trainee action (*śaikṣa-karman*) is the wholesome [action] belonging to the mental continua of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*).
Non-trainee action (*aśaikṣa-karman*) is the wholesome [action] belonging to the mental continua of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee action is that which, setting aside both of those, belongs to other mental continua and is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Karma to be abandoned by seeing is that which is unwholesome and leads to experience in the states of woe. Karma to be abandoned by cultivation is that which is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, and leads to experience in the happy realms. Karma not to be abandoned is that which is mundane, supramundane, and untainted.
Black karma with black ripening is that which is non-meritorious;
white karma with white ripening is that which is imperturbable;
and black-white karma with black-white ripening is that which is meritorious yet unwholesome, due to its lack of opposition.
For thus, while non-meritorious karma has not been abandoned, the establishment of meritorious karma is made;
and karma that is neither black nor white, which is without ripening, conduces to the exhaustion of karma.

That which is supramundane and untainted (*anāsrava*) karma serves as the antidote for the abandonment of all three types of karma; therefore, the crooked karma (*vaṅkakarma*) is that which belongs to the outsiders and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), whether it be wholesome or unwholesome.
Furthermore, the faulty karma (*doṣakarma*) is precisely that which is crooked karma;
it is indeed faulty karma as well.

Furthermore, the action of fault (*doṣakarma*) refers here to whatever wholesome or unwholesome action is performed by ordinary persons who follow the teachings of the righteous but hold perverted views, who abide in their own adherence to dogmatic views, and who are falsely convinced.
The action of turbidity (*kaṣāyakarma*) is that which is crooked action and faulty action; it is also called the action of turbidity.

Furthermore, turbid action (*kaṣāyakarman*) refers here to whatever wholesome or unwholesome action is performed by ordinary persons who follow the teaching but are undecided and possess doubting minds.
Pure action (*śucikarman*) refers here to the wholesome action of ordinary persons who follow the teaching and possess correct certainty and non-doubting minds.

The action of sages (*munikarma*) here refers to the wholesome action—whether of those who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—of the noble ones (*ārya*) who are not ordinary persons (*apṛthagjana*).
According to another interpretation, all three [types of crookedness, etc. belong only to the outsiders (*bāhyaka*), that is, the non-Buddhist heretics (*tīrthika*);
therein, it is "crooked" (*vaṅka*) in the sense of being a wrong practice (*mithyāpratipatti*).
A *doṣa* (fault) is to be understood in the sense of obstructing the manifestation of the qualities (*guṇa*) dependent upon that [basis];
likewise, a *kaṣāya* (corruption) is to be understood in the sense of being an impediment; [and an *ādīnava* (disadvantage) is to be understood in the same way].
What is the disadvantage of actions?
In brief, the disadvantage should be understood as being of seven aspects.

For instance, one who takes life, on account of the basis and cause of taking life, intends harm for himself, harm for others, or harm for both; he produces fault pertaining to the present life and fault pertaining to the future life.
One experiences mental pain and dejection arising from that, pertaining both to the present life and to future lives.
How does one intend for one's own harm?
One who exerts himself toward harming living beings, on that account, incurs execution, imprisonment, loss, or censure.
But he is not able to harm another.
How does he harm another?
By being engaged in that very same way, he harms another.
But he does not incur, on that account, either death or even censure.
How is it for the affliction of both?
