When one, having applied oneself in that very way, afflicts another and, because of that, incurs from the other side either death or even censure.
How does one produce a fault pertaining to the present life? For example, when one intends for one's own harm. How does one produce a fault pertaining to future lives?
Just as one intends for the harm of others,
how does one experience the mental pain and dejection born thereof? One applies oneself to harming living beings if one does not perceive the sixfold disadvantage.
And yet, his taking of life does not succeed as he desires;
rooted in desire and lacking its proper cause, he experiences the mental suffering and dejection born thereof.
Furthermore, the ten disadvantages of immorality should be understood in detail exactly as they appear in the Sūtra.

Moreover, the disadvantages of the four unwholesome courses of action and the fifth, the consumption of fermented and distilled liquors, as related by the Blessed One in connection with the training of a lay follower (upāsaka), should also be understood in detail.
As it is said in the *Nandika-sūtra*: "What is the defilement of birth? The defilement of birth is as follows:"
And it should be viewed through four aspects:
by way of its classification, by way of its calamity, by way of its lack of restriction, and [by way of its nature].
Also by way of conduct.
[The classifications:
Among these, the classification of birth is according to the classification of realms (*dhātu*) and also according to the classification of destinies (*gati*).
It should be understood through the distinctions of different locations, the distinctions of birth, and the distinctions of the world of personal existence.
Therein, by way of the classification of realms,
there is birth belonging to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
In terms of the classification of destinies, there are five kinds of birth within the five destinies.
In terms of the distinction of different locations, birth occurs in thirty-six different locations within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
eighteen in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
and four different locations in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Summing those up, there are fifty-eight births.
According to the distinction of birth, there is birth among humans in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as one of dark birth.

For example, here some person is born into families such as those of the *caṇḍālas*, the *pukkasas*, the chariot-makers, or the bamboo-workers; or indeed into other such low, inferior, wretched, and miserable families, where food and drink are meager and sustenance is difficult to obtain. In this way, one is born into such types of families.
They alone are called unfortunate among humans.
Birth into a pure lineage:

as when someone here is born into a great kṣatriya family, a great brahmin family, or a great householder family; or indeed into other families that are wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments, with abundant assets and implements, abundant fields and property, and abundant stores of wealth, grain, treasuries, and granaries—one is born into such families as these.
These alone are called those who possess human good fortune.
Birth is neither black nor white;
for instance, some person here is born into middle families that are devoid of both [extremes].
Or, there is a threefold birth among those belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*).
Birth as an asura;
birth dependent upon a terrestrial region;
birth dependent upon a celestial palace in the sky.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are three kinds of birth:
the birth of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) with perception (sasaṃjñaka), and the birth without perception (asaṃjñaka).
And birth in the Śuddhāvāsa [heavens].
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are three kinds of birth:

birth among the gods who possess the perception of the immeasurable (apramāṇasaṃjñin), those who possess the perception of nothingness (akiñcanasaṃjñin), and those who possess neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñin).
In that regard, according to the distinction between the worlds of individual existence,
one should understand that there is immeasurable birth for immeasurable sentient beings within the immeasurable world-systems in the ten directions.
[It is called] "calamity" because of its calamitous nature,
as it was said by the Blessed One:
The blood that has flowed and been shed by you as you have run and wandered through the long course of saṃsāra is more than the water in the four great oceans.
For what reason?
Because for a long time you were reborn among the company of elephants; you were reborn among the company of horses, camels, donkeys, goats, buffaloes, boars, and dogs.

In that regard, you have experienced many severings of limbs and members, wherein much blood flowed and was shed from you—just as it is in the case of elephants and other such beings, so it is for humans; just as it is in the case of elephants and others, so it is for humans. Therein, you have experienced abundant calamities concerning mothers, calamities concerning fathers, calamities concerning brothers, calamities concerning sisters, as well as the destruction of kinsmen, the destruction of wealth, and the destruction of enjoyments.
In that regard, a vast amount of tears has flowed and been shed by you;
just as blood and tears are to be seen, so too should the drinking of a mother’s milk be regarded.
Such categories of calamities pertaining to birth are to be understood.
[Indeterminacy:
In that regard, it is indeterminate.

As the Blessed One has said: "For example, if one were to take all the grass, wood, branches, leaves, and so forth upon this earth, reduce them to tooth-sticks four finger-breadths long, and set them out in succession representing each generation of one's parents..."
This is my mother; this is the mother of that mother of mine;
this is my father.
If one were to think, "This is the father of my father," then by this method, those pieces of wood four finger-breadths long would indeed be exhausted and brought to an end very quickly.
Yet, I do not declare that there is a limit to mothers as mothers,
nor a limit to fathers as fathers.
And as it was said: "Whatever being you see who is suffering, possessed of supreme pain and mental distress, you should understand therein: 'We too have experienced such sufferings;
as with sufferings, so too with pleasures.
As it has been said: 'I do not see that spot of earth which is easily found where, after the passing of a long time, you [have not been born]...'"
"Those who have been born, gone, or died before you—

I do not see any being so easily found among you who, after the passing of this long road, has not been your mother, or your father, or your brother, or your sister, or your teacher, or your preceptor, or your guru, or one in the position of a guru."
As it has been said:
"The heap of bones of a single person in one eon would be like this:
it would be like Mount Vipulapārśva, were it to be gathered together."
If they were conjoined, they would neither perish nor become putrid.
[This concerns] the process of occurrence (*pravṛtti*). In that regard, what is the process of occurrence of birth?
The way in which the personal existences (*ātmabhāva*) arise through dependent origination is called "evolution" (*pravṛtti*). [Dependent Origination.
What is dependent origination? The summary verse:]

The body, the entrance, the meaning, the analysis, the sequence, the instruction, the etymology, the nature of conditionality, the classification of the nature of conditionality, and the compendium of the sūtras— thus the final [chapter] is manifold.
What is the body?
In brief, the establishment of dependent origination occurs through three aspects:
namely, how it arises from the prior limit into the middle limit.
And how it arises from the middle limit into the subsequent limit;
and how, having arisen in the middle limit, it proceeds and advances toward purification.
How does one arise from the prior limit into the middle limit, and having arisen, how does one proceed in the middle limit?

It is as follows: here, someone who was previously ignorant, possessed by ignorance, performs and accumulates meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable karma of body, speech, and mind, conditioned by ignorance.
And his consciousness, which follows that karma, persists until the time of death, serving as the cause for the consciousness of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*).
Internal and external craving is present as an auxiliary factor for this consciousness at the time of the production of its fruit.

Having passed away, it brings about a personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) from the past into the present continuum; specifically, through the causal consciousness as a condition, it gradually produces the resultant consciousness of rebirth-linking within the mother’s womb, proceeding through successive stages such as the *kalala* and so forth.

From the moment of the linking of rebirth (*pratisandhibandha*) until the state of decrepitude of the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) within the womb, that karma which was conducive to that birth has given its fruit through maturation (*vipāka*). And that maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) proceeds by depending upon that very name-and-form.
And that [consciousness] exists established upon six bases;
therefore it is said that "consciousness has name-and-form as its condition.

The material sense-faculties existing simultaneously and the mental factors (*nāman*) having just ceased are the respective bases for the six consciousnesses, depending upon which the activity of consciousness continues for as long as life lasts.
The great elements that constitute the sense-faculties of the five material faculties,
the matter produced by the great elements which serves as the physical basis for those faculties,
and the name (nāma) by which the appropriated faculties proceed in a continuous stream, falling within the causal succession.
Combining those two, they become the basis for continued existence.
For in this way, name-and-form has consciousness as its condition, and consciousness has name-and-form as its condition;
they proceed together in the present life like a bundle of reeds, for as long as there is life.
In this way, there is the occurrence of the dependent origination of the formative forces from the prior limit into the middle limit;
and for those that have occurred, there is their activity in the middle limit.
In that regard, this is the sequence of the process for those born from a womb (*jarāyuja*).
For those born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*) and those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), it should be understood that everything is the same except for the mother’s womb.

Among sentient beings with form (*rūpin*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), the distinction is that they appear with all their faculties complete through the apparitional mode of birth (*aupapāduka*).

Furthermore, in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), consciousness proceeds supported by name (*nāma*) and supported by the seed of form (*rūpa-bīja*), while the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-bīja*) proceed supported by consciousness.
From those seeds again, there occurs the manifestation of form in the future, even though it has been severed; this is the distinction here as well.
And by means of meritorious karma, one is born among gods and humans of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
By means of non-merit, one is reborn in the miserable states;
by means of the imperturbable, one is reborn in the realms of form and formlessness.
How does the dependent origination of conditioned phenomena arise from the middle limit toward the subsequent limit, and how does it not so arise? And through its non-arising, there is purification.
That person, having thus arisen at the middle limit, experiences two kinds of results of prior karma.
The internal fruit of maturation and the dominant fruit arising from objects are to be experienced;
yet, due to either hearing false doctrine or former habituation, one becomes deluded regarding both types of fruit.
Being thus deluded regarding the fruit of internal maturation, he does not understand, as it truly is, the production of renewed existence as suffering.
Taking ignorance pertaining to the past and the future as his dominant influence, he performs and accumulates formative forces (*saṃskāra*), as previously described.
As that consciousness performs new karma, it becomes associated with that karma in this very life.
Thus, conditioned by ignorance, the formative forces arise; and conditioned by the formative forces, consciousness arises.
And that consciousness, being the cause in the present life, grasps the fruit of the arising consciousness in the future.
And with reference to all consciousness, they are called the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñānakāya*).
That consciousness is accompanied by the seed of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that leads to renewed existence in the future;
and that seed of name-and-form is also accompanied by the seed of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) that leads to renewed existence in the future.
And that seed of the six sense bases is accompanied by the seed of contact pertaining to future renewed existence;
and that seed of contact is accompanied by the seed of feeling pertaining to future renewed existence.

This, first of all, should be understood as the projecting cause for the intermediate state of renewed existence, by which the entire personal existence—from consciousness up to and including feeling—is projected.

Having projected renewed existence through the very first delusion regarding the fruit of maturation, he then, by means of the second delusion regarding the fruit arising from sense objects, generates craving that takes the sensation of those objects as its support.

Through this craving, he either embarks upon the quest for sensory pleasures or the quest for existence, and thereby adopts the grasping for sensory pleasures, or the grasping for views, precepts and observances, and the doctrine of self.
Once grasping has been adopted, the previous projecting cause—conjoined with and accompanied by craving and grasping—is called "becoming" (*bhava*).

And for one who has passed away immediately after an existence that was comprised of the causes for the production of rebirth, there occurs— either sequentially or all at once— the manifestation of the formative factors beginning with consciousness and ending with feeling, according to the projecting cause as it was projected.
Thus, in this present life, there is craving conditioned by feeling born from contact with ignorance.
With craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises;
with existence as condition, birth arises.
Furthermore, specific sufferings such as old age, sickness, death, and so forth, which have birth as their condition, manifest;
they should be understood as occurring either in a particular place of rebirth or through the persistence of seeds.

Thus, in the middle period, depending on the formative forces (saṃskāra) conditioned by ignorance and craving conditioned by sensation, there is the arising of the formative forces in the future period.

Furthermore, if, by relying on the voice of another or upon the equipment accumulated in the past within this present life, one correctly attends to the two kinds of conditioned phenomena that constitute the fruit, as well as their cause, their cessation,
and the path leading to their cessation; and if, through the sequence of such correct mental attention, one gives rise to right view.
And having become purified regarding the truths, the trainee gradually attains the knowledge and vision of one beyond training.
By means of that knowledge and vision, he abandons both that ignorance and that craving in their entirety.
And through their abandonment, [he abandons] that contact born of ignorance which arises from not knowing that object as it truly is.
That which was to be felt has been abandoned;
through its abandonment, and through the fading away of ignorance, liberation by wisdom is realized in this very life.

The craving and attachment that are associated with the consciousness conjoined with feeling born of contact with ignorance—through the dissociation from that consciousness and through the abandonment of that attachment, liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*) is realized.

Due to the cessation of that ignorance, those formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth, up to feeling (*vedanā*), which previously existed starting from the future limit while that ignorance was not yet abandoned, do not arise;
they become subject to non-arising (*anutpattidharman*).
Therefore, it is said that from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations, proceeding in succession until,

from the cessation of the contact of maturation, there is the cessation of feeling born of maturation. In this very life, from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of the contact associated with ignorance.
Through the cessation of contact associated with ignorance, and through the cessation of feeling born from contact associated with ignorance, craving ceases.
Through the cessation of craving, as previously described, the formations beginning with grasping and ending with despair cease by virtue of being subject to non-arising;
thus, there is a non-occurrence of these formations in the present life.
And because of the non-occurrence [of further existence] in this present life, there is the attainment of nirvana in the realm of nirvana with remainder.
At that time, for him, consciousness-conditioned name-and-form and name-and-form-conditioned consciousness remain, pure and completely cleansed.
As long as his body, together with consciousness, persists, [so it remains].
To that extent, he experiences sensation while dissociated from it, not while associated with it.
And this body of his, together with consciousness, remains for as long as the lifespan projected by prior karma lasts.

When, due to the exhaustion of that lifespan, he abandons the body appropriated by consciousness, his life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is completely exhausted beyond this point of the life-faculty and does not ripen further.

And that consciousness, together with all feelings, having ceased by its own inherent nature in this life and because its causes have previously ceased elsewhere, becomes extinguished without remainder and without reconnection.

This is the realm of nirvana without substrate-remainder, the state of ultimate peace, for the sake of which [one practices] in the presence of the Blessed One, which leads toward nirvana and culminates in nirvana.
They desire the holy life.
Thus, this systematic presentation of dependent origination has been explained in detail through three aspects:
its occurrence from the prior limit to the middle limit, its occurrence from the middle limit to the subsequent limit, and its purification of occurrence within the middle limit.
This is the body of dependent origination.
[The "gateways"]: What is the gateway?
Dependent origination proceeds by way of eight gateways.
Internally, by way of the arising of consciousness;
externally, by way of the production of crops;

by way of the death and rebirth of the world of sentient beings; by way of the dissolution and evolution of the receptacle world; and by way of the support provided by nutriment—taking the ownership of one's own karma as the dominant factor, [one observes] desirable and undesirable karma and its corresponding results.
[The meaning] is by way of the enjoyment of the fruit, by way of power, and by way of purification.
What is the meaning of dependent origination?
The meaning of dependent origination is the meaning of being devoid of a sentient being; when there is the absence of a sentient being, it is the meaning of impermanence;
and when there is impermanence, it is the meaning of appearing only for a brief duration.
When existence is present, there is the meaning of dependence; when dependence is present, there is the meaning of being devoid of agency;
when the state of being devoid of agency is present, there is the meaning of the non-interruption of the continuity of cause and fruit.

When there is no interruption in the continuity of cause and effect, it has the sense of the proceeding of corresponding causes and effects; when there is the proceeding of corresponding causes and effects, it has the sense of the ownership of one's own karma (*karmasvakatā*). For the purpose of elucidating what meaning is the establishment of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) set forth?
This is for the purpose of elucidating the meaning of one's own affliction and purification as they are embraced by causes and conditions.
[The Analysis] What is analysis?
It is that which is ignorance regarding the past.
The sutra is given in detail.
In that regard, what is ignorance concerning the past?
The ignorance that arises when one improperly conceptualizes past conditioned phenomena, thinking: "Did I indeed exist in the past, or did I not exist in the past?
Who was I? Or how was I? is [ignorance].

What is ignorance regarding the future? It is the improper conceptualization of future conditioned phenomena, thinking: "Shall I indeed exist in the future time, or shall I not exist in the future time?"
What is ignorance regarding "what shall I become? and "how shall I become?
What is ignorance regarding the past and the future?
It is the ignorance of one who, inwardly engaging in improper reflection, becomes full of doubt, wondering: "Who am I? Who shall we become?
From where has this sentient being come?
Having passed away from here, where will he go?"
What is internal ignorance? It is the ignorance of one who attends improperly to internal conditioned phenomena by conceiving of them as a self. What is external ignorance?

The ignorance that arises from improperly attending to external conditioned phenomena— which are reckoned as non-sentient beings— as being "mine," is the ignorance regarding the internal and external.
What is it?
It is the ignorance of one who improperly conceptualizes the formative factors belonging to the continua of others as being friends, enemies, or neutral parties.
What is ignorance regarding action?
It is the ignorance of one who improperly conceptualizes an agent of action.
What is ignorance regarding maturation?
The ignorance that consists in the improper conceptualization of the formations comprised within the fruit of maturation as having an experiencer;
this is ignorance regarding the ripening of karma.
What is it?
It is the ignorance of one who conceptually constructs actions and their results in an improper manner (*ayoniśas*) and in a false way.
What is ignorance regarding the Buddha?
It is the ignorance that arises from not attending to, or from attending to erroneously, or from being negligent, or from doubting, or from disparaging the enlightenment of the Buddhas.
What is ignorance regarding the Dharma?
It is the ignorance that arises from not attending to, or from attending to erroneously, or from being negligent, or from doubting, or from disparaging the well-expounded nature of the Dharma.

What is ignorance regarding the Saṅgha? It is that ignorance which belongs to one who does not attend to the Saṅgha’s correct practice, or who attends to it erroneously, or who is negligent, or who is doubtful, or who disparages it.
What is ignorance regarding suffering?

For one who does not attend to suffering as suffering, or attends to it erroneously, or through negligence, or through doubt, or through disparagement— whatever ignorances there are regarding suffering, so too should the ignorances regarding origination, cessation, and the path be understood.
What is ignorance regarding the cause?

It is the ignorance of one who imagines there to be no cause at all, or who improperly imagines an uneven cause—such as Īśvara, primordial nature (prakṛti), the individual self (puruṣa), or other such [factors].
Just as it is with regard to the cause, so it is with regard to the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) arisen from causes.
Furthermore, those are wholesome because they are irreproachable;
unwholesome because they are reproachable;
and to be cultivated because they are beneficial.
They are not to be cultivated because they are harmful;
they are blameworthy because they are black;
they are blameless because they are white.
They are with counterparts because they are mixed.
What is ignorance regarding the thorough penetration of the six bases of contact as they truly are?
It is the ignorance of one who possesses overweening pride and whose mind is perverted with respect to spiritual realization.
Summarizing these, there are twenty modes of ignorance. Furthermore, there is another sevenfold ignorance:

delusion regarding time, delusion regarding entities, delusion regarding transmigration, delusion regarding the supreme, delusion regarding reality, delusion regarding affliction and purification, and delusion regarding overweening pride.
Regarding the twentyfold ignorance and the sevenfold ignorance, by which [categories] should the inclusion of which be understood?
The first [sevenfold] ignorance is included within the first three [of the twentyfold];
furthermore, the second [sevenfold] ignorance is included within the subsequent three.
Again, with three [verses] following the fourth;
again, with four [verses] following the fifth;
again, with six [verses] following the sixth.
By the last one, [the verse] of the seventh [chapter].
Furthermore, there is another fivefold ignorance:
delusion regarding objects, delusion regarding views, delusion regarding heedlessness, delusion regarding the true meaning, and delusion regarding conceit.
As for the twenty exclusive types of ignorance and the fivefold [ignorance], by which [category] should the inclusion of which be understood?
Through delusion regarding views, the inclusion of ignorance concerning the six preceding [links] and regarding phenomena produced by causes should be understood.
Through delusion regarding negligence, the inclusion of ignorance concerning action, its maturation, and both of them should be understood.
Through delusion regarding the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha-sammoha*), there is the inclusion of ignorance concerning the Buddhas and so forth, up to the Truth of the Path.

Through delusion consisting of overweening pride (*abhimāna-sammoha*), there is the inclusion of the last [type of ignorance]. Furthermore, through delusion regarding the object (*artha-sammoha*), the inclusion of all [types of ignorance] is to be understood.
Ignorance (*ajñāna*), non-seeing (*adarśana*), non-realization (*anabhisamaya*), darkness (*tamas*), delusion (*saṃmoha*),
and the gloom of nescience (*avidyāndhakāra*)— these six synonyms for ignorance (*avidyā*) are to be understood respectively in relation to the seven objects of delusion;
the last one corresponds to the object consisting of delusion regarding reality (*tattva*).
Having established the matter in this way, the final synonym for the darkness of ignorance (avidyā) should be understood therein.

There is another way of explaining it. Three synonyms are applied respectively to the opposites of the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī*), the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*), and the wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*). Furthermore, because those very opposites are weak, middling, and intense, there are three other synonyms. Thus, there are six synonyms based on the distinction of opposites and the distinction of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
What are the bodily formations?
They are bodily actions belonging to the desire realm and the form realm, reckoned as meritorious or non-meritorious below and above; furthermore, they are reckoned as imperturbable.
What are the vocal formations?
Vocal action;
the remainder is to be understood as before.
What are the mental formations?
Mental action:
in the realm of desire, that is both meritorious and non-meritorious, but not imperturbable; in the two higher realms, it is exclusively imperturbable.
What is eye-consciousness?

It is that consciousness which, based on the eye-faculty in the future, is the discernment of forms; it is the consciousness that has become a seed permeated by merit, demerit, and the imperturbable, as well as that which arises from those seeds as a result.
Just as it is with eye-consciousness, so should ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness be understood.
This distinction among the various types of representation should be understood as being produced by way of their basis and their object.
Furthermore, that which belongs to the desire realm is sixfold,
while that which belongs to the form realm is fourfold.
That belonging to the formless realm is of only one kind.
What is the aggregate of feeling? It is the entire class of experience,
and it belongs to the three realms.
What is the aggregate of perception? It is the entire class of perceiving. What is the aggregate of mental formations?
What is the aggregate of consciousness? It is the entire class of mental activity consisting of the volitional formation of the mind and the nature of discerning.
These aggregates, too, should be understood as belonging to the three realms.
What are the four great elements?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
These, moreover, are contained within two categories.
What is form derived from the four great elements? It consists of the ten bases of form.

And the form included in the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) consists of the ten forms belonging to the desire realm, the form of the sphere of phenomena that falls under conventional designation (*prajñaptipatita*), and the eight forms belonging to the form realm, as well as the form included in the sphere of phenomena;
all of that too is twofold:
that which exists as a seed embraced by the seed of consciousness, and that which exists as the fruit produced from it.
What is the sense-sphere of the eye?
It is the translucent matter that is the support for visual consciousness, by means of which one has seen, sees, or will see visible forms.
Just as the sense-sphere of the eye is, so too should the sense-spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind be understood according to their respective applications.
Furthermore, for all [these], karma should be explained by way of its designation according to the three times.

That too is twofold: that which exists as a seed comprised within the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and that which exists as the fruit produced therefrom; [this pertains to] the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
There are five [such types] belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*).
The sixth belongs to the three realms.
What is eye-contact?
It is the grasping of an object as beautiful and so forth, arising from the coming together of the three.
Furthermore, these are of two kinds.
They consist of those that have become seeds, being grasped by the seeds of the six sense bases, and those that have become the fruits produced from them;
all those belonging to the desire realm,
and four belonging to the form realm.
One [realm] belongs to the formless sphere (ārūpyāvacara).
All [of these belong to the three realms]: four belong to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), and one belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*). What is pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*)?
It is that which, depending on a sense faculty and its object conducive to pleasure, arises as a pleasant experience, a felt sensation, belonging to the category of feeling.
What is painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*)?
That which is conducive to suffering arises in dependence upon a dyad as an unpleasant feeling. What is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
That which arises in dependence upon a pair of conditions that are neither conducive to suffering nor conducive to pleasure— a feeling belonging to sensation that is neither pleasant nor unpleasant—
consists of three types of conduct pertaining to the desire realm,
and two types pertaining to the form realm, from the third dhyāna upwards.

The neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] from the fourth dhyāna upwards, as far as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, is also twofold: that which exists as a seed comprised within the seed of contact, and that which exists as the fruit produced by it.
What is craving for sensual pleasures?
It is the defiled longing directed toward the formations belonging to the realm of sensual pleasure, by means of which one brings about suffering within the realm of sensual pleasure.
What is craving for form?

What is craving pertaining to the form realm? It is the afflicted longing dependent upon the formations of the form realm directed toward the formations of the form realm, by which one brings about suffering in the form realm. What is craving pertaining to the formless realm?
It is the afflicted longing dependent upon the formations of the formless realm directed toward the formations of the formless realm, by which one brings about suffering in the form realm.
What is clinging to sensual pleasures?
It is the desire and lust for sensual pleasures. What is clinging to views?
Excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it is the desire and attachment toward other views.
What is the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*)?
It is the desire and attachment toward the false resolve regarding rules and observances (*śīlavratamithyāpraṇihita*).
What is the discourse on self? It is the desire and attachment toward the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
By means of this first [discourse], one brings about suffering specifically within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, by means of the remaining [perfections], one [acts] within the triple world.
What is the existence of the desire realm (*kāmabhava*)?

The existence of the prior period belonging to the desire realm, the existence of karma, the existence at death, the intermediate existence, the existence at birth, and the existences as hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, and humans— these are called the existence of the desire realm.
Furthermore, it is produced by the influence of the appropriation of previously performed formative forces and afflictions.
What is existence in the realm of form?
Excluding the existences of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and humans, the remaining should be understood as the existence of the form realm (*rūpabhava*).
What is formless existence?
With the exception of the intermediate state, formless existence should be understood as that which is comprised within the other forms of existence.

With reference to what are the seven existences established—the existences of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, humans, karma, and the intermediate state? They are established with reference to three functions: one is the projecting existence.
Existence that brings about rebirth is one;
existences that experience the fruit are five.
What is birth (*jāti*)?
It is the initial manifestation in the womb-born (*jarāyuja*) and egg-born (*aṇḍaja*) modes of birth.
What is being born (*saṃjāti*)?
What is the fulfillment of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) therein for one who has not yet emerged? What is the entry? It is the emergence from that state.
What is emergence?
It is the growth of that which has emerged. What is manifestation?
In the modes of birth from moisture and by spontaneous generation, there is a simultaneous arising.
What is the acquisition of the aggregates? It is the arising of the five appropriated aggregates within those very modes of birth and stages.
What is the acquisition of the elements (*dhātu*)?
It is the state of those very aggregates (*skandha*) being grasped by causes and conditions.
What is the acquisition of the sense bases (*āyatana*)?

What is the production of those very aggregates? It is their being sustained by other conditions. What is the manifestation of the aggregates? It is the nourishment and accumulation of those very aggregates produced by food.
What is the manifestation of the life-faculty?
It is the persistence of those very aggregates by virtue of the remainder of their lifespan.
Furthermore, what is the summarized meaning of this birth?

It is as follows: the intrinsic nature of birth, that in which one is born, that which is born, those causes and conditions by which it is grasped, and that support—both acquired and innate—by which it is sustained; this is the summarized meaning.
What is "stumbling"?
What is trembling? It is that which arises from the weakness of its basis.
What is graying? It is the discoloration of the hair.
What is the abundance of wrinkles?
It is the contraction of the skin.
What is decrepitude?
What is "sinking"? It is the lack of capacity for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures and the loss of vitality,
as well as the lack of capacity for undertaking resolute efforts due to natural ill-health.
What is the state of having limbs marked by moles? It is the prominence of dark-colored lumps on the body due to the obstruction of symmetry, such as being bent like a curved rafter.
What is the state of having a body that pants with a wheezing sound?
What is the forward-leaning of the body? It is the state of bodily configuration manifested by the posture of walking, as well as the resulting tendency toward heavy breathing;
it is the incapacity of the body to remain upright when one is situated in the posture of sitting.
What is reliance on a staff?
It is the state of dwelling by resorting to the strength of a staff while remaining in a particular posture or mode of conduct (*iryāpatha*).
What is infirmity? It is the state of excessive and frequent sleep while remaining in a particular posture or mode of conduct during sleep.
What is slackness?
It is the lack of capacity to wake up clearly in that very state.
What is decline?
What is the decline of mindfulness and wisdom?
It is the lack of capacity to bring wholesome qualities to fulfillment due to the dullness of mindfulness and wisdom.
What is the transformation of the faculties? It is their natural dullness. What is their deterioration? It is their impairment.
What is the antiquity of those very conditioned phenomena? It is their lack of abundance regarding their objects,
which consists in their final stage leading up to the proximity of death.
What is the state of being worn out? It is the tendency of the physical basis toward disintegration until the end of life, based on its incapacity for functional application.
Furthermore, what is the summarized meaning of old age?

The transformation of the basis, the transformation of the hair, the transformation of nourishment, the transformation of vitality and strength, the transformation of health, the transformation of complexion, the transformation of posture, the transformation of the formless faculties,
the transformation of the material faculties, the passing of the ten stages, and the exhaustion of the lifespan— this should be understood as the summary meaning.
Who are those various sentient beings? They are the hell-beings and so forth. What are the classes of sentient beings?
All those [beings] are indeed [included].
What is death? It is the death of those beings for whom it occurs without the severing of the vital points (marmaccheda).
What is cyavanatā? It is the death of those sentient beings accompanied by the cutting of the vital points (marmaccheda). What is bheda? [It is the dissolution of the body.]
What is the departure from the basis of consciousness?
What is disappearance? It is the cessation of the material sense faculties.
What is the loss of vitality?
It is the state of hiccupping and labored breathing.
What is the loss of heat?
What is the state of motionlessness,
the laying down of the aggregates, and the cessation of the life-faculty?
It is death at the appointed time.
What is death? It is the passing away at the [proper] time due to its conditions. What is the act of dying?
The state of being near death for a long time is another synonym for what is called "death," "the work of Māra," and "the passing away. Furthermore, what is the concise meaning of dying?
What is death;
of which dharma there is death;
how there is death; and what is the time subsequent to that for one who has died.
This is the summarized meaning;
thus should this analysis of the analysis of dependent origination be understood.
[The Sequence: For what reason has such a sequential exposition of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*), beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), been made?
First, there is confusion regarding the object of knowledge (*jñeya-vastu*).
For one who is thus deluded, there arises therein false volitional formation;
from false volitional formation comes perversion of the mind;
and from perversion of the mind comes the binding of rebirth.
From the connection of rebirth comes the completion of the sense faculties;
from the completion of the sense faculties comes the enjoyment of objects through both [the faculties and the mind];
and from the enjoyment of objects comes attachment and the longing for them.
For one who seeks by means of prayer, there is an accumulation of afflictions (*kleśa*).
From the accumulation of afflictions arises the origination of desirable and undesirable karma leading to renewed existence (*paunarbhavika*).
From the origination of the accumulation of karma, [one wanders] in the saṃsāra of the five destinies.
The suffering of origination;
the suffering of aging, death, and so forth produced by that suffering of origination, which has its cause in the transformation of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*);
and the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair, which has its cause in the transformation of sense objects.
Therefore, these twelve limbs were taught by the Blessed One in their proper sequence.

There is another sequential method concerning dependent origination based on two kinds of conditions: the condition of personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) and the condition of the enjoyment of objects (*viṣayopabhoga*).
The condition of personal existence is comprised of six members, and the condition of the enjoyment of objects is likewise.
It is by means of these six alone:
first, one is deluded regarding the self-body through the grasping at a self and so forth;
then, not knowing that the ripening of the fruits of actions is suffering, one performs those actions.
Having done this, he reflects upon it as follows:

"By means of that karma acting as an assistant to consciousness, one brings about three kinds of suffering in the future: that comprised by the arising of the sense faculties, that comprised by their full development, and that comprised by the enjoyment of objects."
With name-and-form ending in contact, having produced craving for feeling conditioned by contact in this very life, one falls into a search conditioned by sense objects;
one undertakes exertion.

By way of exertion, by way of gain and ritual practices, by way of moral precepts and vows, and by way of liberation, one undertakes the search for sensual pleasures, the search for personal existence, the search for liberation, and the search for the conditions for the enjoyment of sense objects.
Falling into false seeking and having committed afflictions and the actions preceded by them, one is born, ages, and dies within the saṃsāra of five destinies.
Another sequential classification consists of three groups of beings:
those who transcend the world, those who desire purification, and those for whom sense objects are supreme.
Therein, the first [type of beings] bring dependent origination to cessation and do not increase it through the white side.

The second type of beings, not knowing the truths as they truly are, dwell frequently with mindfulness established, having performed meritorious, imperturbable, and contaminated karma consisting of cultivation; or else, with mindfulness unestablished, they dwell frequently with a mind permeated by remorse or permeated by the joy of being without remorse.
As before, those who are inferior, middling, or superior produce three kinds of suffering in the future within the place of rebirth in successive order.

For the third type of beings— those existing in the experience born from the enjoyment of present objects— the other six links, beginning with craving and ending with old age and death, are to be understood sequentially as previously described.
For what reason is dependent origination taught by starting with this aging and death in reverse order? It is with reference to the teaching of the method of the truths;
for in that way, birth, aging, and death are categorized under the truth of suffering.

As for what was said by the Blessed One—that phenomena do not have the cessation of name-and-form as their precursor—for what reason is it not stated that they have the cessation of ignorance as their precursor? Because [the designation] is made with respect to those whose minds are liberated;
for in them, in this very life, that which has become the seed and ends with sensation has ceased.
And when one experiences a feeling in the present life, because the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) of craving is uprooted, it does not arise again and thus becomes ceased.
Due to its cessation, those factors that preceded it also become ceased.
In this manner, the causal sequence of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is to be understood.
[Etymological Explanation] For what reason is dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) called "dependent origination"?

The etymological derivation of the word is: "the arising (utpāda) of those who have gone back (pratigatya) into the realms of existence (gati) and are conjoined with the afflictions (kleśa) is dependent origination."
Furthermore, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the arising [of an effect] through the convergence and coming together [of conditions] immediately [after they have ceased],
with reference to the meaning of momentariness. Furthermore, dependent origination is the arising within one's own continuum from a past condition that has not yet relinquished its causal capacity.

This definition should be understood with reference to this meaning: "When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises—and not otherwise. Furthermore, *pratītyasamutpāda* means "arising again and again in a continuous succession";
the sense is "perishing again and again."
Furthermore, having again become a condition, the arising [of phenomena] in a continuous succession within the past time is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
It was said by the Blessed One: "Having realized dependent origination, I shall teach it."
"Having understood" means "having fully awakened to";
consequently, that very designation became established as *pratītyasamutpāda*.
Regarding "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*):
by how many conditions (*pratyaya*) does ignorance (*avidyā*) become a condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)?
It is a condition for those possessing form (*rūpin*) by way of the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
But for those that are formless, they exist by way of three conditions: the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition.
In this manner, the status of the remaining members as conditions should be understood according to their respective application.
For those with form, [they serve] for those with form by way of one condition: the dominant condition.
For formless [dharmas], there are two [conditions] and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
For formless [dharmas], there is one [condition] for those that possess form;
however, for formless [dharmas], there are three—namely, the immediately preceding, the object, and the dominant conditions—for those that are formless.
For what reason or causal condition are these members not conditions?
Because the causal condition is characterized by its own-nature and seed-condition.
If they are not conditions by way of the causal condition, for what reason is dependent origination taught as the relationship between cause and fruit?
With reference to the projecting cause and the productive cause, which are subsumed under the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
How many members are comprised within the projecting cause? From ignorance up to feeling. How many members are comprised within the productive cause?
From craving up to existence:
how many members are comprised within the results of the causes of projection and actualization?
They are, in both the present life and the future life, the factors beginning with consciousness and ending with sensation, as well as the states of birth, old age, and death.

[The Classification of Conditions] Since it has been stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) has appropriate mental attention (*yoniso-manaskāra*) as its cause, for what reason was this exposition of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) not taught at the very beginning?
Because it is not a cause for abandonment and because it is a cause of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
For instance:
that mental attention does not arise in one who is not deluded,
and dependent origination is the cause of affliction.
Ignorance is inherently afflicted, and improper mental attention is also inherently afflicted. The mind defiles knowledge;
however, it is rather through the power of ignorance that it becomes afflicted.
And birth is produced by karma and afflictions;
therein, ignorance is the primary cause of karma within dependent origination.
Therefore, appropriate mental attention (*yoniso-manaskāra*) has not been mentioned for this [ignorance].
For what reason is intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) not stated to be a condition for intrinsic nature?
Because intrinsic nature, when not obtaining other conditions, does not become a nourisher or a producer of intrinsic nature in terms of its defilement;
therefore, it is not so stated.
For what reason are meritorious and imperturbable formations, though performed with discernment, said to have ignorance as their condition?
For one who does not know the conventional cause of suffering, non-meritorious formations arise conditioned by that [ignorance].
For one who does not know the ultimate cause of suffering, meritorious and imperturbable formations arise conditioned by that [ignorance].
Therefore, they too are said to have ignorance as their condition.
When it was stated that karma has greed, hatred, and delusion as its causes, for what reason is it said here to have delusion alone as its cause?
It is because this refers specifically to the causes of meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable karma;
however, only non-meritorious karma has greed and delusion as its causes.

Since bodily and vocal actions are originated by volition (*cetanā*), for what reason are the formative forces (*abhisaṃskāra*)—which have the formative forces as their condition—said to have ignorance (*avidyā*) alone as their condition?
It is because the context concerns the condition for the origination of all formative forces, and because it concerns the condition for the arising of both afflicted and wholesome volitions.
Since consciousness has name-and-form as its condition, for what reason is it said in this context that it has formations alone as its condition?
It is because formations are the defilers of consciousness, the projectors of renewed existence, and the actualizers [of rebirth];
whereas name-and-form is not, because it is merely a condition for the arising [of consciousness] by way of being its support and object.

When name-and-form (nāmarūpa) arises depending on the great elements (mahābhūta) and even contact (sparśa), for what reason is it said that consciousness alone is its condition? Because consciousness is the cause for the new arising of that [name-and-form], whereas the great elements and contact are merely the causes for the support of what has already arisen. Furthermore, when it is stated that the descent of the embryo into the mother’s womb occurs in dependence on the six elements (ṣaḍdhātu), for what reason is only the consciousness-element (vijñānadhātu) mentioned?

For when the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) is present, it is certain that the semen, blood, the primary elements (mahābhūta), and the cavity of the mother’s womb are not deficient; thus, because the element of consciousness is predominant and because this concerns the arising of existence in all modes of birth (yoni), why is it stated here that the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana)—even though they have nutriment as a condition—have name-and-form (nāmarūpa) alone as their condition?
It is because name-and-form is the cause for their arising.
And food is merely the cause for the maintenance and support of that which has already arisen.
As for why contact—which is conditioned by the coming together of the three—is stated to be conditioned specifically by the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*):
it is because, when the six sense bases exist, the other two [factors] are necessarily present; thus, the six sense bases are primary, and furthermore, because the six sense bases include those two.

Since sensations arising from self-aggression, aggression by others, seasonal changes, and those brought about by past karma are all perceived, for what reason are they explained here as being conditioned solely by contact (*sparśapratyaya*)?
It is because contact is the most immediate cause, and because the other conditions are themselves nourished by contact; thus, even those various sensations [are shown to be so].
Because [feeling] arises from contact and does not exist without contact;

and since craving has been described as having ignorance as its condition and as being conditioned by objects corresponding to that [craving], for what reason is it stated here that feeling alone is the condition?

It is because, through the power of feeling, the longing for union with an object proceeds; whereas, through the power of delusion regarding such an object, while failing to understand as they truly are the arising, passing away, and so forth of those feelings, the mind [proceeds] from that [delusion].
They do not prevent it.
Since grasping arises from unabandoned latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and from those phenomena conducive to them, for what reason is it said here that grasping has craving alone as its condition?
It is because one who has given rise to longing and engages in searching awakens the latent disposition and draws in those phenomena conducive to it.
Since it was already stated previously that "existence" (*bhava*) is conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*), for what reason is it said here that existence is conditioned by grasping (*upādāna*)?
It is because, through the power of grasping, that very same karma becomes capable of drawing forth consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so forth, into their respective places of rebirth.
When birth is conditioned by semen, blood, and so forth, for what reason is it said to be conditioned by existence (*bhava*) alone?
Because when existence is present, those other conditions necessarily exist in their entirety; thus, existence is considered the primary condition.
Furthermore, when old age and death are observed even through conditions such as traversing uneven paths or failing to avoid dangers, [existence remains the primary cause].
For what reason is it stated here that [old age and death] have birth alone as their condition?
It is because those other conditions also have birth as their root; furthermore, even when those other conditions are absent, old age and death are still produced by birth.
Among these twelve factors, how many belong to the path of afflictions (*kleśavartman*),
how many to the path of karma (*karmavartman*), and how many to the path of suffering (*duḥkhavartman*)?
Three are the path of afflictions;
two are the path of karma; the remaining ones are the path of suffering.
How many are exclusively causes?
The first one. How many are exclusively fruits?
The last one is a single [member].
How many are both cause and fruit?
The remaining ones.
Furthermore, there is another way of answering this question:
three are exclusively of the nature of cause and fruit,
while two are exclusively of the nature of fruit.
The remaining factors should be understood as being both causes and effects.
How many have individual characteristics? How many have combined characteristics?
Three have individual characteristics.
The factors beginning with volitional formations (saṃskāra) have the characteristic of being interconnected.
For what reason are *saṃskāra* and *bhava* taught as having a combined characteristic?
They are taught in two ways:
because they bestow desired and undesired fruits, and because of the difference in their capacity to bring about rebirth in the various realms of existence (*gati*).
For what reason is it taught in three ways— characterized by consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases in partial conjunction?
It is because of the context of the time of affliction and the context of the time of conception.
And [it is established] by way of the time of its occurrence and its governing authority.
For what reason are the factors beginning with consciousness and ending with feeling, as well as birth, aging, and death, explained in two ways?
It is for the purpose of making known the characteristics of distinct bases of suffering, and for the purpose of illuminating the distinction between projection and actualization.

In the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), what is the meaning of "departure" (*prativigama*)? It is the meaning of the non-abiding of those things that have arisen; it is the meaning of departure.
What is the meaning of "conjunction"? It is the meaning of the coming together of a collection.
What is the meaning of "arising" for conditions?

What is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? What is the state of being dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpannatā*)? It is the nature of arising (*utpattidharmatā*) which consists in the production of ever-new [phenomena] as they are encompassed by the totality of conditions (*pratyayasāmagrī*).
This is the dependent origination of the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, that which is simply the state of having arisen is called "dependently originated" (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
How many members (*aṅga*) are subsumed under the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), and for what kind of suffering in this present life?
Two [links]— birth and aging-and-death—
are comprised solely within the truth of suffering and result in suffering only in the future.
From consciousness through feeling, the [remaining] links exist as seeds.
How many are comprised within the truth of the origin?
The remaining ones.
Is ignorance a condition for the formative forces (saṃskāra) by way of coexistence, or is it a condition as that which has ceased immediately prior,
or is it a condition as that which has ceased long ago?
It should be understood that it is a condition in all three ways.
By way of coexistence, it is the obstructive condition (*āvaraṇa-pratyaya*) with respect to those phenomena that serve as the basis for formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
It is through ignorance regarding that purpose for which one arouses the formative forces that [this occurs].
The immediately preceding ceased [moment] is the generative condition (*saṃjanana-pratyaya*).
Due to ignorance accompanied by wrong views and negligence,

one establishes a state within the continuum that is conducive to the future arising of those [afflictions]; therefore, even though it has long since ceased, it should be regarded as the projecting condition.
How are the formative forces (saṃskāra) to be viewed as the threefold condition for consciousness?
They are the simultaneous condition by way of perfuming the state of the seed;
and subsequently, they are the generative condition by way of being subject to its influence, having ceased immediately prior.
The projecting condition is that which, by way of projection, brings about the production of a fruit in the future.
Just as volitional formations are the condition for consciousness,
so too is consciousness for name-and-form,
and name-and-form for the six sense bases.
The six sense bases are the condition for contact; contact is the condition for feelings; and feelings are the condition for craving. How are these to be understood as being conditions in three ways?
They should be understood as the co-existent condition by virtue of being the causal basis for determination (*adhyavasāna*).
Immediately thereafter, they are the generative condition by virtue of initiating activities such as seeking (*paryeṣṭi*) under its influence.
Because it remains in the continuum in such a way that it is difficult to escape in the future, even though it has long since ceased, it is still designated as a condition.
How is craving (*tṛṣṇā*) a condition for grasping (*upādāna*) by way of being a threefold condition?

Because it is accompanied by desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*), it is the co-existent condition (*sahabhāva-pratyaya*), as it serves as the condition for the inclination toward and settling upon those phenomena conducive to grasping.
Because it exercises control immediately following that [craving], it is the generative condition (*saṃjanana-pratyaya*).
Because it is not released from that [state] and is established in a continuous stream, even though it has long since ceased, it is still the cause for the attainment of death.
How is grasping (*upādāna*) a condition for existence (*bhava*) by way of being a threefold condition?
By way of coexistence, it is the condition of coexistence because it directs that karma toward its respective realm of rebirth.

By way of drawing forth consciousness and the rest into that place of birth through its power, it is the immediately preceding ceased [condition] acting as the generative condition (*saṃjanana-pratyaya*).
The projecting condition is also [effective] even though it has long since ceased, by virtue of being the condition for the capacity to bring about the elements.
How is existence (*bhava*) a condition for birth (*jāti*) by way of being a threefold condition?
It is a simultaneous condition (*sahabhāvapratyaya*) by virtue of perfuming the state of the seed;
it is a condition for production (*saṃjananapratyaya*) by virtue of following its power immediately thereafter, even though it has long since ceased.
The condition for the penetration [of the result] is the actualization of that fruit.
Just as existence (*bhava*) is the condition for birth (*jāti*), so too should birth be regarded as the condition for aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Existence is established in two ways.

Thus, the establishment of the primary members should be understood from the perspective of the action (*karman*) as previously described when it is embraced by grasping (*upādāna*), as well as from the perspective of all the members—from consciousness (*vijñāna*) up to sensation (*vedanā*)—which exist as seeds embraced by grasping.

Is the function of these members of existence (*bhavāṅga*) solely this: namely, that they serve as the successive conditions for the factors beginning with formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and ending with old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), or is there something else as well?
Furthermore, this second function should be understood as the activity of all [factors] within their respective spheres, as appropriate.
Is ignorance the condition for the formations alone, or for the other members as well?
Ignorance is indeed the condition for everything up to old age and death; however, it is specified as the condition for the formations alone in the sense of being their immediate condition.
In this manner, the remaining factors should be understood according to their respective applications.
But it is not the case that lower factors serve as conditions for those that are higher.
For what reason?
Because effort is exerted toward the abandonment of the higher [factors] in order to abandon the higher, and through that abandonment, there is the abandonment of the lower.

Having thus [stated] that one does not [attain] the higher abandonment through the lower abandonment, therefore only those many conditions should be seen as its causes. How is it said: "When this exists, this comes to be"?
In the sense that from a condition which has not been abandoned, something other than itself arises;
how is it said that "from the arising of this, that arises"?
It is in the sense that from an impermanent condition, something other than itself arises.
For what reason does old age and death exist when birth exists?
Why is it said that "old age and death have birth as their condition"?
This applies all the way back to ignorance and the formative forces; by this very designation, it is shown that from a condition devoid of agency, there is the arising of something else.
For what reason is it said that when birth exists, there is aging and death, and that aging and death do not occur elsewhere [than in that context], but rather have birth as their condition?
This applies likewise up to ignorance and the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
By this very designation, it is shown that from a condition belonging to one's own continuum, there is the arising of something else within that very same continuum.
Those phenomena which are conditioned by ignorance are also formations;
or rather, those which are formations conditioned by ignorance may also be so.

However, there may be formations that are not conditioned by ignorance—namely, the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the unobstructed-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) formations of body, speech, and mind—which are conditioned by ignorance but are not themselves formations.
Excluding the limb of existence comprised within formative forces (*saṃskāra*),

those other limbs of existence which have ignorance as their condition— namely, meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formative forces of body, speech, and mind— and excluding these modes, constitute the fourth alternative.
Thus, this is a fourfold alternative:

that which is consciousness conditioned by formative forces may also be such that formative forces are conditioned by it; or, that which is consciousness may also be such that it is conditioned by formative forces.
Consciousness does not have formations as its condition;
rather, with the exception of consciousness itself, it refers to the other members of existence.
Furthermore, that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) and non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) is not consciousness conditioned by formations.
Excluding that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
as well as consciousness conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra*)— whether it be the seed-nature or the fruit-nature that leads to renewed existence—
setting these modes aside constitutes the fourth alternative (*koṭi*).
Following this principle, one should apply it appropriately to the fourfold alternatives (catuṣkoṭika) up to the feeling conditioned by contact.
Whatever feeling is conditioned by feeling, all that is craving;
whatever is craving, all that is conditioned by feeling.
In this case as well, there would be a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
Craving is not conditioned by feeling;
rather, it is that aspiration for higher liberation and that craving which, relying upon the wholesome, abandons craving.
[In this context,] "conditioned by feeling" refers to [the process where] feeling is the condition, and not [all] craving [arising from] feeling is [necessarily] conditioned by feeling.
Dependent upon the feeling born from contact with ignorance, those other factors that arise,
as well as the other members of existence (bhavāṅga),
and craving conditioned by feeling— this defiled craving has as its condition the feeling born from contact with ignorance.
Excluding these modes, there is the fourth alternative.
Whatever has craving as its condition is all grasping; or rather, whatever is grasping has craving as its condition.
In this regard, the latter term should be understood first: while whatever is grasping is necessarily conditioned by craving, there may be that which is conditioned by craving but is not grasping.
Excluding clinging (*upādāna*), it consists of the other factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*),
as well as those wholesome phenomena such as the arousal of vigor that arise in dependence upon wholesome craving.
Whatever has appropriation as its condition is all existence;
or whatever is existence is all that has appropriation as its condition. Indeed, whatever is existence is entirely conditioned by appropriation.
However, there may be that which has appropriation as its condition but is not existence;
namely, the other members of existence (bhavāṅga) excluding existence itself.
Whatever is conditioned by existence (*bhava*) is all birth (*jāti*);
or whatever is birth is all conditioned by existence. Indeed, whatever is birth is entirely conditioned by existence.
But it may be that birth does not have existence as its condition:
namely, that which is the final limb of existence, old age and death, setting aside birth itself;
all that is old age and death has birth as its condition.
Alternatively, all that constitutes aging and death has birth as its condition;
furthermore, all that constitutes birth and death has aging as its condition.
However, there may be something conditioned by birth that is not aging and death.
Sickness, union with the unpleasant, separation from the pleasant, the frustration of one's desires, and the sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair arising therefrom.
Among these factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*), how many are primarily obstacles to the path comprised of right view?
Ignorance (*avidyā*), the mental formations (*manaḥ-saṃskāra*) arising from it, and a portion of existence (*bhava*) are the obstacles.

Just as it is for right view, so it is for right intention, right effort, and for right speech, action, and livelihood—the formative factors of body and speech, as well as a portion of existence, constitute an obstruction.
For right mindfulness and right concentration, the remaining factors should be understood as constituting obstructions.
Among these members of existence (*bhavāṅga*), how many belong exclusively to the side of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and how many belong to both the sides of affliction and purification (*vyavadāna*)?
Four belong exclusively to the side of affliction;
the others belong to both the sides of affliction and purification.
Birth in the miserable states or in the inopportune moments (*akṣaṇa*), or in other such conditions, belongs to the side of affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣya*).
Furthermore, birth among gods and humans that is free from the inopportune moments should be seen as belonging to the side of both affliction and purification (*vyavadānapakṣya*).
As for the remaining members [of dependent origination], they should be seen as belonging to either of those two sides according to their respective application.
In the absence of which ignorance do the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) not come to be? Through the cessation of which ignorance does the cessation of the formative forces occur?
It is through the cessation of that ignorance which persists as the latent tendency (*anuśaya*), the manifestation (*paryavasthāna*), and the origination (*samutthāna*) of the three types.
From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of ignorance; and when that has ceased, from its cessation follows the cessation of volitional formations.
In the absence of which formations does consciousness not arise?
Through the cessation of which formations is there the cessation of consciousness?
Those formations that have been ceased within one's own continuum and for which no antidote has yet been produced.
Furthermore, when there are mental formations, there are bodily and vocal formations;
therefore, when that [mental formation] exists, consciousness has it as its condition.
When that is absent, because of the absence of that, and due to the cessation of its totality, the cessation of consciousness should be understood.
In the absence of which consciousness does name-and-form not come to be?
And through the cessation of which consciousness, moreover, does the cessation of name-and-form occur?
When consciousness, which has become the seed, does not exist, consciousness, which has become the fruit, does not arise.
From the cessation of both of these, there is further the cessation of both name-and-form.
Just as the principle for consciousness and name-and-form is stated, so should it be understood for the remaining members of the chain, down to sensation, according to their respective applications.
Just as it is with the formative forces conditioned by ignorance, so should it be understood for grasping conditioned by craving, and for existence conditioned by grasping.
Just as it is with consciousness conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra*), so should it be viewed for birth conditioned by becoming (*bhava*).
Just as it is with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the others conditioned by consciousness, so it is with aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) conditioned by birth.
In the absence of which feeling does craving not arise?
And from the cessation of which feeling, moreover, does the cessation of craving follow?
This principle should be understood in the same way as that which was stated regarding consciousness conditioned by formations.
Regarding that eightfold dependent origination which was taught, how many of its aspects are manifested by the twelve-linked dependent origination,
and how many are not?
Three aspects are manifested by it.
Two are manifested by a single part; one is manifested by all its members;
the remaining ones are not so manifested.

The gateway of the arising of consciousness and the gateway of the ownership of one's own karma are manifested by a single part; furthermore, the gateway of the evolution of the world of sentient beings is manifested by all its parts.
How many disadvantages are to be seen for one who does not understand dependent origination?
Five: there arises the view of a self.

One gives rise to views associated with the past limit (*pūrvānta*). Just as with those associated with the past limit, so too with those associated with the future limit (*aparānta*), and those associated with both the past and future limits. Firmly adhering to these, possessing grasping (*sopādāna*) and accompanied by torment (*saparitāpana*), one does not attain final nirvana in this very life; this is the fifth disadvantage.
How many benefits are to be seen for one who knows?
By the reverse of this, exactly five benefits are to be seen.
Among these twelve factors, how many factors are substantial entities (*dravya*)?
He said: Nine.
How many do not exist as substantial entities?
Those which remain.
How many have the nature of a single substance? Five. How many have the nature of multiple substances?
As for the remaining [categories]:
how many are obstructions to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)? One.
How many bring about suffering? Five.
How many contain suffering within them?
Five are exclusively [neutral];
how many are exclusively suffering? Two.
How many are to be explained by way of the nature of cause? How many are to be explained by way of the nature of fruit?
How many are to be explained by way of the nature of a mixture of cause and fruit?
The first six links, from ignorance up to contact, are based upon ignorance.
Craving, grasping, and becoming are to be explained as the causal state;
the final two are to be explained as the resultant state.
That which belongs to the future life is to be described as mixed with feeling and has contact as its condition; it is the cause.
That which belongs to the present life has craving as its condition and is the result.
Having made contact the condition for both of these, they are described as being mixed.
How many members bring about desirable and undesirable fruits? How many members bring about the fruit of personal existence?
The first six bring about the former fruit.
The last three produce the latter fruit; one produces both fruits.
How many are accompanied by pleasant feeling?
All except for two members.
How many are accompanied by painful feeling?
Those very same [factors],
with one member set aside;
how many are accompanied by neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
The same principle should be understood here as well, just as it was in the case of pleasure.
How many are not accompanied by feeling?
One member, which is set aside.
How many factors are comprised within the suffering of change?
Those factors accompanied by pleasant feeling, as well as a portion of those factors not accompanied by feeling.
How many are comprised within the suffering of suffering?
Those which are accompanied by suffering, as well as that factor which is not accompanied by feeling, and a portion of that [factor].
How many are comprised by the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)?

Those which are comprised by the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) are necessarily also comprised by the suffering of conditioned formations.
However, there may be things comprised by the suffering of conditioned formations that are not comprised by the other two types of suffering.
Those factors associated with neither-pain-nor-pleasure, as well as that part of the factor which is not associated with feeling.
Are all the factors found in their active manifestation in all births and meditative attainments?
He replied: They are not found.

In the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and in the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the material factors are found, but not the immaterial ones. Furthermore, for one born in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), the immaterial factors are found, but not the material ones.
Could it be that, by relying on the limbs [of yoga], one might attain seclusion from the limbs?
He replied:
It could be that there is seclusion from a portion of them at that time, but not seclusion from all the primary and secondary limbs.
By relying on the factors belonging to the higher stages, [one attains] those belonging to the lower stages.
How many factors are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and how many are non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*)? Three are afflicted; the remaining are of two kinds.
Furthermore, among those that are non-afflicted, a twofold division should be understood based on the distinction between the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
How many are associated with the desire realm?
All of them, taken together and collectively.
How many are associated with the form realm?
It is a portion of all [conditioned phenomena].
How is aging to be seen therein?
It is that which pertains to conditioned phenomena, whether they be those of one in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
They become worn out; their state is one of antiquity and decrepitude.
Just as it is with those associated with the form realm, so it is with those associated with the formless realm.
How many are those belonging to the stage of training (śaikṣa)? None at all.
How many are beyond training?
