None at all.
How many are neither of those in training nor beyond training? All of them.
As for those factors that are wholesome yet contaminated (*sāsrava*), why are they not considered "of one in training" (*śaikṣa*)?
It is not tenable [to call them so] because they have fallen under the sway of active existence (*pravṛtti*).
However, for one in training, wholesome contaminated phenomena are contrary to active existence and are conditioned by clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
How many [defilements] of a stream-enterer are to be said to be abandoned?
A portion of all of them, but not any of them in its entirety.
As it is for the stream-enterer, so it is for the once-returner.
How many factors of the non-returner (anāgāmin) are to be stated as abandoned?
All those belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara);
however, there is no fixed rule regarding those belonging to the form and formless realms (rūpārūpyāvacara).
How many factors are to be said to have been abandoned by an Arhat?
All those belonging to the three realms.
[The Compendium of Sūtras:
By how many explanations is dependent origination taught in those various sūtras?
In brief, by six.

By way of exposition in direct order, by way of exposition in reverse order, by way of exposition of a single part of the factors, by way of exposition of all the factors, by way of exposition of the dark side, and by way of exposition of the bright side.
Dependent origination has been described by the Blessed One as profound.
How is it to be understood as profound?
The profound meaning of dependent origination is to be seen through ten aspects.
Namely, with reference to the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of suffering, the meaning of emptiness, and the meaning of selflessness:
therein, with reference to the meaning of impermanence, they arise from their own seeds;
and depending upon external conditions, they arise from those external conditions.
They arise depending upon their own seeds and from other conditions due to those seeds;
yet, in the production of that [result], there is no striving, no effort, nor any activity whatsoever on the part of either the seed or the condition.
Indeed, neither the seed nor the condition possesses any striving, effort, or activity.
Furthermore, it is not that those two lack the capacity to function as causes;
rather, the factors (aṅga) possess characteristics that are negated from the beginningless past, yet new characteristics arise at every moment.
Moreover, dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is characterized by momentary disintegration.
And they appear as having fixed modes of existence.
In that regard, starting from the meaning of suffering, the members [of dependent origination]—which have the characteristic of being of a single flavor of suffering—appear in three ways.
In that regard, starting from the meaning of emptiness, the members—which are devoid of a sentient being, an agent, and suffering—appear and are taught as if they were not devoid of them.

In that regard, concerning selflessness: the members [of dependent origination] have the characteristic of selflessness in their lack of independence, yet they appear as having the characteristic of a self;
and while in the ultimate sense they have an ineffable intrinsic nature, they possess an intrinsic nature through verbal expression.
It is explained.
By how many knowledges (*jñāna*) is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to be understood?
By two: by the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*) and by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
How [is it understood] by the knowledge of the stability of phenomena?
It should be understood exactly as it was prescribed and revealed by the Blessed One.
How so? Through the knowledge of reality, just as those in training who have seen the path perceive it in its profound meaning.
As it has been said:

"Indeed, dependent origination was not created by me, nor by others; rather, whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of phenomena remains constant—this is the stability of phenomena (dharmasthiti), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
What is this nature of phenomena? What is the stability of phenomena? What is the realm of phenomena?
The fact that it has been established since beginningless time is *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).
The formal establishment of that which is thus established through reasoning by means of words and syllables is *dharma-sthiti* (the stability of phenomena).
*Dharmatā* is the cause for that stability.
Therefore, it is called the cause.
As it was said: "If birth did not exist, would birth occur for anyone at all?
Or, if birth were entirely non-existent, would aging and death, which have birth as their condition, be discerned?
For what reason, then, is intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) here described as having intrinsic nature as its condition?
Because the category of the fruit of one's own seeds is under discussion, the twelve factors beginning with consciousness are [included]; that too is "birth" in terms of its meaning.
And when that exists, those very same factors which have become the fruit are called "birth conditioned by becoming."
In this manner, the remaining factors should be understood according to their respective designations and as they appropriately apply.

Just as it has been stated that all the [other] members [of dependent origination] do not stand in a relationship of mutual conditionality, for what reason is the mutual conditionality of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) established?
Because in the present life (*dṛṣṭe dharme*), consciousness has name-and-form as its condition;
and because in the future life (*samparāye*), name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.

For instance, at the time of conception in the mother’s womb, because they act as mutual conditions, the semen and blood— the physical form— of the mother’s womb, conditioned by consciousness, are grasped as "name" and coagulate into the state of the *kalala*.
Furthermore, that consciousness, conditioned by that name-and-form, obtains its foundation therein.
For what reason does the mind of a bodhisattva, while examining the dark side [of dependent origination], turn back from consciousness and not from the other members?
Because these two are mutually conditioned:
just as name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness, so too consciousness is conditioned by name-and-form; thus, for one who examines it in this way, the mind turns back from consciousness.
However, it did not turn back in the same way regarding the other members [of dependent origination].
In that one case, it is said to have turned back because of the demonstration of their mutual conditionality (*anyonya-pratyayatva*).
But in the context of cessation, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is not the cause for the cessation of the consciousness that leads to rebirth, which is what he subsequently reflected upon.
For what reason are these factors said to be self-made, not made by another, not made by both, nor arisen without a cause?
Because they exist subsequent to their arising,
and because a condition is devoid of agency.
And because of the existence of the efficacy of conditions.
In dependent origination, what corresponds to the sprout of suffering? What corresponds to the nurturing of the sprout of suffering? What corresponds to the tree of suffering?
Consciousness and the subsequent factors, conditioned by ignorance and volitional formations, up to and including sensation, correspond to the sprout.
Craving and the factors beginning with it, ending with existence (*bhava*), which have feeling as their condition, should be regarded as corresponding to the act of maintaining [the flame].
Birth and old age and death should be regarded as corresponding to the tree of suffering. How many members (*aṅga*) should be regarded as corresponding to the wick?
From consciousness up to feeling:
how many members are of the nature of moisture?
Ignorance, formations, craving, clinging, and becoming.
How many members are to be regarded as being like flames?
Birth, old age, and death.
For what reason is dependent origination called "accumulation" from the perspective of the exposition of the dark side?
It is solely because it is the final fruit of the mass of suffering;
and it is the condition for all the [other] members, because it follows upon those other members.
For what reason is dependent origination called "diminution" by way of the teaching on the white side?
Because they involve the progressive abandonment [of defilements] and the prevention of further decline,
and because they serve as the cause for the diminution of the entire mass of suffering.
How many members are called "dharmas with cause"?
The first seven. How many members are called "suffering with cause"?
The remaining five.
Through the cessation of how many factors is the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya) manifested?
Through three.
Through the cessation of how many factors is the cessation of conditions (pratyayakṣaya) manifested?
Because these same three [factors] serve as the conditions for the other members;

how many members are characterized by the exhaustion of sensation? [The answer is] one, because when the afflictions have been abandoned, at the time of the cessation of the aggregates, all sensation ceases right here.
For what reason are seventy-seven consciousnesses established based upon dependent origination?

It is for the purpose of demonstrating the knowledge of affliction together with its causes; for the purpose of demonstrating the afflictions produced by oneself within one's own continuum; for the purpose of demonstrating that the members [of the sequence] from the prior limit are beginningless; and for the purpose of demonstrating the opportunity for the cessation of affliction regarding the members from the subsequent limit.
And for the purpose of elucidating the full comprehension of the contaminated wisdom not included within the [noble] factors:
with respect to these seven causes in each individual factor, seventy-seven consciousnesses are to be understood.
For what reason are forty-four knowledges established?
With respect to the examination of the four noble truths within each individual factor, there are forty-four.
Therein, one born and existing in the desire realm produces, by means of a basis belonging to the desire realm, the eye and ear belonging to a higher stage;
and by means of those, one sees forms and hears sounds belonging to lower stages.

Furthermore, one brings the mind belonging to the three realms into manifestation by means of that very same basis; and when born in the form or formless realms, one brings into manifestation everything except that which belongs to lower levels, just as in the desire realm.

Indeed, for the abandonment of these three kinds of affliction— namely, the affliction of defilements, the affliction of karma, and the affliction of birth— one should understand that there is a sixfold clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
They are as follows:

The realization through reflection, the realization through faith, the realization through ethical discipline, the realization of the truths through the knowledge of realization, the realization of the truths through the knowledge proximate to realization, and the ultimate realization.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the stage with vitarka and vicāra, the stage without vitarka and with vicāra only, and the stage without vitarka and without vicāra are completed.
